title: Vibe-Coded Apps Are a Security Nightmare, but They Don't Have to Be
description: Companies like Softr say they offer vibe coding solutions while mitigating security risks.
fullText:
Vibe coding might be extremely popular, but it comes with some serious security concerns, including exposed databases, leaked APIs, remotely orchestrated prompt injection attacks, and AI scraping. It's enough to raise the question: Is there a version of vibe coding that could actually hold up in a live environment? I spoke with Shiran Brodie, Head of Growth at Softr, for a face-to-face discussion on the challenges and solutions to vibe coding security hassles.

Softr began as a no-code app builder designed specifically for professionals, small businesses, and enterprises to build apps or portals to support their internal workflows. That means handling a ton of proprietary data, where security is always a big concern. The original version has gone through several updates since launch, with vibe coding now one of the platform's core features.

Brodie spoke about the challenges that the company faced expanding into this new space and the solutions that helped get through them. We also talked about how app development platforms like Softr now suggest a hybrid approach that layers vibe coding features on top of pre-built security infrastructure like built-in database management, access control, and developer visibility. But how does this hybrid security system work on a technical level? And more importantly, does it actually hold up in practice?

In 2025, a security firm called Escape DAST analyzed 5,600 vibe-coded apps built using platforms like Loveable, Replit, Base44, and Bolt. More than 2,000 of these apps had security issues, totaling 2,038 critical vulnerabilities and over 400 exposed credentials.

“The problem ultimately is that these platforms are generating raw code from scratch,” explained Brodie. Simplicity is a big part of the appeal with vibe coding, but also the thing that can create security issues down the line. “It can abstract a lot of the complexity that comes with building, but non-technical people don't know what they don't know.”

Also in 2025, Georgia Tech researchers launched the Vibe Security Radar, a platform that pulls information directly from publicly accessible security advisories and traces them back to AI-generated coding platforms and LLMs. Researchers scanned more than 40,000 security advisories, and uncovered 43 critical vulnerabilities across eight vibe coding platforms that led to command injections, server-side request forgery, and authentication bypass. Even in the last few months of 2026, security analysts have discovered massive API leaks from Meta-owned Moltbook and the Hugging Face community. Most of these incidents stem from poorly generated code that didn’t take enough steps to secure private API keys from the open web.

Brodie believes that the problem with vibe coding is that it leaves too much of the core infrastructure up to AI generation, even the mission-critical parts like third-party integrations and permission management systems—which is where most of these vulnerabilities originate.

Instead of letting AI models generate every new app from scratch, Softr retains the same pre-coded backend infrastructure, hosting, integrations, and permission management. Vibe coding features add more design flexibility and smarter workflow automation, but the core systems remain the same.

For example, if you wanted to build an online portal that pulls certain information from your internal company database using an API, Claude Code or Loveable would accomplish this by asking their AI models to write an integration using custom logic, webhooks, and UI wiring. With a platform like Softr, these integrations are available as ready-made components with security best practices already built into them. You can still use vibe coding options to customize their look and functionality, but the core systems and security protocols remain intact.

In development terms, this is called visual scaffolding. Apart from Softr, several other no-code platforms have carried forward this same model, with varying levels of success. Framer, for instance, offers an AI-enabled Workshop extension in its app marketplace. The feature has expanded into Framer’s built-in prompt-based development tool and AI agents that can handle ongoing maintenance tasks. FlutterFlow, a no-code tool designed specifically for building smartphone apps for iOS and Android, also lets you generate pages and components with established security guardrails using AI.

“It's not an iframe,” Brodie clarified, when describing how vibe-coded elements are isolated from the security layer within Softr. Instead, AI-generated code is confined to specific component blocks that allow custom code to exist with restrictions. “These blocks are built to exist within our infrastructure,” she added.

Shadow AI is the AI-era version of a long-standing problem called "shadow IT." When employees put company data in a software platform without IT approval, it opens businesses to data governance and cybersecurity risks. The same goes for AI, except now, it’s no longer limited to a rogue Trello board, but an employee’s personal account running Claude Code or Gemini with full access to proprietary company databases. AI coding platforms offer generous limits even on personal accounts, making it convenient for employees to go off on their own and start building apps on company data without a centralized approval system.

“There's no incentive to exist within company guardrails,” Brodie said. Even when employees disclose their vibe-coded apps, IT leaders are expected to maintain and troubleshoot that poorly generated code even though they’d never pass a regular security audit.

Earlier this year, RedAccess scanned more than 380,000 vibe-coded applications built using platforms like Lovable, Replit, or Base44. They found over 5,000 of these apps publicly accessible on the open web and 2,000 of them actively leaking company data, including customers’ sensitive financial and medical information.

It isn’t enough to fix bad coding practices in large language models or vibe coding tools; instead, companies must implement better access controls and improve visibility for system administrators. If your IT team has a bird’s-eye view of who has access to what and the power to control that access, a scenario where rogue apps and portals leak company data becomes a lot less likely.

Model Context Protocol—or MCP for short—is Anthropic’s open-source standard for securely connecting AI models to external applications and data sources. It’s quickly become an industry staple, more so because of convenience and the fact that it’s free to use. But the problem with MCP connectors is that they inherit the same permission structure as the database or application it’s connected to.

Softr has its own database management system that lets you control what MCPs can see. For example, Brodie uses Claude's MCP connector to read and write directly into Softr Databases, but that only stays safe because her databases are governed by the permissions and rules implemented in Softr. Most vibe coding platforms don’t benefit from the same level of access control.

Vibe coding tools often get blanket access to your raw databases without a permission layer in between, making breaches more likely when attackers use prompt injection attacks. Data is further exposed for companies that need to give third-party vendors and clients access to their vibe-coded applications, where controlling access to company data is a minimum security requirement.

Beyond Softr Databases, the platform offers access to more than 60 pre-coded integrations to platforms like HubSpot, Stripe, and ClickUp. These integrations are already built with security standards in mind, making data leaks less likely. You can also connect Softr to Zapier or Make to benefit from a larger selection of pre-built automations, all of which are more secure than your standard vibe-coded MCP.

There’s a marked difference in the security requirements of a small business or early-stage startup versus a large-scale enterprise operation spanning multiple locations. Small business startups are usually content with basic permission management and data encryption standards, whereas enterprise organizations need GDPR and SOC II compliance, control over data center locations, and stronger access control with multi-factor authentication and single sign-on facilities.

Like Softr, more startups are noticing the enterprise security gap posed by vibe coding and trying to build solutions that offer better visibility and governance options. Retool, a low-code app builder, has obtained SOC II Type 1 certification with its strict role-based access control for AI features and limitations to keep LLMs from touching important databases or infrastructure. WaveMaker promises similar security controls, with LDAP-based authentication, centralized permission management, cross-site scripting prevention, and SSO integration through platforms like Okta to woo enterprise clients.

"No organization wants to hire or train more developers just to keep one internal tool secure," Brodie said. Larger companies expect these things to be handled by an AI coding platform’s native security systems. With multiple major public security incidents rattling the AI coding space, no-code platforms are looking for options to offer users more flexibility, without being plagued by the complexity that made them turn to vibe coding in the first place.

title: 10 Hacks Every In-Flight Wifi User Should Know
description: Connecting to the internet while in the air can be a hassle, but there's a lot you can do to make it easier.
fullText:
Getting (and staying) online while flying has gotten way better over the years, but at the end of the day, you’re still trying to connect to the planet while you're 30,000 feet above it. In other words, it's still going to be a bit of a hassle—but there are things you can do to make it easier. With that in mind, here are some of the best in-flight wifi tricks and hacks.

Even if you get in-flight wifi, it’s going to be slower than what you would have at home or at the airport. You’re not going to be able to stream 4K, high bit-rate video from Netflix—and even if you managed it, you’d probably end up ruining the connection for everyone else.

For movies, shows, or playlists you know you’ll want to have access to on your flight, it’s best to download them ahead of time. Most streaming services have a method to download episodes of shows for local viewing while you’re offline. You can also load video or music files on your phone directly, if you have local copies on your computer or other device.

Many applications will work while offline or with limited internet access, even if they’re normally online web apps. For example, Google Docs can work offline if you head to Google Drive and go to Settings > General > Offline and enable the checkbox to work offline. From there, make sure the specific documents you want to edit are downloaded locally.

This process will be different for other applications, so check the specifics of the apps you use on a regular basis. Many productivity tools have some version of airplane mode access, so even if you lose connection to the internet, you can still keep working.

For some jobs, you need to constantly stay online—or at least seem that way. While your mileage will vary depending on your industry, you can fudge it a bit by scheduling your emails or social media posts to go up while you’re in the air. After all, waiting an hour to respond to an email from your boss can be more acceptable than waiting four.

Most email apps have a tool to schedule your replies, but so do communication apps like Slack. If you spend a lot of time posting to social media, tools like Buffer can help you space out your posts so you don’t end up leaving gaps.

Airlines might be pinching every penny to get by, but on some airlines, you can still get free wifi—as long as you Airlines like Delta and JetBlue offer free in-flight wifi on a number of flights if you log in with your SkyMiles or TrueBlue accounts.

Other airlines like Southwest offer complimentary wifi due to sponsorships from cell carriers like T-Mobile (even if you don’t use T-Mobile for your phone service). Once again, though, you’ll likely need to sign in with your airline rewards account to make use of the perk.

Even if an airline doesn’t offer complimentary wifi, you can sometimes still get it for free through your credit card company. Many credit card providers will either offer discounts on certain airlines’ internet access, or reimbursements after the fact.

You’ll typically see these listed as travel credits or “airline incidentals” credits, but some credit cards offer an annual allotment of fees you can get reimbursed for. In some cases, credit card companies will only reimburse you for fees from certain airlines, but in others it will apply to general travel fees. It’s worth checking your credit card’s perks before booking your travel to see which airlines you might get credit for.

Some airlines will offer free internet access, but only for messaging or other extremely limited services. That might be sufficient for your needs, but occasionally you can also leverage that for broader access than the airline intended.

For example, some users have reported that you can access the Gemini service via the Messages app on Android to do broad searches that all get funneled through a single chat interface, without paying an extra fee. Others have claimed you can use a VPN while connected to a messaging-only network connection to open up full internet access. This will vary based on airline and the types of connections they offer, but it’s worth giving it a shot if you don’t want to shell out for full internet access.

If you do get in-flight access to wifi, it’s still probably going to be pretty speed-limited. You can make watching things easier on yourself by manually dropping your streaming speed where you can.

Sites like YouTube offer tools to limit how much bandwidth you use. On any given YouTube video, click the gear icon and choose Quality to select a lower resolution. Depending on the quality, you might not even notice that much of a hit, but still get better playback and, most importantly, fewer interruptions on other browsing while you do it. Check the other sites you use for similar features.

If you’re struggling to get solid performance with the site-specific tools, you can use speed throttling at the browser level to moderate your bandwidth and make things smoother for everything else.

For example, in Chrome, you can open up dev tools (F12 on Windows, Option+Cmd+I on Mac), then select Network. On this tab, you can click “No throttling” and instead choose a more limited option. This is usually designed to mimic slower internet connections for dev purposes, but throttling your own connection here can force more bandwidth-hungry services like Netflix to chill out, freeing up the plane’s limited bandwidth for everything else you’re doing.

You can also save some bandwidth by utilizing lower-lift modes like Reading mode to just pull the parts of the article you actually need. In Chrome, you can enable this quickly by pressing Alt+Shift+R.

Additionally, you can use ad blocker extensions to cut down on loading unnecessary data. This does mean that, if you use Chrome, it might be a bit of a headache. Whether you choose to use a different browser or live with the versions of ad blocking extensions that work today is up to you.

In-flight wifi is still public wifi, so you should treat it like you’re connecting to any given Starbucks network. At this point, any website that isn’t already using HTTPS should be a little suspect, but even then, that’s not necessarily enough. For any work that’s particularly sensitive, you should enable a VPN to protect your data.

Beyond that, it’s a good idea to make sure you have updated antivirus software running, and use tools like UBlock Origin to block any data tracking. There isn’t much about connecting to in-flight wifi that’s different from any other public network, from a security perspective, but you should still take care to protect your data on any public network to begin with.

title: Seven Surprisingly Useful Mac Apps You've Never Heard Of
description: These lesser-known apps can vastly improve your macOS experience.
fullText:
If your time on macOS is solely spent switching between the well-known apps that everyone uses—your web browser, Notes, Apple Music—then you're missing out. There are a host of more unusual and idiosyncratic apps for Apple's desktop operating system that are well worth digging into.

The apps collected in the list below fall under that description, and while they might not have been installed on millions of Macs or be particularly complex in what they offer, they're all quite useful. Give them a try and see how they can upgrade your macOS experience.

Scrolling isn't particularly hard on macOS, but what if it were even easier? ScrollPods teams up with a connected pair of AirPods to let you scroll up and down webpages, documents, and more with a tilt of the head. It works with anything on screen that can be scrolled.

The utility is simple to set up, and based on my testing, it works quite well. The default sensitivity is just right, with slight head tilts enough to nudge a page up or down, but you can adjust the sensitivity and set up custom gestures for the app through its settings.

You can add some extra functionality to your MacBook trackpad with Slidr: It turns the left side of your trackpad into a brightness slider, and the right side into a volume slider, so you can quickly adjust these key settings without interrupting your typing and scrolling flow.

You're able to take advantage of a free trial before committing to the purchase, so you can see if it works for you. It couldn't be any more straightforward to use: The app runs from the menu bar, and there are options for adjusting the sensitivity and position of the slide gestures, and swapping over the brightness and volume sliders if you prefer.

A picture-in-picture mode can be very useful when multi-tasking, but it's not supported in every app—something Pipiri fixes. Once you've got Pipiri installed, any window on the macOS desktop can be put into a picture-in-picture mode, running on top of your other apps.

So, for example, you can keep an AI agent window or a social media feed visible on screen while you get on with something else. There are lots of options to play around with, too, including the refresh rate of the overlaid window, app hotkeys, and adaptive resizing.

Pipiri (free trial, then $9.70)

Haptyk takes advantage of the hidden accelerometer that's built into every Apple Silicon MacBook keyboard, figuring out how hard you're striking each key and adding appropriate audio. You get mechanical keyboard sound effects, with your existing MacBook keyboard.

I gave the app a go and it works really well: There's zero lag on the sound effects, and you get the same experience across every app. You've got 16 different keyboard sound packs to choose from, plus lots of configuration options (including volume, pitch, and gain).

If you're a regular video caller, then you'll know that subtle feeling of dread that rises up whenever you're called upon to share your screen or to record something you're doing. What browser tabs do you have open? Is an embarrassing notification going to pop up?

Stealthy deals with this with the minimum of fuss, hiding your desktop icons, the desktop wallpaper, and the dock. silencing notifications, and clearing away open app windows you don't want visible on screen. It can also launch automatically when video calls start.

Stealthy (free trial, then $12.99)

There's nothing too revolutionary about Gestimer, but it does a simple job in an intuitive way, and is likely to come in handy more often than you might think. It lets you set timers and reminders by just dragging down the app icon from the macOS menu bar.

There's no messing around with opening up other apps or digging through calendars—it's just click and drag, with the length of the drag controlling the time that's set. There's a persistent countdown in the menu bar, and you get a notification at the appropriate time.

Gestimer (free trial, then $6.99)

Unclack is both simple and useful: It mutes your microphone when you're typing (even more helpful if you've installed Haptyk, above). That means you no longer need to worry about your aggressive typing style distracting other people during video meetings.

It runs quietly from the menu bar and you don't need to do anything to enable or disable it—it just works, and you won't even know it's there. Should you need to talk and type at the same time, you can disable Unclack with a couple of clicks until you need it again.

title: U.S. Treasury is paying $3 billion a day in interest on national debt, says the CBO—having spent $10 billion to prop up the currency of its top lender
description: The CBO reported that net interest on public debt totaled $963 billion between October 2025 (when the fiscal year begins) and July 2026.
fullText:
The government's nearly $40 trillion national debt is now costing the Treasury more than $3 billion a day in service payments, according to a new report from the Congressional Budget Office (CBO). 

In its August budget update, the CBO reported that net interest on public debt totaled $963 billion between October 2025 (when the fiscal year begins) and July 2026. That equates to $96.3 billion a month, or approximately $3.18 billion a day over the 303 days in between.

Interest payments on the debt have grown by $117 billion—or 14%—compared to the same period last year, the CBO added, on account of the debt being "larger than it was in the first 10 months of fiscal year 2025 and because of higher long-term interest rates." The CBO, led by director Phil Swagel, added, "Declines in short-term rates partially mitigated the overall rise in interest payments."

How much is the U.S. spending daily on debt?

What are economists' concerns about rising debt-to-GDP ratios?

Why did Treasury Secretary Bessent intervene in yen markets?

How does Japan's Treasury holdings impact U.S. bonds?

The latest budget update is further evidence for debt hawks who suggest policymakers are heading in the wrong direction when it comes to fiscal responsibility: Deficits totaled $1.8 trillion in the first 10 months of this fiscal year,  $169 billion more than the deficit recorded during the same period last fiscal year.

With that information in mind, the CBO updated its deficit projection for the total fiscal year to $2.1 trillion, $200 billion more than the deficit projected in February of this year.

The value of U.S. debt isn't necessarily a concern for economists—it does, after all, form the basis of the U.S. Treasury market, one of the safest asset classes on the planet. The concern for debt hawks is that the U.S. debt-to-GDP ratio is becoming unbalanced (currently at 122% per the St. Louis Fed), and lenders at some stage will attach a higher risk premium to lending, pushing up interest as a result.

While the bull case is that the U.S. can rebalance by boosting economic growth, bearish concerns range from inflation to the crowding out of public investment by interest payments. Bridgewater Associates founder Ray Dalio has warned as much, saying a "debt-induced heart attack" will be prompted by debt payments crowding out public spending.

The CBO report comes after the Treasury's move last week to backstop the Japanese yen. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent confirmed the move was to help stabilize currency in the region as a whole, telling CNBC, "A stable yen is not only important for the U.S., but very important for the entire region."

The Treasury secretary had been clear in his intention to support the currency: A photo of Bessent's to-do list from a cabinet meeting at the end of July featured a reminder to buy $5 billion to $10 billion worth of the currency.

title: Russian attacks kill 10 in Ukraine as Zelenskyy says Moscow is getting more North Korean missiles
description: Russia attacked Ukrainian cities with missiles, drones and glide bombs Tuesday, killing at least 10 civilians, officials said, as President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Moscow is getting new military help...
fullText:
KYIV, Ukraine (AP) — Russia attacked Ukrainian cities with missiles, drones and glide bombs Tuesday, killing at least 10 civilians, officials said, as President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Moscow is getting new military help from North Korea for its more than 4-year-old invasion.

Zelenskyy said Russian forces used ballistic missiles supplied by North Korea in an overnight attack on the southeastern city of Zaporizhzhia, where a company said seven workers at its steel plant were killed and 21 injured.

Three more people, including a 15-year-old boy, were killed by Russian drones and artillery in the central Dnipropetrovsk region, authorities said.

In addition to the ballistic missiles, North Korea is preparing to deploy more of its troops to Russia, Zelenskyy said late Monday.

Russian President Vladimir Putin and North Korean leader Kim Jong Un signed a strategic partnership agreement in 2024, pledging mutual aid if either country faces aggression.

Kim has sent thousands of troops and huge supplies of weapons to support Putin's full-scale invasion of Ukraine. Some experts say the engagement with Moscow is helping improve North Korea's military capabilities, and Zelenskyy said the battlefield experience would help Pyongyang menace other countries in its region.

Ukraine says Russia is scaling up its production of ballistic missiles, aiming to exploit Kyiv's critical shortage of Patriot air defense interceptors that can stop them, and claims Moscow is preparing to recruit more troops for a new push on the front line that stretches 1,250 kilometers (775 miles) along eastern and southern Ukraine.

"Every step Russia takes — increasing ballistic missile production, bringing in North Korean equipment, preparing for mobilization — all of this shows that Moscow is preparing not for peace, but for escalation," Zelenskyy said on social media.

In an unusual step, Ukraine's air force didn't say in its daily report how many missiles Russia launched overnight. It was not clear whether the omission was deliberate, and Kyiv officials made no immediate comment.

U.S.-led diplomatic efforts to stop the war have fizzled as Washington grew frustrated with the lack of progress and its attention turned to the Iran war.

In an indication that Putin is determined to press on with the invasion, Russia's highest court on Monday ordered that Yabloko, the only political party opposing the war, to be excluded from the ballot in the Sept. 18-20 parliamentary election.

"The Kremlin will not enter serious negotiations or make meaningful compromises on its demands as long as Putin believes that he has a viable military path to achieving his full objectives," the Institute for the Study of War, a Washington-based think tank, said in an analysis Monday.

"Ukraine's Patriot shortages offer Russia an opportunity to cause very serious damage to Ukraine over the coming winter and will therefore contribute to delaying meaningful negotiations and protracting the war," it said.

Russian forces also struck parts of the Ukrainian capital, Kyiv, overnight, according to officials. One strike hit the grounds of a children's hospital, leaving two craters and shattering windows, the State Emergency Service said. Children and medical workers were in bomb shelters and nobody was hurt, it added.

At another location in Kyiv, a Russian strike started a fire in a warehouse that spread across about 1,200 square meters (nearly 13,000 square feet), according to emergency officials.

The Russian Defense Ministry said its forces overnight struck "military industrial facilities and transport and logistics centers" in Kyiv and Zaporizhzhia with "ground-based precision weapons."

It said in a statement that it hit civilian storage facilities housing drones in Kyiv and a metallurgical plant in Zaporizhzhia.

Metinvest, a major Ukrainian mining and metals company with operations in Zaporizhzhia, said seven of its steel plant employees died as staff tried to reach shelters after a warning of an incoming ballistic missile.

The company, which employs tens of thousands of people, said in a statement that the attack damaged its blast furnace and other equipment and forced the plant to shut down.

Russia targeted Kyiv and Zaporizhzhia with Zircon anti-ship missiles and Iskander ballistic missiles, while launching 120 long-range strike drones across the country, Ukraine's air force said.

Meanwhile, the Russian Defense Ministry said its air defenses overnight intercepted nearly 400 Ukrainian drones over 14 regions and Crimea, the peninsula that Moscow illegally annexed from Kyiv in 2014.

Russia's biggest online retailer, Wildberries, said its logistical facilities in the Voronezh region near the Ukrainian border came under attack and caught fire. It added that the fire was extinguished and goods stored there were "largely undamaged."

Ukraine has repeatedly struck Wildberries warehouses and Russian oil facilities in what it says is a strategy to compel Putin to negotiate an end to the invasion.

Ukraine's General Staff said its forces struck an oil refinery in the city of Orsk in Russia's Orenburg region near the border with Kazakhstan, about 1,500 kilometers (930 miles) from Ukraine, causing a fire.

The refinery, with an annual processing capacity of about 44 million barrels of crude oil, produces gasoline, diesel and aviation fuel, among other products. The extent of the damage was being assessed, the military said.

Meanwhile, Romania's Ministry of National Defense said its navy destroyed two drones drifting in the Black Sea about 90 nautical miles (166 kilometers) from the port of Constanta.

The Gerbera-type drones were neutralized by divers using controlled detonations, and some pieces were recovered, the ministry said, adding that Ukraine said the drones were not theirs.

The United Nations, meanwhile, estimates that more than 16,000 civilians detained by Russia during the war are still being "deprived of their liberty," with many held incommunicado and on grounds that don't comply with international law.

"Widespread and systematic torture and ill-treatment" of both Ukrainian civilian detainees and prisoners of war by Russia are continuing, including sexual violence, said Claudia Fuentes Julio, the U.N. assistant secretary-general for human rights.

She spoke at an informal meeting of the U.N. Security Council on Monday to spotlight the plight of civilians and soldiers taken following the Russia invasion.

Edith M. Lederer at the United Nations contributed.

Follow the AP's coverage of the war in Ukraine at https://apnews.com/hub/russia-ukraine

title: Opinion - The Blanche appointment is another Trump win that’s America’s loss
description: He will serve only Donald Trump, not our precious rule of law.
fullText:
Trump ballyhooed the appointment of Todd Blanche to become the nation's 88th attorney general with the exaggerated claim, "Todd Blanche is a STAR, and everyone knows it!"

It is to the shame of the U.S. Senate that Blanche is now confirmed. It is the worst appointment of the second Trump administration. Yes, you heard me — worse than Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy, Jr., Director of National Intelligence Tulsi Gabbard or Homeland Security Secretary Kristi Noem put together, because he will serve only President Trump, not our precious rule of law.

Sen. Bill Cassidy (R-La.), who cast the deciding vote, said in an absurd statement that Blanche "is not perfect … but the choice is not between perfection and Mr. Blanche," it is "between Mr. Blanche and another acting attorney general who … may not be as good as Mr. Blanche."

Blanche has proved himself a petty bureaucrat jumping at Trump's call; a lawyer of distinction he is not.

Ask the more than 1,200 of Blanche's Department of Justice colleagues who urged the Senate to reject his nomination. Ask the 35 former federal judges from across the country who have argued he committed a fraud on the court. Incumbent federal judges have said that the Justice Department under his aegis is no longer entitled to the presumption of regularity. He has lied to the courts once too often. In July, a judge forced Blanche's prosecutors to withdraw subpoenas served on New York Times reporters at their homes, finding serious irregularities.

Under Blanche, grand juries have refused to return indictments. The government reportedly could not persuade a single grand juror to sign off on proposed criminal charges against six Democratic lawmakers who released a video encouraging members of the military to refuse illegal orders. A grand jury refused to indict a man for assault who threw a sandwich at a federal agent.

It's not that he lost. It's about what kind of attorney general prosecutes cases like this. Where is the judgment?

Blanche tried to install Lindsey Halligan as the U.S. attorney in the Eastern District of Virginia to mount a vindictive case against Trump's enemy, former F.B.I. director James Comey. But judges, finding she had been improperly appointed, dismissed the case against Comey, as well as a separate one Halligan tried to bring against New York Attorney General Letitia James. Comey later moved to dismiss a ridiculous second indictment, in which he was charged with photographing an arrangement of seashells on a beach.

Before leaving the Justice Department, Halligan kept using the U.S. attorney title, despite the court's ruling. Blanche defended her actions in a response that displayed, as a presiding judge put it, "a level of vitriol more appropriate for a cable news talk show."

Under Blanche, the Justice Department has suffered a flight of career attorneys. Seasoned lawyers who worked on Trump prosecutions have been fired. Others have flocked for the exits, finding that politicized prosecutions are inconsistent with principled governmental service.

The 50 Senate Republican votes to confirm Blanche came after his appointment was nearly derailed when Sens. John Cornyn (R-Texas) and Thom Tillis (R-N.C.) threatened to vote against him over the deal he struck this spring to resolve Trump's questionable legal claims against the IRS.

They wanted written assurances that the Justice Department would not move forward with aspects of the settlement, including a proposed $1.8 billion slush fund for people like the Jan. 6 insurrectionists who claimed they were victims of "politicized" prosecutions under Obama and Biden. The slush fund was the kettle calling the pot black.

Both senators said that Blanche had allayed their concerns in statements issued last Sunday purporting to impose limits on the deal. The statements were worthless. As Tillis switched his vote in favor of Blanche, he seemed to acknowledge that they could be reversed by the president.

Several GOP lawmakers said they were somewhat reassured by the "concessions" Tillis and Cornyn had extracted from Blanche. Strange because even if the anti-weaponization fund isn't revived, Trump can still make payouts to allies through individual settlements. Blanche has also essentially left in place the deal that shields the president, his sons and their businesses from past tax claims. The release is said to be worth $600 million.

"There is enough weasel room in these documents to drive a truck through," said Sen. Sheldon Whitehouse (D-R.I.).

Then, there is the elephant in the room: the Epstein files, with the drip-feed, heavily redacted disclosure Blanche handled, not to mention his callous mistreatment of Epstein's victims. A New York Times report by Maggie Haberman and Jonathan Swan exposed that Blanche handled the Epstein case as a matter of politics, and key decisions were made by Blanche in collaboration with the White House.

In 1940, Attorney General Robert Jackson declared in the prosecutor's creed that, "the citizen's safety lies in the prosecutor who tempers zeal with human kindness, who seeks truth and not victims, who serves the law and not factional purposes, and who approaches his task with humility."

Blanche has been confirmed to serve "factional purposes." If he is not "perfect," he should not have been confirmed.

James D. Zirin is a former federal prosecutor in the Southern District of New York and a published legal analyst.

title: GOP senators rally behind Thune in response to Trump jabs at leader
description: Senate Republicans are rallying behind Senate Majority Leader John Thune (R-S.D.) after President Trump declined to support the GOP leader serving another term following the midterm election. Many Rep...
fullText:
Senate Republicans are rallying behind Senate Majority Leader John Thune (R-S.D.) after President Trump declined to support the GOP leader serving another term following the midterm election.

Many Republican senators say Thune will have their full support, even if Trump backs a challenger, because of the Senate leader's refusal to abolish the filibuster to advance Trump's top legislative priorities, such as the Safeguard American Voter Eligibility (SAVE America) Act.

"There's a lot of respect for John Thune. There's a lot of recognition of how he works and how difficult his job is and a belief that he's doing it really well under difficult circumstances," said Sen. Jerry Moran (R-Kan.).

Moran said Republican senators have been willing to yield to the president on a lot of issues but that they would draw a line against letting Trump push Thune out of his job or pick a replacement.

"I also think there are some things where the Senate seems willing to accede their privileges, but I think who our leader is, there's a real sense that that belongs to us," he said.

Even Senate conservatives who have ratcheted up pressure on Thune to keep the upper chamber in session during the August recess to debate the SAVE America Act acknowledge that Thune has had to navigate a political minefield as GOP leader.

"It's a hard job, it's really a hard job," said Sen. Rick Scott (R-Fla.), a leading proponent of the SAVE America Act.

Asked if he continues to have confidence in Thune despite the growing criticism from the White House, Scott noted that presidents often get frustrated with the Senate's 60-vote hurdle to passing their legislative priorities.

"I'm sure if I were president of the United States, I would be frustrated if everything I wanted didn't get done. So that's probably pretty common," the Florida senator said.

Sen. John Kennedy (R-La.) said he's doesn't "know of any movements to replace" Thune even though Trump has repeatedly expressed frustration over his agenda getting bogged down in the Senate.

"I think the president and John like each other. I think these are tough issues and they obviously disagree over things like the filibuster," Kennedy said.

Trump last week insisted in an interview with Punchbowl News that Republican voters are "not angry at me, but they are angry at Republicans" in Congress.

But even Trump's allies on Capitol Hill aren't buying that claim.

"I think Republicans are angry at all of us, I mean the voters. I think the voters are angry, period. And I think they're angry most about … cost of living, and I think that's what this election is going to be primarily about," Kennedy said.

"One of the reasons that the democratic socialists are winning elections is because they stand for something. Now what they stand for sucks, but a lot of their support is coming from young people who don't know history," the Louisiana senator continued.

GOP lawmakers think Trump has caused political headwinds for their party by not being more attuned to the affordability crisis, which Trump downplayed as a "hoax" issue driven by Democrats.

And while Trump has traveled around the country to talk about his economic accomplishments, he is prone to veering away from his script to hit on hot-button political issues, such as calls to pass the SAVE America Act to avert fraud in the upcoming election.

Thune has tried to shrug off Trump's criticisms in recent weeks, but they're becoming tougher to downplay as the president continues to suggest that the Senate GOP leader isn't getting his job done and that voters aren't happy with Republicans in Congress as a result.

Thune said he almost "expected" Trump to withhold his endorsement for him serving another term as Senate leader.

"That's probably to be expected," Thune said with a trace of resignation in his voice.

And Thune argued just as the Senate was leaving that his Republican colleagues have done a lot of heavy lifting to get the president's agenda passed, disputing Trump's accusations that they're not doing their jobs.

Thune said he and other Senate Republicans feel they are getting a lot done for Trump.

"I think we've had a really productive run. There are a couple things I said right from the very beginning are going to be difficult if not impossible — frankly more impossible — to do," he said of Trump's calls to pass the SAVE America Act and abolish the filibuster.

"That's the reality I have to deal with," Thune said of Democratic opposition to voting reforms and Republican opposition to lowering the threshold for passing legislation from 60 votes to a simple majority.

The GOP leader said the president is "entitled to his views," and Thune is "fine with that," but he argued getting Attorney General Todd Blanche confirmed despite strong reservations from a handful of GOP senators, coupled with the prolonged absence of Sen. Mitch McConnell (R-Ky.), was a "good, solid win for the team and obviously … not an easy one."

"We'll keep grinding away and let the chips fall where they may," Thune added.

One Thune ally said Trump's public criticism of the Senate leader is a tactic he is using to put "pressure" on Thune to pass as much of the president's agenda as possible and predicted it could "change" after the election.

Even so, Trump's refusal to say whether Thune is "still the man for the job" — coupled with White House press secretary Karoline Leavitt's statement that Trump's "patience is running out" with Thune's job performance — has fueled the appearance that their personal relationship is on shaky ground.

Thune has winced or hinted at his frustration at times when asked about the latest rumble of dissatisfaction from Trump but has mainly stayed focused on enacting as much of his agenda as possible before Democrats have a chance to win back control of one or both chambers of Congress.

Yet a growing number of Senate Republicans see Trump and his low approval ratings — especially on the economy — as a bigger political problem than strategic decisions made by Thune and his leadership team.

GOP lawmakers are seeking to distance themselves from Trump ahead of the November election as polls show independent voters moving away from the president and Republican voters losing enthusiasm for him.

More than half the Senate GOP conference pushed back against the Justice Department's proposal to establish a nearly $1.8 billion "anti-weaponization" fund for Trump's MAGA allies at a fiery meeting with Blanche in May.

GOP senators also quashed Trump's push for $1 billion in funding for the new 90,000-square-foot White House ballroom and are now currently resisting his call for immediate passage of a budget resolution to fund the unpopular military conflict with Iran.

A group of Senate Republicans last week bristled over the White House intervening in a stopgap spending bill to fund the government until Dec. 11 by adding language to delay the implementation of a ban on hemp-derived THC products — a policy rider that deeply divided their conference.

One GOP senator fumed the move was "not rational," given the uproar it created within the conference, to delay the implementation of the ban by only a month.

"I don't understand why this is an issue. What's the heartburn over just a few weeks? They say there's someone very close to the White House who has an interest in this," the lawmaker added, referring to media reports that White House chief of staff Susie Wiles's son-in-law, Bret Worley, is the CEO of companies that make hemp-derived intoxicating gummies and vapes.

GOP senators vented their complaints over the hemp-products rider to White House staff during a closed-door meeting but later acceded to the White House's will on the issue by voting early Saturday morning to table an amendment sponsored by Sen. Ted Budd (R-N.C.) to strip the White House-backed hemp language from the government funding stopgap.

"This issue has got everybody in the conference spun up," the senator added. "If the president were to veto a CR [continuing resolution] over this? Wow. But that's kind of the worry."

title: Chinese rocket carrying satellite explodes seconds after launch
description: A Chinese rocket set to launch a satellite into orbit blew-up seconds after liftoff Monday, marking the relatively rare failure for a rocket considered the workhorse of Beijing’s space program.
fullText:
A Chinese rocket set to launch a satellite into orbit blew-up seconds after liftoff Monday, marking the relatively rare failure for a rocket considered a workhorse of Beijing's space program.

The Long March 7A rocket erupted into a massive fireball just 85 seconds after blasting off from the Wenchang Space Launch Site on the island of Hainan on Monday night, video showed.

Unlike other successful launches, the incident appears to have been downplayed on China's state media with scant mention of the explosion.

State news agency Xinhua confirmed the failure three hours after the launch, saying "the rocket experienced an anomaly during flight." The cause is under investigation, it added, without providing further information.

On Chinese social media, video of the launch was mainly limited to state-affiliated content, while videos posted by users appeared to be removed or deprioritized from searches on popular platforms Xiaohongshu and Douyin.

Chinese leader Xi Jinping has ambitions to make China a world leader in space science by 2050, and the country's locked in an intense competition with the US on multiple fronts, including reusable launch technology, moon research and satellite launches.

SpaceX founder Elon Musk, who has watched a number of his own rockets explode after launch during testing, commented on X saying: "Rockets are insanely hard."

Long March 7A is a satellite delivery rocket designed by China Academy of Launch Vehicle Technology, a subsidiary of China Aerospace Science and Technology Corporation, the main state-owned contractor for China's space program.

This was to be the Long March 7A's 18th mission – it's only failed on one previous occasion, during its maiden flight in 2020. The second attempt in March 2021 succeeded, with images showing crowds that had gathered to witness the launch.

Wenchang, home to one of China's major rocket launch sites, is known for its space tourism. Tourists and residents often gather at Wenchang Space Launch Viewing Center and other locations to watch launches where there's a clear view.

Gasps could be heard on one video posted online after Monday's failed launch, as the rocket appeared to break apart midair just after 8 p.m.. The rocket was carrying the Zhongxing-4B or ChinaSat-4B, to provide radio, television and other communications services to users around the world, according to Chinese state media.

Following the failure of the Long March 7A on Monday, the much-anticipated launch of the Zhuque-3, planned for Tuesday morning at Jiuquan satellite launching station, was delayed, according to Yicai, a Shanghai-based financial news outlet citing sourced information.

The Zhuque-3, developed by Chinese private rocket company LandSpace, is the country's first serious attempt to build a reusable launch rocket. It made its first voyage in December 2025, but the first stage of the rocket caught fire before crashing near the target recovery site.

Last month, China successfully recovered the first stage of a carrier rocket during an orbital launch test – a breakthrough for the country's reusable rocket program. In that test, the first-stage booster returned to a floating platform about six minutes after ⁠the separation of its first and upper stage, according to state broadcaster CCTV.

"This mission … signifies a historic breakthrough in China's reusable rocket technology and a solid foundation for accelerating the improvement of China's space access capabilities," the rocket-maker China Aerospace Science and Technology Corporation said in a post to social media at the time.

Unlike the Zhuque-3, the Long March 7A is a three-stage rocket that's not designed for re-use.

Measuring almost 200 feet (60 meters) in length, the rocket has four boosters and the capacity to send seven metric tons of payload to geostationary transfer orbit (GTO) – approximately around 22,000 miles (35,405 kilometers) above the Earth's surface.

CNN's Fred He contributed to the reporting.

title: Russia frees ailing ex-US Marine Robert Gilman from detention
description: Russia on Tuesday freed a former American Marine who had been jailed in the country since 2022, U. In a social media post, Trump said Russia agreed to release Robert Gil...
fullText:
WASHINGTON, Aug 11 (Reuters) - Russia on Tuesday freed a former American Marine who had been jailed in the country since 2022, U.S. President Donald Trump said.

In a social media post, Trump said Russia agreed to release Robert Gilman, 32, for humanitarian ‌reasons after discussions with Russian President Vladimir Putin, adding that the ailing American would arrive at Joint Base Andrews near Washington on Tuesday night.

"I am ‌proud to announce that American Citizen Robert Gilman, a former United States Marine, is coming HOME!" Trump said. "We appreciate this decision, and the fact that Russia asked for no one in return — No exchange ​took place."

The White House and the State Department had urged Moscow to release Gilman so he could receive medical treatment in the United States. U.S. officials said Putin approved a pardon for him.

Gilman was being held in a prison in Voronezh, about 340 miles (550 kilometers) south of Moscow. The exact circumstances of his health are unclear.

But Eric Lebson, chief strategy officer of Global Reach, an advocacy group representing Gilman's family, told Reuters last week that Gilman was moved in late June from the prison hospital to the psychiatric ward ‌of a civilian emergency hospital in a catatonic-like state assessed ⁠as a "dissociative stupor."

A U.S. official who spoke to Gilman said he was walking and talking.

"All things considered he seems to be in good shape," the official said.

Trump's post included a photo of a gaunt-looking man on a plane surrounded by a group of ⁠smiling people carrying an American flag. The president said he had spoken to Gilman, who requested a cheeseburger upon landing.

"I will take care of that!" Trump said.

Gilman will be evaluated on the flight by four doctors, said the U.S. officials, who spoke on condition of anonymity.

After that, Gilman is likely to be flown to a rehabilitation center in San Antonio, Texas, for ​medical ​treatment, the officials said.

ARRESTED OVER POLICE OFFICER INCIDENT

Gilman, who served in the U.S. Marines from August ​2019 until August 2020, was traveling by train when he was ‌arrested in January 2022 in Voronezh, Lebson said.

He was detained for allegedly kicking a police officer while drunk, according to Russian state media.

However, his father, Vladimir Gilman, who emigrated to Massachusetts from Russia, wrote in an October 2024 Boston Globe op-ed that the charges were false.

His son, he said, had fallen ill when the incident occurred and accidentally kicked the officer. The officer was uninjured, dropped the charges, and did not present evidence at Gilman's trial, he wrote.

Robert Gilman was sentenced to 4-1/2 years in jail. He was one of at least 10 Americans known to be imprisoned in Russia.

The U.S. officials said a Russian senior official, Yuri Ushakov, informed Trump aides ‌last week that Putin had agreed to sign a decree pardoning Gilman for humanitarian purposes, given ​Putin's friendship with the president.

The release resulted from intense negotiations over the weekend by U.S. and ​Russian officials. The U.S. did not exchange any Russian prisoners in order to ​gain Gilman's release and no concessions were made, the officials said.

"It's a goodwill gesture," one official said.

Trump thanked U.S. envoy Steve Witkoff, ‌senior director for counterterrorism Sebastian Gorka, his son-in-law Jared Kushner, ​and U.S. special envoy for hostage response Adam ​Boehler for making the release possible.

U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio said Gilman is among 100 U.S. citizens whose freedom Trump has helped secure during his second term in office. Rubio said the U.S. appreciated the "positive step," but called for the release of other Americans who he said were unjustly ​detained in Russia, including Stephen Hubbard.

Hubbard, a retired schoolteacher, was ‌sentenced in October 2024 to almost seven years in a penal colony after a court found him guilty of serving in a Ukrainian territorial ​defense unit against Russian forces, tasked with manning a checkpoint.

title: Chelsea face Sociedad in Champions League qualifying
description: Chelsea will face Spanish side Real Sociedad in the Women's Champions League third qualifying round, with the first leg of the tie on 26 August.
fullText:
Chelsea will face Spanish side Real Sociedad in the Women's Champions League third qualifying round.

The Blues will be at home for the first leg on 26 August, with the return fixture in Spain a week later on 2 September.

Having finishing third in the Women's Super League last season, eight-time WSL champions Chelsea will have to beat Sociedad in order to seal their spot in the competition's league phase.

Sociedad finished their Liga F campaign in third, 21 points behind league winners Barcelona.

Chelsea, who were beaten in the Champions League final by Barcelona in 2021, were seeded for Tuesday's draw which took place at the House of European Football in Nyon, Switzerland.

In the other ties, Paris St-Germain take on Eintracht Frankfurt, Real Madrid play Ajax, two-time winners Wolfsburg face Inter Milan and Juventus have been drawn against Austrian side St Polten.

WSL champions Manchester City and runners-up Arsenal have already qualified for the league phase, along with defending champions Barcelona.

title: Who is prospective new Celtic signing Hassan?
description: BBC Scotland takes a look at Egypt winger Haissem Hassan, who seems poised for a move to Scottish champions Celtic.
fullText:
Having burst on to the World Cup stage this summer, breakout star Haissem Hassan now appears bound for Celtic.

The Egypt winger is reportedly set for a medical in Glasgow after Celtic agreed an initial £6m transfer fee, external, that could rise to £9m, with Real Oviedo.

It would end a saga and take Celtic's haul of new recruits this summer to three as the hugely-important Champions League play-off with LASK looms large.

Martin O'Neill has stated his desire for quality over quantity in replenishing a squad that has lost more than a dozen players since last season's league and Scottish Cup double success.

So, why have Celtic zoned in on Hassan and what will he bring?

Celtic hope to complete Hassan deal soon - Scottish gossip

'Celtic fans are going to fall in love with him' - Hogh makes his mark

Hassan played just 126 minutes at this summer's World Cup, but it was enough to send his reputation rocketing.

He did not feature in any of Egypt's Group G matches with head coach Hossam Hassan later revealing it was down to a paperwork delay in registering the former France youth international.

The 24-year-old was finally unleashed as a second-half substitute in Egypt's last-32 penalty shootout win over Australia - before delivering a standout performance against Lionel Messi's Argentina.

A left-footer deployed on the right flank, Hassan started the last-16 match and set up Mostafa Zico's goal, skipping past Enzo Fernandez before drilling in a precise delivery to help put Egypt 2-0 up.

However, it was the Egypt's infamous disallowed goal in their agonising 3-2 defeat by the defending champions that showcased Hassan's direct running and dynamic dribbling qualities.

Bursting forward from the right-back area, he evaded two challenges in a 60-yard run before threading a pass through for Mohamed Salah, who teed up Zico.

Across his two World Cup performances, Hassan registered nine dribble attempts at a rate of 6.4 per 90 minutes.

If Celtic had hoped to keep their interest in the winger under the radar, that prospect was blown out of the water with his impact on football's biggest stage.

Hassan was born in France and represented Les Bleus at Under-17 and Under-18 level before switching allegiances and making his senior international debut for Egypt, his father's birthplace, earlier this year.

He started his club career in central France at Chateauroux, featuring initially for their B team and then the senior team in the lower leagues.

A move to Spain's Villarreal followed in 2020 where he turned out for their B team, then went on loan to Mirandes before returning to the Yellow Submarine for his first taste of top-flight football in La Liga.

Another loan, to Sporting Gijon, followed and Hassan stayed in the second tier before a move to Oviedo in 2024.

He helped the club win promotion in his first season, scoring four goals and setting up three, but the going was far tougher in La Liga last term.

Hassan contributed three assists and couldn't muster a goal in 37 appearances, 20 of those from the start, as Oviedo finished bottom to immediately drop back down.

His xG (expected goals) of 0.15 last season hints at a paucity of clear chances in a team that were the lowest scorers in the division by a distance.

Kasper Hogh is an out and-out-striker, while fellow new arrival Camilo Duran, who can play wide or through the middle, is left-footed but has been deployed on the right wing in Celtic's opening two games of the season.

That right-wing berth would likely become Hassan's, with Duran shifting over to the left in place of Yang Hyun-jun.

Manager O'Neill has also hinted at playing two up top, which would mean a Hogh-Duran front pairing and Hassan providing ammunition on the right with Yang on the left.

That would give Celtic's attack a similar look to that of the Gordon Strachan era, when Shunsuke Nakamura and either Aiden McGeady or Shaun Maloney operated as inverted wingers, supporting a central pair of strikers - typically Jan Vennegoor of Hesselink with Giorgios Samaras or Scott McDonald.

Celtic's link-up play really stretched Kilmarnock in the 5-1 weekend win, with hat-trick hero Hogh coming deep and going long to combine with his team-mates.

The wingers and midfielders got into advanced positions throughout, with three different players providing assists for Hogh's goals.

Adding Hassan would offer Celtic a fresh and exciting option in a fluid attack.

title: Ulster captain Henderson to miss start of season
description: Ulster captain Iain Henderson will miss several months of the new season after hip surgery during the summer.
fullText:
Ulster captain Iain Henderson will miss several months of the new season following hip surgery.

The 34-year-old, who won the last of his 86 Ireland caps against New Zealand in November, missed the end of the northern province's season through suspension.

A red card against the Stormers in the United Rugby Championship (URC) resulted in a three-game ban that included the Challenge Cup final defeat by Montpellier in Bilbao.

The second row made his Ulster debut in April 2012 and first appeared for Ireland against South Africa in November of the same year.

A two-time tourist with the British and Irish Lions, he was named captain of his province following Rory Best's retirement in 2019.

Ulster start their URC season at home to Edinburgh on 25 September and Henderson is not head coach Richie Murphy's sole injury concern.

Bryn Ward (shoulder), Juarno Augustus (ankle), and Jude Postlethwaite (knee) have all also had surgery during the off-season and, according to the province, "are currently undergoing a period of rehabilitation".

title: China's car sales extend slide as shift accelerates to overseas markets
description: China's car sales fell for a 10th straight month in July, though the pace of decline eased, contrasting with strong export growth as automakers step up overseas expansion
fullText:
BEIJING, Aug 11 (Reuters) - China's car sales fell for a 10th straight month in July, though the pace of decline eased, contrasting with strong export growth as automakers step up overseas expansion to offset ‌cut-throat competition in the world's largest auto market.

The decline underscores broader strains in China's economy, where sluggish ‌household spending has left exports accounting for a greater share of growth.

Sales at home slid 21.1% last month from a year earlier to 1.47 million ​vehicles, while exports rose 88.2% to 923,000, data from the China Passenger Car Association (CPCA) showed on Tuesday.

"The downturn has proved more severe than we had expected. We had anticipated a noticeable improvement in July," said Cui Dongshu, secretary-general of the CPCA, attributing the weakness to elevated fuel prices that have weighed on gasoline-powered vehicle sales and subdued demand for entry-level sedans.

For the first seven months of the year as a whole, domestic passenger vehicle sales declined 20.5%, equivalent to about ⁠2.65 million fewer vehicles than in the same period a year earlier.

Automakers have stepped up efforts to expand abroad, particularly in Europe, Southeast Asia, Latin America and the Middle East, creating a pronounced gap between domestic and overseas demand.

In the domestic market, some carmakers ​are ​also piling into the premium segment with bigger, feature-packed models, including ​Xiaomi's extended-range SkyNomad SUV series.

"Replacement demand has moderated ‌after the subsidy-driven pull-forward, while consumers have become increasingly selective given frequent product launches and a more competitive market," HSBC analysts said in a note in July.

The pressure is evident among industry leaders. BYD, the world's largest EV maker, has been grappling with a slowing home market, yet record overseas shipments in July helped lift its global sales for a third consecutive month.

But not everyone is suffering, even in the home market.

Stellantis-backed Leapmotor, one of BYD's fastest-growing ‌challengers, reported global sales of more than 100,000 vehicles in July, more ​than double a year earlier.

Analysts say it is catering better for current ​consumer demand.

"What consumers want are vehicles with strong ​value for money, not necessarily premium models," Cui said. "Automakers want to move upmarket, but consumers are ‌looking for affordability."

title: Fighting relegation & eyeing promotion? Championship set for six-team play-offs
description: The Championship play-offs expand to six teams this season. Here's a closer look at how it may pan out and the thoughts of those involved.
fullText:
Derby County, Millwall (twice), Middlesbrough and Blackburn Rovers all have something in common which could be worth in the region of £150m this season.

Across the past five seasons those teams finished eighth in the Championship table - a decent year but with no reward at the end of it.

All that will change for the upcoming 2026-27 campaign with seventh and eighth being enough to get you into the play-offs for a shot at reaching the Premier League.

Clubs finishing third and fourth will progress directly to the semi-final - as has been the case in previous seasons - while a one-legged quarter-final will be played with fifth at home to eighth and sixth hosting seventh.

Semi-finals will remain as two legs and the final will still take place at Wembley at the end of May.

Will this new format change the way teams approach the season which gets under way on Friday? How likely is it a side finishing seventh or eighth will actually win through? And, is it fair?

When announcing the decision to extend the Championship play-offs in March, the English Football League said the aim was to "increase the number of competitive fixtures during the closing stages of the season".

Last season, three teams went into the final day of the campaign vying for the sixth and final play-off spot. The top eight was already decided with just the order to be sorted. As it turned out, Wrexham finished seventh and Derby eighth.

On the last weekend of the 2024-25 season, five sides had a shot at the last two play-off berths but only Middlesbrough, who were ninth, would have had a chance of breaking into the top eight had they been working under the new rules.

Staying with the new regulations, had they been in place for the 2023-24 season only ninth-placed Coventry City would have been in with a shout of overhauling Middlesbrough in eighth.

Of course, managers might change their approach if there is more chance of snagging a play-off spot as the season progresses - picking different players or making alternative signings in January if a top-eight finish is still realistic.

"I thought the system worked pretty well previously - I think we'll have to see how it pans out," Portsmouth boss John Mousinho said.

"I didn't think there was an issue but we'll see how it goes. I think since the introduction of the play-off system, it's been wildly successful."

Clubs vote in favour of six-team Championship play-off

'I understand why more teams want golden ticket' - Championship reaction to play-offs extension

Since the Championship play-offs were tweaked in 1989 to only include the teams finishing third to sixth, the side coming sixth has been promoted just seven times.

Three of the first six (Crystal Palace, twice, and Blackpool) were immediately relegated.

Hull City's promotion last season made them the seventh and came as something of a surprise - they were the first sixth-placed outfit to go up for 16 years.

Between them, Wrexham and Derby managed only three wins in 16 games against the sides who qualified for the play-offs last term. That ratio would appear to make it unlikely either would have gone all the way in the post-season competition.

Prior to the new season, the lowest play-off spot available was in League Two with seventh enough to sneak in.

But the seventh-placed side has only gone up seven times from 38 attempts. Championship sides will also face that extra one-off game before the semi-finals.

Despite the odds being against seventh or eighth actually winning promotion, there are still reservations about even allowing them to compete.

Lyle Taylor, a play-off winner with Nottingham Forest, Charlton Athletic and AFC Wimbledon feels it is rewarding mediocrity.

"If you're talking about going down to eighth, you could have a team with 10 or 11 fewer wins than the one finishing third," he told the BBC podcast 72+.

"Are you therefore deserving of being in the same post-season competition as that team? No, this is a meritocracy isn't it?"

Former Huddersfield Town play-off winner Tommy Smith added: "I get that it gives more teams a chance to compete, but I can't help feeling some of the teams who end up competing could have a chance of getting to the Premier League over a team which finishes third and amasses an enormous amount of points.

"I think back to Sheffield United just missing out on the automatics and then losing to Sunderland in the play-off final (having finished 14 points ahead of them in 2024-25).

"I don't know how that sits with me, a team finishing eighth could be in the Premier League over a team finishing third."

At the 2026-27 EFL season launch in Manchester, several EFL players and managers gave their thoughts on the change.

Nigel Clough, manager of League One side Mansfield Town, expected the format to be used in League One and League Two in future seasons, but was not keen on the expansion.

"If you come third and are 20 points away from eighth and in the same competition for the last few games, that does seem a little bit unfair, but it does keep the season alive for so many teams," he said.

"With how close League One was last year, you could be fighting relegation and trying to make the play-offs at the same time. How far do you take it?

"There must be a reward for your 46 games. I know there is for the top two, but maybe going to top eight is a bit far for my liking because if you are the third-best team after 46 games you should get some reward."

Derby striker Rhian Brewster, whose side finished eighth in the Championship last season, said: "It will be good as some teams will have slow starts and kick on and could have a chance of getting in the play-offs this year and going up.

"It is going to be harder but you could be near the bottom and go on a run and finish eighth or seventh. You want to finish first or second, but if you end up in the play-offs then win the play-offs."

Burnley and former England defender Kyle Walker played in the 2009 Championship play-off final.

He was featuring for Sheffield United, who had finished third in the league, and they lost 1-0 in the Wembley final to Burnley.

He was in favour of the new format and said: "I think it's good, more chances for more people, but first of all you don't want to be involved in the play-offs.

"I've been involved in it and it's a roulette, anything can happen. Make sure you make a gap between first, second and let the rest deal with it themselves."

Blackburn manager Tony Mowbray scored in the 2000 Championship play-off final as his Ipswich Town side beat Barnsley 4-2 to win promotion into the Premier League.

"I think it's good and keeps the dreams alive for fans and a lot of football teams. You could be sitting 10th, 12th or 14th but still be three points off the top eight and two wins back-to-back and you can catapult yourselves in," Mowbray said.

"People have to dream, they have to have a reason why they want to go and believe they can still do it. For me, it's only positive. The argument is you could have a team finishing eighth and getting promoted, but good luck to them.

"Sunderland when they scraped through the play-offs [in 2025], Coventry in the semi-finals over two legs were the better team but Dan Ballard got them through with a header right at the death.

"Then, at Wembley, Sheffield United might have been the better team over 90 minutes and they [Sunderland] got there. Then they spent £180m and are now playing in Europe so it can happen to any team."

The new format means one third of the Championship will be able to point to some sort of 'success', be that automatic promotion, going up via the play-offs, a Wembley appearance or just a top-eight finish.

It could heap even more pressure on managers (there were 13 managerial changes in the division last season) and on owners to invest more money in pursuit of the Premier League riches.

"It depends whether it dilutes it too much and, all of a sudden, the side that finishes eighth and maybe is a long way off the side that finishes third ultimately gets a chance to go into the Premier League and what knock-on affect that has," Portsmouth boss John Mousinho told BBC Radio Solent.

"It'll be very interesting to see if and when that does happen."

Sheffield United's poor start to last season saw them lose eight of their opening nine matches but, following the reappointment of Chris Wilder, they were 15th, within nine points of the top six and, perhaps more pertinently only three short of eighth, with 11 games remaining.

Mousinho thinks the Blades are an example of what the extension of the play-offs can offer for those who might have previously started planning for the next campaign.

"For sides competing at the top of the bottom half currently, or who maybe want to compete and get in the top half, it's a good thing because eighth is a realistic target whereas sixth previously was a bit of a leap," he said.

"The acid test will be if a side does finish seventh or eighth and is maybe a long way off the top four but does get promoted to the Premier League.

"In other leagues I think you can bridge the gap a bit more easily, but in the Championship to the Premier League there is a big gap there.

"I'm sure if a side does do it there'll be no complaints but it'll be a good one to keep an eye on."

title: Rocky Flintoff hits first professional century for Lancs
description: Rocky Flintoff, the 18-year-old son of legendary former England all-rounder Andrew, hits his first professional century for Lancashire.
fullText:
Lancashire 443-6 (50 overs): Jennings 156 (127), Flintoff 123 (76)

Somerset 269 all out (39.2 overs): Lammonby 68 (58); Aspinwall 4-42

Rocky Flintoff, the 18-year-old son of legendary former England all-rounder Andrew, hit his first senior professional century in Lancashire's One-Day Cup match against Somerset at Taunton.

The right-hander dominated the bowling in crashing 10 fours and seven sixes in a superb 123 from 76 balls in Lancashire's 443-6.

Somerset were then bowled out for 269 in response after George Balderson and Tom Aspinwall claimed four wickets apiece despite a battling 68 from Tom Lammonby.

Lancashire finished second in Group A on 20 points - behind leaders Leicestershire Foxes on net run-rate - and will play Durham at Old Trafford in the quarter-final on Friday.

After coming in at 138-3, Flintoff was the aggressor in a brutal partnership of 214 with Keaton Jennings and reached his century from just 65 deliveries.

Also capitalising on a flat pitch and a Somerset attack depleted by The Hundred, Jennings made 156. Lancashire's total was their best in List A cricket.

But the century is the latest landmark moment in the young career of Flintoff.

He became Lancashire's youngest player when he made his debut aged 16 years and 113 days in the One-Day Cup in 2024, a week after becoming England Under-19s' youngest centurion with a ton against Sri Lanka.

He followed that by becoming England Lions' youngest century-maker, in a match against Cricket Australia in January 2025, beating his father's record.

Injuries have also hampered the teenager's progress.

He missed last winter's Under-19 World Cup with England and had to withdraw from The Hundred in 2025, having been signed by Northern Superchargers where his father was coach.

After reports linking him with a move away, Flintoff signed a new two-year contract extension with Lancashire in March.

He has still only played four first-class matches for the Red Rose county - the most recent in 2024.

But, after beginning the season playing for Lancashire's second XI and featuring again for England Under-19s, he has found opportunity and form in the One-Day Cup, which has effectively become a second-tier competition played below The Hundred.

Flintoff has made scores of 33 not out, 41 not out, 34 and 61 not out around dismissals for nought and one in his six previous matches.

Against Somerset, whose XI also featured spinner Archie Vaughan, son of former England captain Michael, Flintoff was particularly destructive in hitting sixes over straight mid-wicket in a fashion reminiscent of his father.

Andrew played 79 Tests, 141 one-day internationals and seven T20s for England and was part of the iconic 2005 Ashes series win.

It was announced last week he has stepped down as coach of England Lions.
