title: Women's football shouldn't be penalised by Uefa boycott - Nandy
description: Culture Secretary Lisa Nandy says women's footballers should not be "penalised" by a potential boycott of next month's Under-20 Women's World Cup.
fullText:
Culture Secretary Lisa Nandy says women's footballers should not be "penalised" by a potential boycott of next month's Under-20 Women's World Cup, as hosts Poland say they have received no notice of any withdrawals from European teams.

European governing body Uefa and its 55 members have threatened to boycott Fifa competitions over its president Gianni Infantino's plan to sell off stakes in the World Cup.

Poland are due to host the tournament from 5-27 September, but are not the only Uefa nation involved - with England, Italy, Spain, Portugal and France all due to take part.

The Polish Football Association (PZPN) told BBC Sport on Tuesday that it had so far "not received any information regarding the possible withdrawal of any participating team from the tournament".

It added: "We believe that the current situation will be resolved swiftly, allowing young players from across the world to compete in Poland.

"Our priority remains to ensure the best possible conditions for the competition and for all participating teams. For many of these young players, this tournament represents an important milestone in their sporting careers, and we remain fully focused on delivering an event worthy of their talent and commitment."

Last week, the French Football Federation (FFF) said it intended to compete at the U20 World Cup while the Portuguese Football Federation (FPF) also told BBC Sport that "so far, the Under-20 team is complying with the planned programme", including a friendly fixture against England later this week.

England's Football Association has not confirmed whether it will field a team for the World Cup. However, as things stand, coach Lydia Bedford's Young Lionesses squad are continuing preparations for the tournament.

The map showing world's division over Infantino

Trump says it would be 'terrible mistake' to remove Infantino

Nandy told the BBC that she wants to see Infantino resign over his Fifa Forward Enterprise (FFE) proposal, under which stakes in the World Cup and other competitions would be sold to private investors.

"We support the [English] FA in saying that football belongs to its fans, enough is enough, and it is time for a change at Fifa," Nandy said.

"I think [Infantino] should go, the time is up."

But she added she would not support a boycott of the U20 World Cup.

"I am not generally in favour of sporting boycotts full stop, because I think they divide people from one another, I think they unfairly penalise athletes and competitors who are not responsible for the reason that these boycotts take place," she said.

"What I would like to see actually is football coming together, resolving this, a change of leadership, a change of direction and a very clear message that football belongs to its fans and it will not have women and girls penalised when the women's game is going from strength to strength. And our Lionesses are leading the world in that."

title: Violent crime up in DC despite Trump boast of National Guard presence
description: Washington DC 2026 crime numbers show varying results from the National Guard deployment, which was ordered by President Donald Trump last year.
fullText:
President Donald Trump said during his State of the Union address in February that Washington DC has "almost no crime anymore" thanks to his deployment of the National Guard last August.

They were comments he took a step further in July, when he said DC has gone to levels of "NO CRIME" under his leadership.

The president is right; overall crime is down in DC. Fueled by a 53% drop in motor vehicle theft and a 37% decrease in theft from automobiles, there has been 23% less property crime in DC from 2026 to 2025, according to police data.

But numbers provided by the Metropolitan Police Department tell a different story, one that shows violent crime numbers are up this year.

Here's a look at the 2026 violent crime numbers in Washington DC and how they compare to 2025, with the National Guard deployment to continue through the entirety of Trump's presidency.

Trump's assertion that crime has been wiped out in DC falls short when compared to DC police statistics.

As of Aug. 10, there were 1,655 reported instances of violent crime in the city — 55 more than the same period from last year.

Most of that increase is due to a sharp upswing in reports of assault with a deadly weapon. There is a 41% increase in such activity, with 767 cases so far this year.

The data does show homicides are down — 67 cases this year, compared to 97 on this date in 2025 — but the summer has seen a dramatic increase.

There have been 32 homicides since the beginning of June, including nine in the past two weeks, police data shows.

While DC's homicide rates have improved, data shows that they're actually down throughout the country.

"It's really hard to parse out any effect of the federal deployment in DC, necessarily, because it is a city that was already seeing really strong declines," Jeff Asher, co-founder of the data analytics firm AH Datalytics, told USA TODAY earlier this year.

From 2024 to 2025 — less than half of which featured the National Guard's deployment — violent crime was down 29% in DC. There were 274 homicides in 2023 and 187 in 2024, and the city saw another decrease last year with 127 homicides.

title: Sunrisers hammer Super Giants to reach knockouts
description: Sunrisers Leeds secure their spot in the knockout phase of The Hundred at the expense of opponents Manchester Super Giants after an emphatic 41-run victory.
fullText:
The Hundred women's competition, Old Trafford

Sunrisers Leeds 166-4 (100 balls): Sutherland 62* (36); Villiers 2-25

Manchester Super Giants 125-8 (100 balls): Scrivens 31 (24); Jonassen 3-21

Sunrisers Leeds secured their spot in the knockout phase of The Hundred at the expense of opponents Manchester Super Giants after an emphatic 41-run victory at Old Trafford.

Set 167 to win in favourable batting conditions, the Super Giants' chase never got going - even retiring one of their players out in desperation - as they froze in the baking Manchester sunshine.

Jess Jonassen, who claimed 3-21, did the early damage for the Sunrisers when she captured the key wickets of Smriti Mandhana and Richa Ghosh for 28 and 13 and the Super Giants never recovered.

The Sunrisers leapfrogged the Super Giants into the top three and will face Southern Brave in the Eliminator at The Oval on Friday.

Trent Rockets await the winner of that match in Sunday's final at Lord's.

The Sunrisers bowling attack - backed up by some superb fielding - exerted scoreboard pressure despite the best efforts of Grace Scrivens, who top-scored for the Super Giants with 31 off 24 balls.

Such was the desperation during their reply that Kathryn Bryce was retired out by the Super Giants after making 15 from 14 balls.

Remarkably, it is the second time Bryce has been out this way in The Hundred, having been retired out while playing for the Manchester Originals against Northern Superchargers in August 2024.

Former Australia skipper Meg Lanning also struggled for timing before she was bowled by Jonassen for 10 after chewing up 15 deliveries.

The end of the game became a procession as Annabel Sutherland and Deepti Sharma claimed 2-17 and 2-21 respectively.

Earlier, the Sunrisers had posted 166-4 thanks to an unbeaten 62 from Sutherland.

Opener Phoebe Litchfield had set the tone after she whacked 27 off 12 balls before miscuing a pull to mid-wicket off Mady Villiers.

Australia all-rounder Sutherland continued the momentum when she arrived at the crease - hammering three sixes and six fours in her 36-ball innings.

Sunrisers skipper Dani Gibson chipped in with a useful 24 off 13 balls before she was snared by Villiers, who finished the pick of the Super Giants attack with 2-25.

The action switches to Sophia Gardens and Edgbaston on Wednesday with two double-headers as Welsh Fire host London Spirit while Birmingham Phoenix are at home to MI London.

Fire's women face Spirit at 11:30 BST while Phoenix play MI London at 15:00, although all four sides cannot make the knockout stages.

Fire's men still have hopes of making the Eliminator, though, but must win big against Spirit in their match at 15:00 to boost their net run-rate.

MI London need to do likewise in their fixture at Phoenix at 18:30 if they are to sneak into third place.

title: Grand Slam Track athletes deny Johnson claim they have been paid
description: Athletes promised thousands of pounds in payments for participating in Grand Slam Track events are still waiting for their money.
fullText:
Athletes promised thousands of pounds in payments for participating in Grand Slam Track events are still waiting for their money, despite organisers saying they had all been paid.

Agents and sports-management companies told BBC Sport athletes are yet to receive money they are owed, despite GST founder Michael Johnson saying he had "got the athletes paid" after a "catastrophic capital issue" caused by investors pulling out.

Four-time former Olympic champion Johnson launched GST in 2025 with the promise of lucrative prize money and salaries.

Originally scheduled for four marquee meets, the final event in Los Angeles was cancelled and organisers voluntarily filed for bankruptcy in the US in December.

In an interview in the Telegraph, external on Saturday, Johnson admitted that as GST ran into financial trouble, he used his own credit card to purchase athlete flights and hotel rooms.

The 58-year-old said he was hurt by accusations he "secretly" paid himself $500,000 (£375,000) days before the season collapsed - a claim a GST representative said at the time was "unfounded and false".

"I'm happy to clear it up, because it's the most hurtful thing and the exact opposite of what was reported," Johnson told The Telegraph.

"Our credit card was full at Grand Slam Track, because we were facing significant cash-flow issues.

"I instructed our travel team to put it on my credit card, and I would be reimbursed for it. So, what I received was reimbursement."

But Johnson's claim those who were owed money by GST had received it was premature.

A company acting on behalf of athletes said they had not received any payments, nor had they been contacted to be told when they were due.

Johnson's representatives conceded the money had not yet reached the athletes and said the American had not intentionally set out to deceive people by saying it had.

It is understood the reported $11m (£8.1m) owed to creditors - including athletes - is being held by a third party.

BBC Sport has contacted the American firm believed to be holding the money but it is yet to respond. It is unclear how long it will take to pay the athletes.

Several high-profile athletes were owed payments of more than £100,000, including British former world 1500m champion Josh Kerr and Olympic 400m silver medallist Matthew Hudson-Smith.

Johnson has been a pundit and commentator for the BBC since 2001 but has not worked for the broadcaster since the 2024 Olympics as he focused his attention on GST.

title: Criticism of empty seats and ticket prices at the Europeans
description: Nearly 10,000 seats were empty at Birmingham's Alexander Stadium on Monday.
fullText:
Nearly 10,000 seats were empty at Birmingham's Alexander Stadium for the European Athletics Championships on Monday evening.

A crowd of 13,623 watched as Britain's 24-year-old sprinter Amy Hunt stormed to her first senior international title, in a stadium that has a capacity of 23,000.

Athletics supporters blamed ticket prices, with some describing them as "extortionate", while BBC commentator Steve Cram commented that spectator numbers were a "little disappointing".

But Birmingham 2026 organisers said they were "delighted" with ticket sales, which have "far surpassed" their targets with "Friday, Saturday and Sunday evening sessions approaching sell-out, with several other sessions close to capacity".

On Monday, Category A tickets for the home straight cost £150 with no concessions for juniors.

For the men's 100m final on Tuesday, those same seats cost £110, again with no concessions - while a similar ticket for the same final in Rome two years ago was 88 euros (£75).

It is Britain's first time hosting the championships in their 92-year history.

The Alexander Stadium was 55% full on Monday morning, 59% full by the evening and 56% full on Tuesday morning, according to figures from the organisers.

Jenny Meadows, Keely Hodgkinson's co-coach, posted on social media to say: "Believe it's full for some final evenings but a shame we couldn't fill the stadium for the duration."

British Olympian Sharron Davies also took to social media: "We must bid for more events but we must make it affordable, so we get to enjoy it first hand, fill stadiums, support our athletes, promote our country & inspire generations to come to love sport."

Davies also criticised how official food vendors in the stadium were selling pork rolls for £18.50 and hot dogs for £15.

During coverage of the Women's 100m final on Monday night, BBC commentator Cram added: "Little disappointing in terms of spectators I have to say that, particularly down the back straight there.

"There's not many people at all in those stands. I'm sure Birmingham is going to get to grips with these champs pretty quickly."

Chris Brown was in the stadium on Monday evening, where he photographed rows of empty seats.

Speaking to the BBC, the 40-year-old said: "I think they have the pricing for the weekdays a little off. The cheapest tickets are £26, which is reasonable and most people have bought those and the back rows are full.

"Maybe they should invite everyone down to the lower seats to at least make it look good on TV.

"The view from the £40 to £26 tickets is pretty much the same, so that price category has become rather redundant. £110 for the best seats I think is reasonable for a weekend evening session, but not mid-week.

"But also, the Commonwealth Games may have had an impact, as not many will attend both and both are in the UK within the same fortnight.

"There are many fans in attendance in Birmingham who are international, which is great to see, but it's disappointing that many Brits haven't bothered."

Adam Hilton travelled from Manchester to Birmingham for Saturday's evening session.

The 34-year-old paid £120 for two tickets for him and his girlfriend - but said he "doesn't feel [it was] value for money" and he would consider no longer going if there was an option to get a refund.

"Seeing the opening day [Monday] felt very disappointing to see the empty seats, especially in the evening session," he said. "In summer, with the good weather, you'd like to see it full-ish.

"It's a shame, as it seems to be a trend across most sports where fans are seemingly being priced out of events that should be way more accessible.

"For the first European Championships in the UK ever, you'd except to get bums on seats - and a lot of kids who could then learn to love the sport and take it up going forward, especially when there's a major event outside of London."

Hilton joined others who have criticised the lack of transport infrastructure around the stadium, with the nearest train station a mile's walk away and shuttle buses ferrying fans from the city centre.

Hilton, who drove, said he could only find a parking space two miles (3km) away.

One athletics fan urged organisers on social media to "fill the place" with "cheap door tickets".

Another said they decided against buying tickets as it would cost his family "more than a holiday" when travel and accommodation for one night was factored in.

But a Birmingham 2026 spokesperson expressed delight at the ticket sales which "have far surpassed our targets".

"Friday, Saturday and Sunday evening sessions are approaching sell-out, with several other sessions close to capacity," they added.

"There are still opportunities to be part of the championships at incredibly good value.

"After a fantastic opening day of competition, we're looking forward to welcoming many more spectators to Alexander Stadium throughout the week and sharing more memorable moments of world-class athletics."

title: What potential Bezos deal would mean for Liverpool
description: Why investment by a group including Jeff Bezos would not make a marked difference to Liverpool's spending power - and might sit uneasily with fans.
fullText:
The fourth-richest man in the world is trying to buy a stake in your club. Surely that has to be good news?

Yet Liverpool fans, who still bear the scars of the Tom Hicks and George Gillette era, are viewing the potential high-profile investment cautiously.

The man in question is billionaire Amazon founder Jeff Bezos, who is part of a consortium that is in advanced talks to buy a 30% stake in the club.

Bezos, according to Forbes, has a personal fortune of about $257bn (£190bn).

To put that into context, last year Liverpool announced record revenues of £703m - but Bezos is worth 270 times that.

With scant information about the group's plans or long-term intentions, supporters have cause for caution - especially with the end of the Hicks-Gillette era still vivid in the minds of many.

So who might be the winners from the deal? Will it be the club, the consortium or Liverpool's owners Fenway Sports Group (FSG)?

This is what the investment would mean in reality - and why it could happen.

When FSG bought Liverpool for £300m in 2010 the club were, according to CEO Billy Hogan, "literally on the brink of bankruptcy".

On top of the purchase price, FSG have since facilitated intra-group loans of about £218m, meaning a total outlay of about £518m.

Sixteen years later, the proposed sale of 30% would mean FSG received £1.35bn, with the club valued at £4.5bn - 13 times what it was worth in 2010 when FSG bought it from Hicks and Gillette.

"It's a great deal for FSG," football finance expert Kieran Maguire told BBC Sport.

"They generate more than £1bn from the deal and still keep control - this represents the best of both worlds."

Such a huge increase in Liverpool's value has required investment off the pitch as well as success on it, including building a new training ground and redeveloping the stadium.

A 30-year title drought was ended in 2019-20, another Premier League was won in 2024-25 and a sixth Champions League was claimed in 2018-19.

This is not the first time outside money has been accepted by FSG, with global sports investment firm Dynasty Equity purchasing 3% for an undisclosed amount in 2023.

Maguire added: "This follows the approach of City Football Group of letting in minority investors to recoup the original purchase price and more."

But even if the minority investment goes through, the Premier League's Squad Cost Ratio financial rules mean supporters should not expect Liverpool to start spending a lot more on transfer fees.

Funds to spend on transfers are directly related to income generated via commercial activities rather than an owner's wealth.

"The deal could be a straight share sale by FSG to the new group, in which case there would be no financial implications for the club itself," Maguire added.

Bezos stepped down as CEO of Amazon five years ago but remains one of the company's biggest shareholders.

He also owns aerospace company Blue Origin, venture capital firm Nash Holdings and the Washington Post. More recently he created Prometheus, an artificial intelligence company which last month invested £330m in a British AI start-up.

As if to underline the scale of his financial resources, only last week he filed to sell 15 million of his remaining Amazon shares with a market value of about £3.1bn - double the value of the consortium's offer for a stake in Liverpool.

Bezos has been linked with sports investment for some time, but usually American sports franchises which are either more expensive or not open to offers.

He was reportedly interested in the Seattle Seahawks, who were sold for £7.3bn, external recently. The Washington Commanders, another NFL franchise said to be of interest, were sold for £4.6bn in 2023.

Buying a stake in Liverpool would give the 62-year-old a slice of one of the most iconic global sports brands for a small fraction of his fortune.

But would Liverpool be a status symbol or a true investment?

It is not as if Liverpool are unknown in the United States, either. Research company GWI has reported that Liverpool have 26 million supporters in the US, and the fastest-growing fan base.

It is no surprise, then, that the Reds had their pre-season tour in the States.

The deal would continue a theme of US investment into the Premier League, with 11 of the 20 teams this season having majority control from America - Liverpool included.

That's not to mention Ryan Reynolds and Rob Mac - formerly known as Rob McElhenney - at Wrexham, and Tom Brady's Birmingham, in the Championship.

FSG bought into Liverpool at the most opportune time, with the club struggling financially.

But even at this point Hogan says there is "a huge opportunity still" to invest in "the biggest and most popular sport in the world".

It taps into the reason why US money continues to pour into the English game - namely prestige, and the chance to grow not just in this country but around the world too.

Facebook co-founder Eduardo Saverin, who is reported to be worth $32bn (£23.7bn), is also involved is the consortium.

Then there is Amit Bhatia, who had been a director and co-owner of Queens Park Rangers for the last 18 years until he relinquished his ownership stake in the Championship club on 21 July.

It is against Football Association regulations to have a substantial interest in more than one club, so the timing of Bhatia's move appeared to confirm he is involved in the Liverpool deal.

Hogan has suggested there is no prospect of FSG entertaining a full sale of the club, but Maguire believes if the initial investment goes well, that could change.

"If Bezos et al like the kudos and attention that part owning as big a brand as Liverpool brings," Maguire said. "Then a full acquisition becomes a possibility, if the price is right."

Liverpool fans consider the club to have a specific set of values, centred around its working-class roots.

When FSG attempted to raise season ticket prices last season, fans' group Spirit of Shankly (SOS) launched a campaign called 'Not a Pound in the Ground'.

It urged fans to buy food and drink from local businesses in the Anfield area rather than inside the stadium. It worked, forcing the club to cut the size of their planned price rise.

SOS has doubts about the proposed investment and has raised a number of concerns.

"We would like to know what the buying consortium will get in return for their 30% stake," an SOS spokesperson told BBC Sport.

"Specifically, what would be the level of involvement in the control of the club and will they take a seat or seats on the board?

"And of huge importance, what due diligence is being done on the potential consortium of investors?

"Does this potential consortium have the best interests of the club at the forefront or is it a 'trophy' buy?"

SOS' ethos is in contrast to the concerns that have been raised over the way Amazon workers have been treated.

A Trades Union Congress report, external issued in 2020 highlighted "long, gruelling shifts with unreasonable productivity targets and unfair shift patterns" and "unacceptable working conditions".

In 2024, more than 200 workers took part in two days of strike action at the Amazon site in Birmingham as part of a long-running dispute over pay and union rights. Amazon said it regularly reviews its pay to ensure it offers competitive wages.

In February this year, the Washington Post announced it would be laying off one-third of its work force, sharply scaling back the paper's coverage of sports and foreign news.

Gareth Roberts, Liverpool season ticket holder and host of the Late Challenge LFC podcast, told BBC Sport he had concerns.

"How Amazon have treated unions and workers isn't particularly palatable," Roberts said. "Is he simply going to ramp up the name of Liverpool in order to make as much money as possible?"

The painful experience of the Hicks-Gillette ownership endures, hence the reluctance to throw support behind this possible new investment without more information.

"People wonder why Liverpool fans do scrutinise things like this so much," Roberts added. "We only have to wind back to the ownership of Hicks and Gillette to see why.

"They put Liverpool in dire straits, in a financially unsustainable position.

"We want the club to be run well, we want the club to be run sustainably and we want people to care about it and to care about the fans. It's as simple as that."

So while the investment would give Liverpool some very wealthy new co-owners, it wouldn't necessarily make a marked different to their spending power - and might sit uneasily with at least some of the club's fans.

title: Colombia building collapses on camera as earthquake brings death, destruction
description: Video posted to social media shows a building crumbling in Pereira, Colombia, as a magnitude 7.4 earthquake struck western Colombia, killing at least 111 people.
fullText:
A harrowing video captured the moment a building collapsed as a magnitude 7.4 earthquake struck western Colombia early Monday, killing at least 111 people and injuring 87 others.

The video shows the building shaking and crumbling as onlookers scream before the structure ultimately gives way.

Colombian President Abelardo De La Espriella declared a state of emergency as rescue crews searched collapsed buildings across several cities, according to Reuters.

"The ​national government has all of its capabilities deployed to protect lives, assist affected communities and ⁠deliver aid wherever it is needed," De La Espriella said. "The first priority is rescuing the people trapped under the rubble."

Exclusive: Franklin Graham Visits Emergency Hospital Treating Venezuela Earthquake Victims

The U.S. Geological Survey said the earthquake struck near San Jose del Palmar in Choco at a depth of about 107 kilometers, or 66 miles. The U.S. tsunami warning system said there was no tsunami threat.

The quake struck just days into De La Espriella's presidency, presenting his new administration with its first major crisis.

"The Trump Administration is closely monitoring the large earthquake that struck Colombia and stands ready to support the people of Colombia and President @ABDELAESPRIELLA's Administration," Secretary of State Marco Rubio wrote on X.

Rubio urged Americans in Colombia to enroll in the State Department's Smart Traveler Enrollment Program and follow the U.S. Embassy in Bogota for updates.

Multiple Deaths Reported, Dozens Of Buildings Damaged Following Magnitude 7.4 Earthquake In Western Colombia

WATCH: COLOMBIA EARTHQUAKE VICTIMS FLEE IN TERROR AS DEBRIS FALLS FROM BUILDING:

Some of the heaviest losses were reported in western Colombia.

At least 40 people were killed in Risaralda, home to hard-hit Pereira, while 27 were killed in Valle del Cauca, where Cali is located, The Associated Press reported, citing authorities.

Nine deaths were confirmed in Choco, two in Caldas and one in Antioquia, according to the outlet.

Cali, one of Colombia's largest cities, suffered extensive damage. Mayor Alejandro Eder said more than two dozen structures had collapsed and people remained trapped, prompting the city to request additional disaster-response teams from Bogota and Medellin.

"At this point, two people have already been rescued alive, one elderly woman and one young girl. There are more people trapped," Eder told Blu Radio. "We have at least 12 critical points and 25 collapsed structures that we are responding to."

The quake's epicenter was near San Jose del Palmar, in Choco, a sparsely populated province on Colombia's Pacific coast. Choco Governor Nubia Carolina Cordoba-Curi said there were injuries and significant damage in Quibdo, the provincial capital, and warned residents about aftershocks.

Colombia's civil aviation authority said flights were suspended at airports in Pereira, Manizales, Quibdo, Armenia, Cartago and Buenaventura while inspectors checked for structural damage.

The country's disaster agency said the quake, which occurred at 7:34 a.m. local time (8:34 a.m. ET), was felt across much of Colombia, triggering evacuations and reports of damage.

Venezuela was hit by devastating twin earthquakes in June, which killed more than 6,000 people, mostly on the coast near the capital, Caracas.

title: All-powerful Trump tells America, ‘Nothing bad can happen’
description: Trump signed an executive order aimed at reducing the number of childhood vaccines.
fullText:
Just one of the wild actions and comments on Donald Trump's manic Monday would rank among the most notorious things another president ever did.

Often, the round-the-clock cacophony from the White House seems expressly designed to stifle public comprehension of each individual act planned to irrevocably change the country and the world.

This was certainly the case on a day that fulfilled some core goals of the Trump base but also helped to explain the plunging presidential approval ratings that have Republicans looking with dread toward the midterm elections.

It all started when one of the president's former personal lawyers, now Appeals Court Judge Emil Bove, swore in another of the president's former personal lawyers, Todd Blanche, as attorney general.

This was peak Trump. Nine years after the president asked James Comey for loyalty — as the fired former FBI chief told it — one of his ultimate loyalists was on Monday installed in a Senate-confirmed position at the pinnacle of US justice.

Blanche was with Trump in some of his darkest moments as he faced multiple criminal and civil charges before winning back the White House. Some Trump subordinates, like former Attorney General Pam Bondi, stumbled when striving to prove their loyalty. But Blanche has already demonstrated fealty — one reason his critics fear him and wonder whether he'll act a spiritual successor to Trump's McCarthyite lawyer Roy Cohn.

As Blanche was clapped by staff back into his agency, more of the president's men gathered by the Resolute Desk. He was about to act on a feeling he's harbored even longer than his quest to make the DOJ his boutique law firm.

Trump then signed an executive order aimed at reducing the number of childhood vaccines. And he administered a fresh dose of unscientific falsehoods, baselessly claiming vaccines cause autism and that little children had had inoculations the size of soda bottles poured into their bodies. At one point, he suggested that the measles, mumps and rubella vaccine could be "quite lethal" — amid a year when the US has recorded the most measles cases in more than a quarter-century. It was hard not to get flashbacks to his erratic Covid-19 pandemic news conferences.

But America's most powerful public health official and vaccine skeptic, Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., insisted: "This is what gold-standard science means."

Trump confirmed he'd recently spoken to new Federal Reserve Chair Kevin Warsh, but denied a Wall Street Journal report they'd had multiple conversations. The president has left no doubt he wants Warsh to lower interest rates. "If it was up to him, it would be different, but he has a board," Trump said, raising doubts about the central bank's independence.

The president also weighed in on the triumph of progressive and democratic socialist candidates in Democratic primaries ahead of the midterm elections: "We have jihadists being elected all over the place."

The president's latest inflammatory comment about Muslim candidates appears to herald a viciously negative fall campaign. He didn't specify who he was talking about, but his remark came a week after Abdul El-Sayed won the Michigan Democratic Senate primary.

When he turned to Iran, the president showed how the once-intricate US foreign policy process has ceded to the wish-casting of the commander in chief who declared a war won after a few days that is now in its sixth month. And he claimed the Strait of Hormuz, an oil exporting choke point effectively controlled by Iran, is "opened now." The Windward Maritime Intelligence Operations Center said Monday that only seven vessels had crossed the strait in the previous 24 hours. Before the war, the waterway often saw more than 100 ships a day.

Each of these examples show how Trump has degraded the institutions of US government and purged them of experts, bureaucrats and officials who don't share his idiosyncratic worldview.

Many Trump supporters argue that he's making good on his vow to dismantle a corrupt administrative state that has long thwarted conservative presidents. Others promote the idea of an all-powerful presidency and 

In some ways, the maelstrom of business across the Oval Office desk Monday mirrors the deeply centralized decision-making process developed for years by the future president at the Trump Organization, where he was the sole source of authority. But Trump's critics see his hands-on style as the behavior of a wannabe authoritarian and argue his hunch-driven style of leadership is a recipe for disaster.

It's hard to make a case that Trump's approach is working for anyone outside his most loyal support base, despite his claim in an interview with Punchbowl News last week that "a lot of people are saying I'm one of the greatest presidents ever."

In a recent CNN/SSRS poll, only 21% of Americans said Trump's military action in Iran had helped the US. Many analysts believe he's led the US into a stalemate against a much weaker nation.

His crusade to dominate the Justice Department is one of the personal fixations — along with his monument-building program — that help explain why a record-high 73% of US adults said in that same CNN survey that he hasn't paid enough attention to the country's most important problems.

And according to polling from the health policy nonprofit KFF, an 81% majority of US adults say they are confident that MMR vaccines are safe for children. A small sector of Trump's base, however, has long bought into the anti-vaccine movement.

Some of the institutionalists who Trump disdains warned on Monday evening that his increasingly unchecked presidency is dangerous.

"It is simply astonishing that this administration would continue to respond to ongoing measles outbreaks and the return of other vaccine-preventable diseases by playing politics with children's lives," said Dr. Richard Besser, president and CEO of the Robert Wood Johnson Foundation and former acting director of the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention.

David Axelrod, who served as a counselor to Barack Obama, told CNN's Erin Burnett that a president's words "can send armies marching and markets tumbling." But they can "also jeopardize people's health because the president has enormous sway. … It's really, really dangerous."

But Trump is beyond listening. Explaining his vaccine policy, he seemed both to encapsulate his attitude to unchecked power and to tempt fate.

"Nothing bad can happen from what we're doing," he said. "Nothing bad can happen."

title: US missile strike reportedly hits container ship off Pakistan
description: A U.S. helicopter reportedly fired a missile at a Panama-flagged ship's rudder after it attempted to evade a blockade.
fullText:
(NewsNation) —  Three crew members were killed in a suspected attack by Iran-backed Houthis on a cargo ship in the Bab el-Mandeb Strait Tuesday, while a container ship was hit by a missile off Pakistan in a suspected U.S. attack, Reuters reports.

The deaths aboard the Egyptian-owned Tihamah, if confirmed, would be the first deaths in a Houthi strike on shipping since the Iran war began on Feb. 28. Yemeni sources told Reuters two Pakistani crew members and one Indonesian crew member were killed.

The Houthis have not claimed responsibility for the attack.

According to the sources, the crew lost control of the ship after an unknown projectile hit it and was later approached by Yemeni coast guards.

Yemeni forces then came under fire, according to U.K. maritime risk management group Vanguard.

The incident occurred while the ship was at anchor northeast of Perim Island, Yemen, British maritime security group Ambrey told Reuters.

The Panama-flagged container ship Vela Nova was reportedly struck by a missile off Pakistan while sailing toward the Gulf of Oman.

The Wall Street Journal reported a U.S. helicopter fired a Hellfire missile at the ship's rudder after it allegedly attempted to evade a U.S. blockade targeting Iran-linked shipping. U.S. Central Command has not immediately commented.

If confirmed, it would be the 12th vessel attacked by U.S. forces since the blockade was announced in April and the third since it was reimposed July 14.

Shipping through the Bab el-Mandeb Strait and Red Sea has dropped more than 50% since an earlier wave of Houthi attacks began in 2023, according to Reuters.

Traffic has fallen further since the Houthis announced a maritime blockade last month, with an average of 32 ships per day passing through the strait last week, compared with about 50 before the blockade.

Traffic through the Strait of Hormuz has also sharply declined. Only six vessels passed through Monday, compared with a 10-day average of about 11 and prewar levels of roughly 130 to 140 ships per day.

The U.S. and Iran are both facing economic challenges tied to the conflict over the Strait of Hormuz.

On Iran's side of the ledger, the U.S. naval blockade is severely limiting Tehran's ability to sell oil on the global market. Its currency is collapsing, much of its industrial capacity has been damaged or destroyed, and inflation is reportedly nearly 88%.

President Donald Trump believes squeezing Iran's economy through sanctions and the naval blockade could ultimately bring the regime back to the negotiating table.

"They're broke. They have no money," Trump told reporters. "You know, Iran is broke, totally broke. And, they're not paying their soldiers. They have inflation of 300%."

The U.S. economy is faring far better than Iran's. However, American consumers are still feeling the effects of the conflict, especially at the gas pump, the grocery aisles and in the job market.

Wage growth is now outpacing inflation, reversing the trend seen in April and May. However, food and energy prices remain elevated.

Inflation is currently running at about 3.5% — still above the Federal Reserve's 2% target. Gas prices are up roughly 13 cents from last month and nearly a dollar from a year ago.

The White House has dubbed its campaign against Iran "Operation Economic Fury." Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent called this component the "financial equivalent" of a bombing campaign as the countries that buy oil from Iran or bank with it could be sanctioned.

The administration has threatened sanctions against countires that buy Iranian oil or do business with its banks. But experts say sanctions could take longer to have an impact than the disruption caused by the largely closed Strait of Hormuz.

Richard Nephew, a former Obama administration Iran sanctions official, told the Associated Press the strategy is also weakened by the Trump administration's shifting goals, which have included preventing Iran from obtaining a nuclear weapon and addressing the Strait of Hormuz.

Still, former Bush administration official Juan Zarate told the Associated Press sanctions and the U.S. naval blockade give Washington significant economic leverage.

title: New transmission from animals likely caused Congo-Uganda Ebola outbreak, study says
description: The ongoing Ebola outbreak in Democratic Republic of Congo concerns a previously unseen variant of the rare Bundibugyo species of the virus, indicating it stemmed from a new
fullText:
DAKAR, Aug 11 (Reuters) - The ongoing Ebola outbreak in Democratic Republic of Congo concerns a previously unseen ‌variant of the rare Bundibugyo species of the virus, ‌indicating it stemmed from a new transmission from animals to humans rather ​than from variants linked to earlier outbreaks, a new study said.

• Researchers from Congo, Uganda, Belgium and other countries analysed the genetic make-up of virus samples from 22 patients in Congo ‌and Uganda and ⁠found the outbreak strain was genetically distinct from previous Bundibugyo Ebola viruses seen in outbreaks in ⁠2007 and 2012.

• The findings, published on Monday in the journal Nature Medicine, suggest the outbreak began with a fresh animal-to-human ​transmission ​event and was then spread ​between people.

• The study did ‌not identify the animal source of the outbreak, but Ebola viruses are known to spill over periodically from infected animals to humans.

• The genetic analysis helped confirm that cases detected in Uganda were linked to the outbreak in Congo.

• ‌The study's authors said wider access ​to testing and virus sequencing could ​help detect future Ebola ​outbreaks earlier and improve efforts to contain ‌them.

• There is no approved vaccine ​or treatment ​for Bundibugyo, although candidate vaccines and treatments are under development.

• The outbreak was declared on May 15 and has ​surpassed 2,000 deaths, ‌with 4,381 confirmed cases so far, according to ​the latest government data.

title: Spotify to distinguish AI artists from real people – and stop recommending them
description:
Music streaming platform creates ‘AI persona’ label that will appear on profiles and track listings in crackdown on fake performers
Spotify is to label AI artists and exclude them from algorithm recommendations as part of a crackdown on fake performers.
The world’s largest music streaming platform is creating a label for AI-generated artist identities called “AI personas” that will appear on the artist profile and on track listings on playlists.
 Continue reading...
fullText:
Music streaming platform creates ‘AI persona’ label that will appear on profiles and track listings in crackdown on fake performers

Spotify is to label AI artists and exclude them from algorithm recommendations as part of a crackdown on fake performers.

The world’s largest music streaming platform is creating a label for AI-generated artist identities called “AI personas” that will appear on the artist profile and on track listings on playlists.

It means that from September AI-generated artists such as the Velvet Sundown will carry the persona label and will be blocked from personalised recommendations by default. The aim is to differentiate these deepfake artists from real performers who might lose out on streams to artificial rivals.

Spotify said: “True artist-fan connection can only be built on a foundation of trust and authenticity. In music, that means listeners need to be able to trust that the artist behind the music is who they say they are. That’s more essential than ever in the age of generative AI.”

Last year Spotify revealed it had removed 75m spam tracks from its platform over a 12-month period as AI tools created a flood of fake music. Spotify’s legitimate catalogue stands at 100m tracks.

Spotify will allow music creators to reveal if their identities are AI-created – and will then label them as an AI persona – but it will not rely on self-disclosure alone. The company said it would use human review and AI investigative tools to determine if artists were fake. Although the new rule technically applies to AI “identities”, Spotify says AI-generated profiles are invariably a front for AI-made tracks as well.

The company said: “Listeners have been clear in telling us that they don’t like seeing an artist profile that seems human, only to find out that the persona is AI-generated.”

Last year there was debate about the origins of the Velvet Sundown – a 70s-style US rock band – before the band’s social media channels confirmed the subterfuge. A statement described the group as an AI creation that was “somewhere in between” human and machine.

The Velvet Sundown has 117,000 monthly listeners on Spotify but its page has no clear AI labelling, although the artist profile describes the four-piece as a “synthetic music project”.

In January there was further discussion about Sienna Rose, a soul singer who entered Spotify’s viral top 50 but did not appear to be real, having never played a gig or released any videos despite releasing a prolific burst of material over a 10-week period. The Spotify profile for Rose, who has more than half a million monthly listeners, does not clarify whether she is AI or not.

title: Meta faces expensive child safety reckoning
description:
Also: Google executives jump ship in race for AI dominance
Hello, TechScape readers! Danielle Abril, editor of the Guardian’s Reworked series on AI and the future of work, filling in for Blake Montgomery this week. Major legal battles against Meta over child safety are playing out in courts across the US – and the tech giant is losing. Recent rulings raise big questions about social media companies’ responsibility to their youngest users. Meanwhile, more key executives have jumped ship from Google as it battles OpenAI and Anthropic in the race for AI dominance, and Meta’s smartglasses face a fearsome backlash.
fullText:
Also: Google executives jump ship in race for AI dominance

Hello, TechScape readers! Danielle Abril, editor of the Guardian’s Reworked series on AI and the future of work, filling in for Blake Montgomery this week. Major legal battles against Meta over child safety are playing out in courts across the US – and the tech giant is losing. Recent rulings raise big questions about social media companies’ responsibility to their youngest users. Meanwhile, more key executives have jumped ship from Google as it battles OpenAI and Anthropic in the race for AI dominance, and Meta’s smartglasses face a fearsome backlash. Let’s dig in!

The pressure on social media giants including Meta is mounting, as courts work through a growing pile of cases and deliver devastating, expensive rulings, one after another. Meta’s repeated losses underscore how serious the child safety crisis has become for social media companies and may force them to change how they operate to avoid further costly legal exposure.

The latest blow came last week, after a New Mexico court hit Meta with an order to pay $567m into a teen mental health fund to remediate the harm its platforms have caused children. The penalty adds to the $375m fine already on the court’s books after a jury determined in March that Meta negligently permitted damage to children’s mental health and hid what it knew about child sexual exploitation on its platforms. In a Los Angeles court, also in March, Meta was held liable for $4.2m in damages for designing platforms that addict and hurt children. The California case paved the way for hundreds of plaintiffs who have filed similar cases, which could cost Meta billions and force major changes to its products.

But New Mexico is just the latest of many headaches in store for social media companies including Meta. The company is facing 42 lawsuits filed by states across the US, plus thousands more, along with YouTube, TikTok and Snap, brought by state attorneys general, school districts and individual families.

At the center of the battle is the growing concern that social media companies harm its youngest users with addictive features that propel issues such as depression, anxiety and suicidal thoughts. The plaintiffs’ goal is to hold companies accountable and enjoin them to change their products – everything from stricter age verification to usage limits and safety banners promoting protection features.

“This is a cautionary tale of hubris,” said Karen North, a professor at University of Southern California who studies social media. Tech companies “seemed to believe they had safe harbor, and this wasn’t their problem”.

Government-ordered remedies are a partial fix at best. For example, the New Mexico court ordered Meta to improve its age verification tools, which use artificial intelligence to analyze signals such as the ages of users’ friends and the content users post and consume. It also asked Meta to develop a prediction model that could determine if users were under the age of 13. These measures will probably flag more underage users for better protection.

But broadly, AI has a track record of misprofiling people, which will probably leave some underage users undetected. Meanwhile, inadequate age verification checks have left Australia’s ban on social media for children under 16 largely ineffective, according to recent research. Only a small percentage of those surveyed were required to provide official ID, and a significant portion said they bypassed the restrictions by using a fake account or a VPN.

Meanwhile, tech companies are already skirting some trials through private settlements. Last week, TikTok settled three lawsuits from young people over claims its app harmed their mental health. Last month, a lawsuit filed against Meta in Los Angeles was dropped after the plaintiff settled with YouTube, TikTok and Snap. In June, companies reached a settlement with a Kentucky school district that sued over platforms’ addictive designs that caused harm.

Children’s safety on social media is no longer a peripheral issue for tech giants. It’s a growing risk to companies’ bottom lines. And the outcome of a federal case against Meta, brought by attorneys general from 29 states set for trial later this month in Oakland, California, could set the tone (and price) for the thousands of cases ahead.

But, as North says, child safety is probably the tip of the iceberg. “At what point do they decide you don’t have to be a child to be harmed?” It starts with “young people and then vulnerable people and then all people”.

Google’s AI division is facing an internal leadership shuffle amid a heated external talent war, as frontier labs race to build the most capable large language models and capture the biggest market share.

News broke last week that Google’s DeepMind CEO, Demis Hassabis, is stepping down from day-to-day leadership of the famed AI unit. He will serve as the chair of DeepMind, chief scientist for Google parent Alphabet, and continue as the CEO of Isomorphic Labs, the drug discovery company that spun off from Google. Meanwhile, Google’s current chief scientist, Jeff Dean, a 27-year veteran, and three colleagues are leaving to launch Discovery Loop, a startup the tech giant is backing. The news caused the company’s stock to drop 4%, and it had yet to rebound as of this newsletter.

The executive shake-up follows the exits of other key leaders, several of whom have jumped to competitors in the last year, and reports of poor morale and delayed releases – Gemini 3.5 Pro is months late and counting. With executives exiting and releases delayed, the pressure to keep pace is only mounting, especially as Google continues to trail OpenAI in the AI race.

ChatGPT is still decidedly in the lead, with 1.11 billion monthly users as of May, according to data from the market intelligence firm Sensor Tower. While Gemini has steadily started to close that gap, with help from a strong Android user base and integrations across Google’s ecosystem, it lags behind with 662 million monthly users in the same month. Claude, meanwhile, has seen a spike in growth this year but trails both at 245 million monthly users, though Anthropic has captured more business customers and higher margins than OpenAI by focusing its bot on coding and technical tasks.

Still, while Google’s exits may be among the most senior and seemingly consequential, they’re part of a broader turnover happening across AI labs as competition for a minuscule pool of top talent intensifies. Which labs can hold on to those major players will shape who leads the AI race in the future.

title: When MAGA met FIFA: Inside Trump’s cosy relationship with Gianni Infantino
description: President Trump has given his full backing to embattled Infantino as the FIFA president faces ongoing pressure to step down
fullText:
President Donald Trump has thrown his weight behind embattled FIFA President Gianni Infantino as the football chief faces ongoing pressure to resign.

The U.S. president warned FIFA that it would be a "terrible mistake" to even consider ousting Infantino, amid widespread backlash over the latter's plan to sell off stakes in the World Cup and other competitions.

"He is fantastic, having just presided over the most successful World Cup, by four times, ever presented," Trump wrote on Truth Social. "If he is gone, it will never be as successful or profitable again!"​

Swiss-born Infantino has been criticized by a slew of organizations and world leaders, including UEFA, Europe's football governing body, Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney and British Prime Minister Andy Burnham.

Below we look at the history of Infantino and Trump's relationship as the pair continue to support each other on the world's stage.

Trump and Infantino's relationship can be traced back to 2018, two years after both he and Infantino won their first presidencies.

The commander-in-chief hosted the FIFA president at the White House after the U.S. won the right to co-host the World Cup.

During the meeting, Infantino handed Trump red and yellow penalty cards and joked that the commander-in-chief could use them against the press.

The pair later met again in Davos in 2020, where they dined together.

Infantino was invited by Trump to the White House that same year for the signing of the Abraham Accords, which normalized relations between several Middle Eastern countries and Israel.

Trump and Infantino appeared to grow closer during Trump's second term as the 2026 World Cup drew nearer.

Ahead of the world's biggest football tournament, Trump was handed the inaugural FIFA Peace Prize by Infantino in December 2025.

​In a press release detailing the award, FIFA credited Trump for his "pivotal role" in promoting peace between Israel and Palestine.

​The award was handed to Trump just months after Venezuelan activist María Corina Machado won the 2025 Nobel Peace Prize, despite the U.S. president insisting that he was deserving of the accolade.

Earlier this year, Infantino attended a meeting of Trump's Board of Peace and confirmed that FIFA would build an academy and a 20,000-seat stadium in Gaza.

"We don't have to just rebuild houses or schools or hospitals or roads," Infantino said at the event. "We also have to rebuild and build people, emotion, hope and trust. And this is what football, my sport, is about."

Once the world's biggest football tournament began, Infantino and Trump became embroiled in a slew of controversial moments.

During the contest Trump confirmed he had called Infantino personally after U.S. player Folarin Balogun was handed a red card during a match against Bosnia and Herzegovina.

"I said, 'Gianni, I'd like to make a recommendation: Let the guy in the game,'" Trump said, recalling the phone call. "No, I didn't say that. I said I'd like to wage a complaint. And actually…I had no idea what was gonna happen."

Balogun was eventually allowed to play with the U.S. team in a match against Belgium, which ended in a victory for the latter country.

In a statement, Infantino said that the decision to allow Balogun to play was taken by the FIFA Disciplinary Committee and that all of FIFA's judicial bodies are "independent."​

Infantino also said that he explained to Trump that "there was an ongoing legal process involving FIFA's independent judicial bodies and that the case would be decided in due course by the competent bodies."​

When the tournament came to a close, Infantino was seen ushering Trump off stage when he awkwardly lingered on stage following Spain's victory over Argentina in the final.

A White House insider told The New York Post in July that Trump wanted Infantino to become the United Nations' next secretary general.

The insider claimed that Trump believes Infantino is "respected by everyone around the world" and that he has a "special ability to bring people together."

After the 2026 tournament eneded, Infantino came under fire over a plan to create a $20 billion subsidiary to run the World Cup and other events, with 20 percent of the subsidiary's shares being offered up to investors.

The plan was dropped after it drew anger and widespread international criticism.

In a scathing open letter, UEFA, CONCACAF and the Asian Football Confederation called for an independent review into Infantino's plan, which they described as a "profound failure of judgement."

Some countries, including Mexico, Morocco and Argentina, have backed Infantino.

In a statement, FIFA claimed that there were attempts to "undermine" Infantino, who is seeking re-election in March next year.

description: The Ohio State Buckeyes have an impressive crop of five former U-18 National Team stars joining their roster for 2026-27, a group that will keep the Buckeyes' women's hockey team in contention for a national title.
fullText:
Ohio State's incoming class of recruits for the 2026-27 season have one thing in common: they've all starred for their U-18 national teams.

It includes Team Canada captain Hayley McDonald, and Slovakian senior national team standout Ema Tothova. Ohio State has added more international talent recently with a strong pipeline through Sweden, and they'll get an influx of those players again in 2027-28 in Ebba Westerlind and Tilde Sundnas Grillfors.

After falling to Wisconsin in back-to-back national championship games, the Ohio State Buckeyes are looking to get back on top this year, and with the core of young returnees like Hilda Svensson, Maxine Cimoroni, Sanni Vanhanen, Joy Dunne, Mira Jungaker, Jenna Raunio, and Jocelyn Amos, coupled with their newcomers, Ohio State will again be a contender.

She's won gold and silver as a member of Canada's U-18 national team and this year captained Canada at the U-18 World Championships scoring nine points in six games. A power forward coming out of RINK Academy, McDonald will bring her heavy game and rounded attack to the Buckeyes. Expect her to contibute immediately similar to the impact Maxine Cimeroni had last year.

At 5-foot-10, Tothova has size, but bounced between leagues in two different countries at various levels. She dominated playing for Bratislava in the EWHL, and had a good stint with HV71 facing some tough competition in the SDHL. Moving to Ohio State next season will be good for Tothova, whose upside is immense. She had six points in five games at the Division 1A World Championships for Slovakia, her fourth World Championship appearance.

A top four defender for Canada's U-18 national team, Viel is a two-way defender who can play a heavy game. She is most valuable in her own zone as a shutdown, physical blueliner, but is capable offensively, and makes good decisions at the offensive blueline. Her game grew in three seasons in the OWHL, including this season on a strong Nepean Wildcats team. Future pro in the making.

The Saskatoon product has good offensive instincts. She is a two-time member of Canada's U-19 national team, and this year served as an alternate captain, producing nine points in six games for Canada. She played alongside McDonald at RINK Academy scoring 26 goals and 48 points in 26 games this season. Korte projects as a top six forward for Ohio State in short order.

Houweling put up incredible numbers for Shattuck St. Mary's this season posting a 0.98 GAA and .940 save percentage along with 10 shutouts in 25 appearances, and posted a pair of shutouts for Canada at the U-18 World Championships in her only two appearances. Houweling was also Alberta's starter at the Canadian U-18 national championships. With Ohio State's past three starting goalies — Amanda Thiele, Raygan Kirk, and Hailey MacLeod — now in the PWHL, the door is wide open for a goaltending battle at Ohio State with Houweling having the opportunity to challenge for starts sooner than later.

title: Royce White predicts the outcome of his WNBA bid after speaking to his legal team
description: Royce White is not done yet, as he continues to fight for a place to play in the WNBA next season. Former NBA first-round draft pick Royce White has largely pivoted away from basketball and into far-right politics, running as a Republican candidate in Minnesota.
fullText:
Royce White is not done yet, as he continues to fight for a place to play in the WNBA next season.

Former NBA first-round draft pick Royce White has largely pivoted away from basketball and into far-right politics, running as a Republican candidate in Minnesota.

Recently, he sparked intense controversy by announcing plans to declare for the 2027 WNBA Draft. White claims to meet self-identification standards and argues that current collective bargaining rules allow his entry, intending to test the league's eligibility policies regarding transgender athletes.

He has warned that any attempt to block his participation will spark a massive court fight, while the league and players' union have largely dismissed the move as a publicity stunt.

Speaking to Scoop B, Royce White plans to go all the way in his bid to land a place in the WNBA, with a 'huge legal battle' the expected outcome in all of this.

"I saw that the WNBA commissioner made a comment today. So, that's to be expected. They're the masters of spin and PR, aren't they? I've been through this before with the NBA, but my legal team is looking into every avenue.

"I think it's going to end up being a huge legal battle, to be honest, and probably a necessary one. But I don't really see what the big deal would be.

"I think the league would get much better, and certainly I'm the prospective number one pick, right?"

This isn't the first time White has threatened legal action against a major sports organization. His brief NBA career derailed primarily over battles with the league regarding mental health accommodations for his severe anxiety and fear of flying.

Now, White is positioning his potential lawsuit as an ideological crusade rather than a sports dispute.

title: Palace co-owner spoke to McNeil's partner before move
description: Crystal Palace co-owner and chairman Steve Parish contacts Dwight McNeil's partner before the midfielder's move to the club.
fullText:
Crystal Palace co-owner and chairman Steve Parish contacted Dwight McNeil's partner before the midfielder's move to the club on Tuesday.

McNeil has completed a move to Palace and signed a four-year contract in a swap deal that involved Brennan Johnson moving to Everton.

McNeil, 26, nearly moved to Selhurst Park in the January transfer window when Palace agreed a loan-to-buy deal.

That deal would have turned into a £20m permanent move, only for the transfer to fall through when the required paperwork could not be completed in time, even though McNeil had already passed a medical.

After the deal fell through, McNeil's partner Megan Sharpley was critical of Palace, writing on Instagram: "We live in a world where everyone is aware of how big a problem mental health is.

"So, in football, why do we find it acceptable because these young men are on a lot of money and that's OK to mess and toy with their mental health and that it's just part of the job?

"To have something promised to you, to have been dragged along on an emotional rollercoaster and to be toyed with until the final minute. For that to be torn away from you at the last second with absolutely no explanation has hurt more than I can say."

BBC Sport understands that Parish reached out to smooth things over before this week's deal was completed.

McNeil joined Everton from Burnley for £20m in July 2022 and scored 15 goals in 128 games for the Toffees.

Palace have won the FA Cup, Community Shield and Uefa Conference League in the last two seasons.

"The lads have had some great success over the last two seasons. It's something that I want to be a part of, so I'm really looking forward to getting started," McNeil said.

Parish said McNeil is "a player with proven ability in the Premier League".

Johnson signed for Palace in a £35m deal in January but struggled to find form and made 26 appearances in all competitions without scoring.

The Wales winger joined Tottenham Hotspur from Nottingham Forest for a fee in excess of £45m in 2023 and scored their winning goal in the Europa League final last May before moving to the Eagles.

title: REPORT: Inter Milan, Spurs in talks over Djed Spence sale
description: The Djedetentiary might be moving to Italy.
fullText:
Well, we kinda thought this might be coming. Numerous reporters and transfer mongers, including Fabrizio Romano (sigh) are now reporting that Inter Milan and Tottenham Hotspur are in negotiations for the potential sale of Djed Spence. Romano is reporting that Spence is keen on a move to Italy, and other reports a potential sale of around €40m (£34.5m).

It feels weird to consider selling a World Cup bronze medalist who was, honestly, one of the most impressive players on that World Cup squad, but here we are. I was listening to the Game is About Glory podcast this morning and one of the hosts made the suggestion that Roberto De Zerbi might think that Spence, while an excellent defender, might be a little too dribbly a fullback for RDZ's tactics, which rely on short, quick passing to progress the ball up the field.

That could very well be the case but selling Spence means Tottenham have a fullback corps of Destiny Udogie, Souza, Pedro Porro, and… various other players playing out of position, like Micky van de Ven and Archie Gray. Selling a fullback who can provide relief on both sides of the pitch feels weird, but then again, Spurs will only rarely play more than one match a week, and Djed is clearly looking for a starting role somewhere. I don't know if he gets that here unless Udogie or Porro are injured or out of action for a significant amount of time.

There's no deal in place yet and we know Inter are going to try and cheap out on the transfer fee. They actually do have some money, but not a ton of it and they have conflicting priorities this summer, so it'll be interesting to see whether a deal can be made. But Spence seems to want this, and if we can get a decent price for him it'll be sad but quite possibly the correct decision. We'll see.

title: Celtics-Heat Rivalry Lands Coveted NBA Christmas Day Stage
description: The Boston Celtics and Miami Heat will renew one of the Eastern Conference’s fiercest rivalries as part of the NBA’s loaded Christmas Day schedule.
fullText:
Celtics-Heat Rivalry Lands Coveted NBA Christmas Day Stage originally appeared on NESN. 

The NBA is giving the Boston Celtics a familiar opponent for one of the biggest games of the regular season. Boston will face the Miami Heat on Christmas Day as part of a five-game showcase on ABC and ESPN, the league officially announced Monday.

The complete schedule also includes the San Antonio Spurs against the New York Knicks, the Philadelphia 76ers against the Los Angeles Lakers, the Oklahoma City Thunder against the Minnesota Timberwolves and the Denver Nuggets against the Golden State Warriors.

Every matchup offers considerable star power, but Celtics-Heat carries something the others cannot manufacture: years of genuine animosity and postseason history.

Boston and Miami have repeatedly collided with championships at stake. Their latest meeting will arrive on one of the NBA's grandest stages, giving the Celtics another national opportunity to display their reshaped roster.

Christmas dinner may have to wait in New England.

Few Eastern Conference matchups have carried more weight over the past 15 years. The Celtics and Heat met in the playoffs six times between 2010 and 2024, including four appearances in the Eastern Conference finals. Miami won the conference finals meetings in 2012, 2020 and 2023, while Boston broke through in 2022.

OFFICIAL: Christmas Day Schedule 🚨

Spurs vs. Knicks
Heat vs. Celtics
76ers vs. Lakers
Thunder vs. Timberwolves
Nuggets vs. Warriors

Watch the NBA on Christmas Day on ABC & ESPN!

The rivalry added another chapter during the first round of the 2024 playoffs. Miami stunned Boston by making a franchise playoff-record 23 3-pointers in Game 2, but the Celtics responded by winning the next three games and eliminating the Heat in five. Boston went on to capture its record-setting 18th NBA championship.

The personnel surrounding the rivalry has changed over time, but the intensity has remained. Miami has consistently embraced the challenge of facing Boston, while the Celtics know better than to overlook an organization that has repeatedly caused them postseason frustration.

That history should give the Christmas Day meeting a playoff-like edge even though it will arrive relatively early in the season. Neither team will need additional motivation.

The Christmas matchup also gives the NBA another opportunity to feature Boston's new star combination. Jayson Tatum and Paul George will enter the season as the leading faces of a reworked Celtics roster. George's arrival gives Boston another experienced wing capable of scoring from multiple levels, creating his own shot and defending several positions.

Their partnership will receive national attention immediately. Boston already is scheduled to open the season Oct. 20 against Cade Cunningham and the Detroit Pistons on NBC and Peacock. Adding a Christmas Day meeting with Miami reinforces the league's belief that the Celtics remain one of its biggest attractions.

The game also could offer a valuable measuring stick. By late December, Tatum and George should have enough time together to move beyond the adjustment stage. The Celtics' offensive roles, closing lineup and defensive identity should be clearer than they will be on opening night.

Miami will be eager to test all of it.

The Heat have built their reputation on toughness, defensive discipline and an ability to make favored opponents uncomfortable. Those traits have made them particularly dangerous against Boston, regardless of each team's regular-season record.

A Christmas win would not settle any postseason questions, but it could provide an early psychological advantage if the rivals meet again when the stakes are even higher.

MORE: Celtics Handed Immediate Test In NBA Season Opener

Celtics-Heat is only one piece of an impressive holiday lineup.

Victor Wembanyama and the Spurs will face the defending champion Knicks. LeBron James and the 76ers will meet the Lakers, creating one of the day's most fascinating individual storylines.

The Thunder and Timberwolves will provide a matchup between Western Conference contenders before Nikola Jokic and the Nuggets face Stephen Curry and the Warriors.

All five games will air across ABC and ESPN.

Boston's inclusion is hardly surprising. The Celtics have become a Christmas Day fixture because of their enormous fan base, championship history and consistent place among the NBA's most prominent contenders.

The opponent makes this appearance feel different.

Miami is not just another team on Boston's schedule. The Heat are responsible for some of the Celtics' most painful playoff exits, while Boston has delivered its share of disappointment in return.

The rivalry has survived changing rosters, different coaches and shifting expectations. It now gets another national showcase with families across the country watching.

For the Celtics, Christmas Day will bring an opportunity to make another statement about their championship ambitions. For the Heat, it will offer a chance to disrupt Boston's holiday and remind the Eastern Conference that this rivalry remains as dangerous as ever.

The presents can be opened in the morning. By the time the Celtics and Heat take the floor, no gifts should be expected.

title: MotoGP to hold 2027 season launch event in Brazil
description: Rio de Janeiro has secured the rights to host MotoGP’s 2027 season launch event, a year after Brazil returned to the championship’s calendar
fullText:
MotoGP's new 850cc era will kick off with a special season-launch event at Rio de Janeiro on 21 February 2027.

As reported by Motorsport.com last month, the entire MotoGP grid will travel to Brazil at the start of next year to mark the launch of the new season.

The main event will take place at Botafogo Beach, with the famous Sugarloaf Mountain serving as the backdrop

The launch will precede the opening round of the 2027 campaign, which will take place on 5-7 March at the Buriram International Circuit in Thailand.

Carmelo Ezpeleta, CEO of MotoGP Group, said: "The MotoGP Season Launch has become one of the defining moments of the year for our championship, bringing together every team, rider and manufacturer as we begin a new season.

"The enthusiasm shown by Brazilian fans during our sold-out return to Goiania in 2026 confirmed the extraordinary connection between MotoGP and Brazil.

"Following the success of our recent season launch events in Bangkok and Kuala Lumpur, Rio de Janeiro provides the perfect stage to continue raising the bar, combining iconic locations, passionate fans and world-class entertainment.

"We look forward to delivering our biggest and most spectacular MotoGP Season Launch yet."

Following in the footsteps of Formula 1, with which it now shares an ownership structure, MotoGP hosted a special fan-focused season launch on the streets of Bangkok in 2025.

The inaugural event was a success, convincing Dorna (now MotoGP Sports Entertainment Group) to turn it into an annual fixture.

A second season-launch showcase was held in Kuala Lumpur at the beginning of this year, with riders performing wheelies and stoppies in a closed-off stretch of road in front of thousands of fans.

For 2027, MotoGP is placing even greater emphasis on its season launch event, with the year marking the introduction of new 850cc machines. The bikes will feature reduced aerodynamic influence and no ride-height devices as part of a major overhaul of the technical regulations.

Miami had initially emerged as the venue of choice, before MotoGP zeroed in on Brazil. The South American nation returned on the calendar in March this year, with Goiania hosting the first Brazilian GP in two decades.

title: La Liga club send clear message to Barcelona over defensive target: ‘We were offered €14 million and we said no’
description: Barcelona have been linked with a move for Racing Santander defender Jorge Salinas since the start of the summer transfer window.The Spanish teenager saw his stock rise with his performances for his n...
fullText:
Barcelona have been linked with a move for Racing Santander defender Jorge Salinas since the start of the summer transfer window.

The Spanish teenager saw his stock rise with his performances for his nation at the Under-19 Euros, and more clubs have joined the race for him.

Barça and Racing had a disagreement on the value of the release clause in Salinas' contract before July, with the Catalan club not moving forward since.

The versatile defender remains on the Blaugrana's radar, but the gap between the two clubs has become increasingly difficult to bridge as Racing hold firm on the player's €16 million release clause.

As quoted by SPORT, Racing sporting director Chema Aragon revealed that the club have already turned down an offer worth €14 million for Salinas.

"We have already been offered €14 million and we said no," Aragon said.

Barcelona remain keen on Jorge Salinas. (Picture credit: Instagram/@jorgesaliiinas)

While Aragon stopped short of confirming which club made that bid, the message was very clear from the Racing director.

Aragon reiterated that Racing's position has not changed.

"If someone comes, brings the €16 million and the player likes the club, he will leave," he explained.

Barcelona have been following Salinas since June and are understood to have an agreement with the player over personal terms.

Their initial proposal consisted of €6 million fixed, another €2 million in variables and the possibility of including a player on loan.

That was never enough to convince Racing. The Cantabrian club also have no intention of lowering the price by accepting players as part of the deal.

"It could be that we are interested in a player, but one thing will have nothing to do with the other. We are not going to mix the two operations," Aragon said.

Salinas has a €16 million release clause. (Picture credit: Instagram/@jorgesaliiinas)

Perhaps most importantly for Barcelona, Racing are warning that the price will not fall as deadline day approaches.

"Today he is only sold for €16 million. Tomorrow, if we can, for €16.1 million. The closer we get to the end of the market, the more demanding we will be," Aragon added.

It is clear that Racing see exactly how special a player they have in their ranks and want to extract every possible penny from his sale.

For Barcelona, meanwhile, spending such a significant amount on a relatively unproven defender might not be a feasible option this summer.

Although the Catalan club are keen on signing the 19-year-old, it is unlikely to happen this summer unless the newly promoted club change their tune.

If not, Barça should let Salinas stay at his current club and keep track of how he progresses through the course of the season.
