title: Opinion - ‘But Biden’ excuses are just admissions Trump has failed
description: An opinion piece argues that Donald Trump has failed to deliver on his promises during his second term and criticizes supporters who continue to blame previous administrations like Joe Biden and Barac...
fullText:
We have all had the similar experience over the last year. When talking about how bad things are going in this country, whether in-person or online, with either family, friends or strangers you will inevitably get hit with an excuse that begins, "But Biden …"

It seems that no matter how badly things are going, President Trump, his administration, his army of cable news talking heads, podcasters, influencers, and regular supporters have a default excuse. "But Biden," then fill in the blank is supposed to shut you up and accept that the current train wreck should be much, much worse.

It really doesn't work anymore, does it? I mean, back in January 2025 and the early part of the second Trump term, it was very much a safe way to explain why his "day one" promises didn't come to fruition right away. But inflation has gone up since the end of Biden's term. Prices have gone up, the war with Ukraine did not end, we started a whole new war with Iran that was also won on Day One (but not really), gas has skyrocketed, and the list goes on.

It is now August 2026. More than 560 days have passed since Trump took office again. He has attained more power, surrounded himself with yes-men, has a Republican House and Senate, a 6-3 tilt on the Supreme Court, and no excuse to fail. But here we are, with Trump polling in Biden territory and trying to convince Americans that things are going great. And yet, when pressed, Trump and company keep defaulting to how bad things were under Biden.

A leader takes accountability for his job and his mistakes. The effect of tariffs didn't have the impact that Trump promised, they hurt American businesses and our international trade relations. How badly? Well companies were refunded $100 billion and Trump still keeps pursuing this folly. It is hard to defend Trump as this point, but people still do so by blaming someone else.

We have all dealt with kids that haven't learned how to take responsibility for their actions. There is always someone else to blame because they believe that their parents, teachers or other adults will believe them.

Sometimes kids will be caught red handed and still try to blame others. It is funny when they are young but aggravating when they get older. Now we are dealing with adults who can't seem to take account of the fact that they voted for a disastrous president. We have seen countless Trump voters still blame others for Trump's sole failures.

From Biden to Barack Obama to Hillary Clinton to just about anyone, it has gotten quite pathetic that people just can't come to terms with the fact that he has messed up.

The Iran war should be a breaking point for any American. No one likes the theocratic regime in Iran, but Americans were very reluctant to get involved in yet another war in the Middle East. And yet, Trump plunged the country headfirst into a war with no plan and no realistic goals or endgame.

Here, the excuses begin with "But Obama," in that the Iran nuclear deal that President Barack Obama negotiated was horrible and needed to be withdrawn from. This ultimately led to us attacking Iran. It is a bit curious that the man who brags that he has mastered the art of the deal didn't even try to fix the alleged problems of the Obama deal and resorted to bombing instead. But here we are.

We all know there is no way Trump will ever hold himself accountable. His bizarre statements where he claims that we are in a "golden age" and everyone loves him is a testament to his worsening mental acuity. But we should stop entertaining those who still make excuses.

In the run up to the midterms, expect a lot of "buts" — "but Biden," "but Obama," "but Kamala," "but Clinton," "but the Democrats," "but Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez," "but Zohran Mamdani," et cetera. Such excuses will be spouted by many looking to deflect, unwilling to admit that the horse they backed is lame. Democrats must pounce without pulling any punches when it comes to these excuses from MAGA land.

Whenever Trump or his acolytes start to excuse him for his failure with this sort of whataboutism, politely tell them that using past politicians to excuse Trump's current mess is already an admission that he has failed. He asked for complete power and the voters handed it to him. If he was unable to improve the situation over the predecessors he was criticizing, then he has failed.

When a president fails, it means our country is in bad shape. And you can't argue that our country isn't in bad shape. There is no need anymore to blame others for our current condition. Using Biden, Obama, or anyone as an excuse at this point is an admission that Trump has failed.

Joslin Joseph is a recipient of the Military Reporters and Editors award for Best Commentary-Opinion. A graduate of Harvard and Ohio State, he is a Marine veteran who served in Iraq. He currently lives in Anaheim, Calif.

title: Former gang leader accused of ordering Tupac Shakur's killing goes on trial. Here's what to know
description: The trial of a man accused of orchestrating the killing of Tupac Shakur started this week with jury selection, almost 30 years after the rap legend was gunned down near the Las Vegas Strip.  Duane “Ke...
fullText:
LAS VEGAS (AP) — The trial of a man accused of orchestrating the killing of Tupac Shakur started this week with jury selection, almost 30 years after the rap legend was gunned down near the Las Vegas Strip.

Attorneys began vetting potential jurors Monday for the case, which centers on one of the hip-hop world's defining moments and enduring mysteries. Seven potential jurors were asked to return Thursday afternoon as attorneys continue the selection process Tuesday and Wednesday. A total of 16 jurors will be selected for the monthlong trial.

Duane "Keffe D" Davis, 63, has pleaded not guilty to murder with a deadly weapon with the intent to promote, further or assist a criminal gang in the rapper's death. At the time, Davis was a leader of the South Side Compton Crips in California.

Family members of Shakur were among those who gathered at a Las Vegas courthouse for the beginning of jury selection, which could continue through much of this week.

"Whoever had anything to do with it, whoever set it up, whoever had any hand in it should be locked up in prison," said Shakur's cousin, Kendrick Lesane.

Thirty years after his death, Shakur remains a cultural icon and is considered one of the most influential and versatile rappers of all time.

Shakur's death at age 25 came as his fourth solo album had sold 5 million copies.

He was in a BMW on Sept. 7, 1996, with music mogul Marion "Suge" Knight when a white Cadillac pulled up at a red light. Shakur, who was in the passenger seat, was shot multiple times and died six days later, while Knight survived.

The case went cold until recent years, when public statements and a tell-all memoir from Davis in 2019 revived it. He was arrested in 2023.

Davis sat next to his attorney during the trial in Clark County District Court while Nevada Judge Carli Kierny asked a group of 75 potential jurors whether they have any medical issues, language barriers or conflicts with serving in a trial scheduled to last about a month.

Binu Palal, the county's chief deputy district attorney, listed names of people involved in the case to see if potential jurors were familiar with them, including Knight and Sean "Diddy" Combs.

Questions posed to the potential jurors included their favorite books and movies, if they had any connections to a gang, and whether they had listened to Shakur's music. One man said he used to.

Meanwhile, Davis sat quietly and appeared calm, occasionally whispering to his defense attorney, Michael Sanft, as jurors responded to questions.

Davis said that if he's convicted, he wants the judge to decide his sentence, not the jury.

Prosecutors are not accusing Davis of pulling the trigger that night, and the trial likely won't confirm who did. Instead, prosecutors plan to show that Davis made the calls that led to Shakur's death and provided the gun.

Davis co-wrote the memoir "Compton Street Legends," which vividly describes the shooting. The book says Davis obtained a handgun from an associate and tossed it into the back seat of the Cadillac but did not say who fired the fatal shots.

Orlando "Baby Lane" Anderson, Davis' nephew, has long been considered the suspect who pulled the trigger, but charges were never brought against him. He died two years after Shakur in an unrelated gang shootout in Compton.

Two others — Deandrae "Freaky" Smith and Terry "Bubble Up" Brown — were in the car with Davis and Anderson, but they have since died as well.

Fans of the rapper expressed relief in social media posts that the trial was finally underway.

"This case been hanging over hip hop for so long, feels strange to see it actually moving," said one commenter on a Reddit forum for Tupac fans.

"He'd only be 55 if he was alive now," another Reddit user wrote. "Brings it home how young he was, imagine how much music he would have made by now, how many movies."

Prosecutors expect to call between 35 and 45 witnesses, ranging from people who saw Shakur moments before he was shot to those who were in both Shakur and Davis' orbits at the time.

The witness list includes former Las Vegas Mayor Oscar Goodman and members of Shakur's family. However, not everyone on the list will testify.

Prosecutors expect to call Denvonta Lee, who was affiliated with the South Side Crips.

In grand jury testimony, Lee said that rival gangs, the Crips and Mob Piru, were tied to dueling record labels Death Row Records and Bad Boy Records.

Though he wasn't there that night, Lee also testified that Anderson didn't have a clear shot, so Smith took the gun and did the shooting. He also said Davis was in charge and gave the gun to Anderson, who then gave it to Smith.

Davis' defense attorney is expected to call a handful of witnesses, including one expert in the area of false confessions and coercive interrogation techniques.

One of the potential witnesses is in a California prison. Knight is serving a 28-year sentence for running over and killing a Compton businessman in January 2015. He previously said he would not testify in Davis' case.

As the only other living eyewitness who was in one of the two vehicles that night, Knight's testimony could be key.

Sanft, Davis' defense attorney, told The Associated Press that Knight would be a good witness for Davis' defense if he testifies.

Fans have also speculated whether Combs will testify, but his name isn't on any witness lists. He is serving a four-year prison sentence in New Jersey following his conviction of prostitution-related charges.

In his book, Davis alleged Combs wanted Knight and Shakur dead and offered Davis money to kill them. Combs has long denied any involvement.

title: Ousted Syrian dictator Bashar al-Assad sentenced to death in absentia
description: The ex-president is convicted of committing war crimes and crimes against humanity during the country's civil war.
fullText:
A Syrian court has sentenced ousted dictator Bashar al-Assad to death in absentia, after convicting him of committing war crimes and crimes against humanity during the country's civil war.

It is the first conviction against Assad, who fled from Damascus to Moscow with his family after his regime was overthrown in December 2024, ending his family's five-decade grip on power.

Assad's cousin and the former head of political security in southern Syria's Deraa province, Atef Najib, was also sentenced to death. He had been put on trial and appeared wearing a striped prison uniform inside a cage in the courtroom as the judge read out his sentence.

Deraa is widely seen as the birthplace of the uprising against Assad's rule.

In March 2011, the detention and alleged torture of a group of teenagers accused of writing anti-government graffiti sparked protests in the city, which were met with a violent crackdown by security forces.

That response helped ignite nationwide demonstrations that escalated into civil war in which hundreds of thousands of people were killed.

Syria's interim government began trying officials associated with the Assad regime, which ruled the country for more than 50 years, earlier this year.

Najib is one of the highest-ranking officials to be put on trial.

He was convicted of crimes including murder, "the intentional killing of children under 15" and "torture leading to death".

The court also sentenced six former military and security officials in absentia to death, including Bashar al-Assad's younger brother, Maher. He ran the army's elite Fourth Division and also fled to Moscow when the regime fell.

The others convicted include former defence minister Fahd al-Freij.

Nouha al-Masri has spent 15 years waiting for this moment.

She is not just part of the five person prosecution team, she is also a plaintiff in this case.

Masri lost her brother during the March 2011 crackdown and massacre at Al-Omari Square in Deraa.

"The verdict reflects the magnitude of the sacrifices we made, the sacrifices of the martyrs, the suffering and pain of the victims, the missing, and the detainees," she told the BBC.

"We have been waiting for 15 years to reclaim even a small part of our rights, for all those who have spilled our blood, committed crimes, violated our rights, killed, and tortured us."

For Masri, the verdict is a new chapter.

"Our demand is that this not be the end of the trials... In the new Syria, there will be no impunity from this day forward."

Syria trial seen as first step on long road for Assad's victims

The phone book that led us to Assad's spy chief in hiding

Calls for justice and accountability in Syria grow after Assad's fall

It remains unclear whether Syria's new authorities will be able to secure Bashar and Maher al-Assad's extraditions from Moscow.

It is not the first move against Assad by Syria's new leadership.

An arrest warrant was issued against him last December on charges of murder and torture.

He left for Russia as forces under Ahmed al-Sharaa - now Syria's president - swept to power in a rapid, 11-day campaign that brought down the Assad dynasty.

Since then, the new government has detained numerous former officials and security personnel, though most senior figures from the old regime, including Assad himself, remain out of reach in Russia.

Attempts by Syrian opposition figures to pursue Assad through courts in Western countries during the final years of his rule did not lead to any convictions.

Assad came to power in 2000 after the death of his father. The second son of Hafez al-Assad, he was not destined to be Syria's ruler until his brother, Basil, died in a car crash in 1994.

Part of the Alawite minority, he continued to favour their dominance in many roles in the military, security and intelligence agencies.

Much of his rule was defined by the civil war.

Additional reporting by Lana Antaki in Damascus.

title: Watch Out for These Fake Fraud Alerts From Apple and Amazon
description: That browser pop-up isn't a legitimate security alert.
fullText:
If you get a security pop-up while you're browsing online alerting you to an unauthorized charge attached to one of your accounts, don't panic, and don't act impulsively. Scammers are currently using these alerts to impersonate Apple and Amazon support (and possibly others) to convince people that their accounts have been compromised and need to be verified to prevent further fraudulent activity. Naturally, this is just a ruse designed to gain access to your device or accounts, which will do far more damage than the fake alert itself.

This campaign, described by Malwarebytes Labs, starts with a browser pop-up that appears on top of Apple's or Amazon's website. The alerts are designed to look like legitimate notifications and state that the user's Apple ID or Amazon account was recently used to make a $149.99 purchase. Targets are urged to call the support number listed—the same on both pop-ups—immediately to prevent further unauthorized activity. The scammer on the other end of the line may try to convince you to download a tool that provides remote access to your device, hand over credentials, or even pay a fee to protect your account.

If you Google the number listed in this specific campaign, you'll find a fake Amazon support website ("amazonhelp[dot]support") set up by fraudsters to make the scheme look more legitimate—of course, the real Amazon customer service site is hosted on amazon.com. Other scam hallmarks present here include manufactured urgency, technical jargon, and a dollar amount that's just enough to get your attention but not so high that it seems like an obvious fake.

First things first: no legitimate company will send you security alerts via browser pop-up. If there's an issue with your account, you may receive an in-app notification or an email, though you should always be wary of the latter, as it's also a common vector for scams. To confirm whether these alerts are real, log into your account by going directly to the website or app and check your message history or activity log.

It's also worth noting that you won't dispute fraudulent charges with customer support over the phone. In fact, you're far more likely to deal with your bank or credit card issuer directly for this, and you may actually get a fraud notification from a financial institution first in the event of a suspicious purchase. Calling a number from a browser pop-up is not the way. Do not give out account information to anyone over the phone unless you have verified the number, such as by clicking through the company's app, and initiated the call yourself.

Finally, these fake pop-ups may be the result of malicious ads, browser redirects, or compromised sites, all of which are used in phishing campaigns. If you're served one, exit the tab immediately and do not click or engage with it further.

title: Johnson tipped to thrive under Moyes at Everton
description: Wales forward Brennan Johnson is tipped to thrive under David Moyes following his switch from Crystal Palace to Everton.
fullText:
Lee Trundle has tipped Brennan Johnson to thrive under David Moyes at Everton following his switch to the Merseyside club from Crystal Palace.

The Wales forward has signed a four-year deal with the Toffees as part of a swap deal that saw Everton winger Dwight McNeil move to Selhurst Park.

Former Wrexham, Swansea City, Bristol City and Leeds United forward Trundle believes the 25-year-old possesses the talent to win over the Everton faithful.

"With Johnson coming in, I think that's a great signing and he's someone I'm excited about," he said on the BBC's Feast of Football podcast.

"I think Moyes will get he best out of him, I think Moyes is a good manager for him.

"I think he'll go in, and once he starts scoring, I think the fans will take to him.

"I think he'll love being at a club like Everton because once you get in and score those goals, the fans will idolise you, especially because that's what they've been crying out for."

Everton and Palace complete McNeil-Johnson swap

Belief but work to do - Wales' two years under Bellamy

Johnson has operated in various roles during his career, including on the wing, at wing-back and as a striker.

But Trundle, an Everton fan, feels Moyes could deploy the former Tottenham Hotspur, Lincoln City and Nottingham Forest man as a number nine given the inconsistency of current first-choice duo Beto and Thierno Barry.

"If you look at Everton, they create a lot of chances, they just don't take the chances," said Trundle.

"I think if he's in those positions to get those chances, he takes more of them."

He added: "He will go in behind, he'll score goals himself and create himself as well."

Johnson was part of the Forest side who gained promotion from the Championship under Welshman Steve Cooper in 2021-22.

He won the Europa League during his time at Spurs - scoring the winner against Manchester United in the final - and lifted the Conference League with Crystal Palace last season.

Despite Everton's 31-year trophy drought, ex-Wales striker Nathan Blake feels Johnson - who joined Palace in a then club-record deal in January - will have to hit the ground running at Hill Dickinson Stadium.

"Everton fans are demanding," he said.

"Whether you like it or not, it doesn't matter if you haven't won a trophy for a long time, that's a big club. I think there'll be more demand on him there.

"Having Moyes and [assistant manager Billy] McKinlay could be a good thing, but if he doesn't produce in the first 10 to 15 games, it catches up with you.

"The coaching and the experience of Moyes and his backroom staff, they'll coach him to improve."

Having been close to joining Palace in January, McNeil has signed a four-year deal with the Eagles.

The 26-year-old scored 15 goals and registered 19 assists in 128 games across all competitions during his four-year spell with the Toffees.

But Trundle feels the time was right for the "inconsistent" former Burnley winger to depart Everton.

"With McNeil, when he was at Burnley, I used to love him. He used to go past people," he added.

"He came to Everton, there's a different expectation. Even though Everton haven't won anything since 1995, there is an expectancy that you should be doing more from the fans.

"It doesn't help that you've got Liverpool as your neighbours and they've had all that success.

"So, for me, I don't know whether he got lost a bit at times. You could see there was a player in there, but he was inconsistent compared to the way he was at Burnley."

title: Can Lawson keep seat for 2027 season? - F1 Q&A
description: BBC Sport F1 correspondent Andrew Benson answers your latest questions.
fullText:
Formula 1 cars will be back on track next week when the Dutch Grand Prix at Zandvoort takes place from 21-23 August.

In the meantime, you can get your F1 fix as our correspondent Andrew Benson answers your latest questions.

As a Kiwi, I'm biased - but clearly Liam Lawson's been performing at Racing Bulls so far this year, and he's currently 'best of the rest' in the driver standings. Thoughts on his future in F1, particularly before the 2027 season? - Isabella

Lawson is having a strong season.

Given Racing Bulls have the fifth quickest car on average this season, and Lawson is considerably the more experienced of their two drivers, 'best of the rest' in the championship behind the drivers from the top four teams is exactly where he should be.

However, Lawson's issue - in terms of prolonging his career in F1 - is recent history, and his current team-mate.

Arvid Lindblad is a rookie this year, but he is already proving pretty much a match for Lawson. As team principal Alan Permane puts it, the team have "two quick guys" who are "incredibly close" in performance.

Lindblad is trailing in the championship by 20 points, yes, but on pure pace there is little to choose between them.

Lawson leads the qualifying head-to-head 6-5 at races where a fair comparison can be made but, on average speed, Lindblad is actually slightly ahead - by 0.017secs.

That's impressive for a rookie in this context.

Equally, Isack Hadjar was more impressive than Lawson in 2025 - hence Red Bull's decision to promote him in favour of Yuki Tsunoda for this season.

In terms of whether he is a candidate for a move up the grid, Lawson will not find it easy to recover his reputation from the two poor races he had alongside Max Verstappen at the start of 2025, after which Red Bull took the decision to demote him back to Racing Bulls and swap him with Tsunoda.

Once there, Lawson was pretty comfortably beaten by Hadjar.

As for this season and the future, Permane points out the goal of him and his team is to "develop drivers" for Red Bull.

If Red Bull were still run by the old regime of Helmut Marko and Christian Horner, there would be no hope of Lawson getting another chance in the senior team.

The modus operandi of the new leadership, of Red Bull team principal Laurent Mekies and soon-to-be head of the young driver programme Gwen Lagrue, and how they view Lawson in all this context, remains to be seen.

Five things we've learned from first half of F1 season

Listen: Chequered Flag Extra - mid-term report

How does F1/the FIA decide where to have sprint races? Silverstone - with a big crowd in every day - was great this year but other races this season didn't look like they had full stands on the Friday and Saturday. - Phil

The location of the sprint events is ultimately decided by Formula 1 as the commercial rights holder. The FIA - the sport's governing body - does formally approve the calendar, but that's essentially a rubber-stamping exercise.

From F1's point of view, primarily it wants the sprints to take place on tracks that will provide an exciting qualifying session and race.

After that, it's about spreading them evenly through the calendar so there are not too many bunched together.

Of course, there are commercial considerations, too. A track has to pay more to host a sprint. But F1 says it would not take the money if it thought it was the wrong place for a sprint.

Then there is the question of the tracks themselves and whether they want a sprint or not. This will be because they feel they can get more spectators through the gate, and/or provide better value for money.

Silverstone managing director Stuart Pringle was keen to have a sprint this year because they want to "deliver as much value as possible for the ticket price", and a sprint means spectators get two races and two qualifying sessions on one weekend.

Pringle said: "We felt it was well worth the additional cost [on the race fee] to give more action."

He pointed out there was a total of 500,000 spectators at the British Grand Prix over the four days in 2025, and 564,000 in 2026.

"The [extra] 64,000 was primarily Friday and Saturday, and we do put that down to the sprint," he said.

Which F1 drivers could consistently challenge for a world title in inferior cars? My wife and I can only come up with four: Ayrton Senna, Michael Schumacher, Fernando Alonso and Max Verstappen. Do you agree? - Martin

It's hard to challenge for a title in an inferior car, and the number of drivers who can do it is limited as a result. Essentially, it is only the very best.

At first glance, your list looks decent, but you have left out two huge names - Lewis Hamilton and Alain Prost.

Prost's most exceptional season was in 1986, when he beat the two Williams drivers - Nigel Mansell and Nelson Piquet - to win his second world title in what was clearly an inferior McLaren.

There is also a very strong case that Hamilton did not have the best car with McLaren in 2008 (or he and Alonso in 2007), given what was learned subsequently about the relative performance of Ferrari drivers Felipe Massa and Kimi Raikkonen when they were team-mates to Alonso.

The point being that Hamilton and Alonso were extremely closely matched, while Alonso comfortably beat both Massa and Raikkonen, so if Ferrari could compete for a title against McLaren in those years, it could only be because their car was better.

Even in 2017 and 2018, when Hamilton won, the Ferrari was the better car for a large part of both those seasons before Mercedes hit their stride.

The stand-out year relevant to this question is 2012, when Alonso drove his best season and took the title fight to the final race in what was statistically the fourth quickest car.

That was an absolutely extraordinary achievement, and it is rightly celebrated. Even more so when you realise that had only one of two incidents for which Alonso was entirely blameless not happened, he would not have lost out to Red Bull's Sebastian Vettel.

That's a reference, of course, to Alonso being taken out at the start of the Belgian and Japanese Grands Prix by collisions with Lotus drivers - Romain Grosjean in Spa and Raikkonen in Suzuka.

Alonso also arguably won in 2005 in an inferior car, but then it depends what "inferior" means. The Renault was not as fast as Raikkonen's McLaren on balance, but it was certainly more reliable.

As for the rest, no argument with Max Verstappen after coming so close against Lando Norris and McLaren last season, which was Alonso 2012-esque.

Senna won the title in 1991 in a McLaren that was inferior to the Williams FW14 being driven by Mansell, although the Williams suffered significant reliability problems that helped him.

And he also probably did it in 1990 - in his McLaren compared to Prost's Ferrari - given Senna's pace advantage over Prost when they were McLaren team-mates in 1988 and 1989.

Schumacher? Arguably the Benetton was an inferior car to the Williams in 1995, but then he was consistently a superior driver to Damon Hill and David Coulthard, both of whom made a bit of a hash of that season.

Williams also probably had an advantage for the second half of 1994, once they had got on top of the aerodynamic problems that thwarted the start to their season.

But would Schumacher have beaten Senna in 1994 had the Brazilian not been killed at Imola? Unlikely.

And it's hard to argue any of his Ferrari titles were won in an inferior car.

Beyond that, there are not many obvious cases when the champion did not have the best car.

Exceptions would be years massively skewed by circumstance.

One example is the tragic 1982 season, when it was a toss-up between Ferrari and Renault for the fastest car. After Gilles Villeneuve died and team-mate Didier Pironi suffered horrendous injuries, and with Renault afflicted by reliability issues, Keke Rosberg came through to take the title for Williams despite winning only one race.

Or 1979, when the championship scoring system was a bizarre split calculation when only the best four scores from the two half-seasons could be counted, and the Williams FW07 made its debut too late for Alan Jones to challenge Jody Scheckter and Villeneuve in the generally inferior Ferrari 312 T4.

Leonardo Fornaroli looks like another Russell/Leclerc/Piastri calibre driver based on his F3 and F2 performances. If he was to land an F1 seat, where is the most likely place he would end up? - Harry

Fornaroli is the reigning F2 champion, and won F3 the previous season. He has been a member of the McLaren driver development programme since the end of last year.

The Italian has done two practice sessions for McLaren - in Barcelona and Austria this year - as well as two what are known as 'TPC' tests - in older cars - for McLaren in Portimao, and Haas in Jerez.

There are not that many seats up for grabs next year and the driver market is on hold for a large part until it becomes clear whether Max Verstappen is going to leave Red Bull.

If Fornaroli is to get a seat, though, it seems most likely it would be at Haas, where Esteban Ocon's place is under threat.

Haas, however, already have Toyota-contracted Ryo Hirakawa and former Alpine driver Jack Doohan on their books.

Teams always talk about getting "the right balance" of the car. What does that mean specifically, and how do they go about getting it? - Ivor

The car's balance is how a driver experiences its behaviour through a corner.

Does it slide at the front or back (respectively, understeer or oversteer), does it slide differently at different points of the corner, and is the behaviour consistent or unpredictable, etc?

Every driver has their preference as to how they want the car to feel, and the closer the car is to that ideal, generally the quicker they will be.

F1 cars are highly sophisticated prototypes with a number of complex factors affecting how they behave in the cornering phase, which can be broken down into multiple sections making up the time from the moment the driver hits the brakes, to when the car is straight again after the corner.

As a result, there are many different ways in which a car's behaviour can be changed.

These include - but are in no way limited to - the level of downforce chosen at front and rear, the settings for the suspension and differential, and brake pad and disc material.

Drivers can also affect the balance with their driving style. For example, how they enter the corner, when they turn in, how they turn in, how they operate the throttle and brakes on corner entry and so on.

title: Are Man Utd judged differently to other WSL sides?
description: Manchester United are one of the biggest clubs in the world, but is the women's team really judged differently as a result?
fullText:
Manchester United's women's side were in the headlines again last week for the wrong reasons following the departure of former manager Marc Skinner.

The club have been heavily criticised for their apparent lack of investment in the women's team since it was reformed as a professional outfit in 2018.

Quiet transfer windows, high-profile departures, a lack of silverware and scrutiny over facilities have been well documented.

Sources at the club have voiced frustrations over their treatment in the media and it escalated last season when The Athletic were banned, external from asking questions in a post-match huddle with Skinner.

Manchester United are proud to call themselves one of the biggest clubs in the world, but are they judged differently as a result?

Have Man Utd lost faith in their women's team?

Find interviews and extra content on the BBC Women's Football Weekly feed

Skinner's departure came after months of hints at his frustrations over the lack of investment in his squad.

His side finished inside the Women's Super League's top three on two occasions, reached three successive FA Cup finals, delivered a first major trophy and made it to the quarter-finals of the Champions League at the first time of asking.

Some criticism towards Skinner came from United's own fanbase, as they held banners up at Leigh Sports Village calling for his sacking in 2024.

Unhappiness also appeared to be based on their performances against their WSL top-three rivals Arsenal, Chelsea and Manchester City, rather than just results.

Meanwhile, media repeatedly pointed out the club's lack of investment, which followed ex-manager Casey Stoney stepping down in 2021 because of growing concerns over a lack of resources and the state of facilities.

United took so long to form a professional women's set-up that when they did in 2018 - hiring Stoney as manager and recruiting a number of Lionesses, including current Manchester City captain Alex Greenwood to play in the second tier - the assumption was they intended to battle it out with England's elite.

But eight years on, they have delivered just one major trophy and are in danger of slipping below their rivals again this season.

High-profile reports on United's inadequate training facilities circled in 2024 when the women's team were moved out of their Carrington training site and into temporary buildings to make way for the men's first team.

Co-owner Sir Jim Ratcliffe's comments about the women's team were also scrutinised. Speaking to the United We Stand fanzine, Ratcliffe described the men's team as the "main issue" and referred to the women's side as "girls" and "an opportunity".

United also lost a number of key first-team members of staff.

Former assistant coach Martin Ho is now enjoying success as Tottenham manager and was joined by goalkeeping coach Ian Willcock in April, while another former assistant, Charlotte Healy, became head coach at WSL 2 club Bristol City last year.

Big-name players, including England duo Alessia Russo and Mary Earps, as well as Spain full-back Ona Batlle, were allowed to leave on free transfers.

This summer, they lost their star striker Melvine Malard to rivals Chelsea and are yet to sign a replacement, although the £850,000 fee will prove useful.

Given the talent at United's disposal during their eight-year existence, it is understandable that questions have been asked over the club's inability to keep hold of them.

United's reputation, built on the history of the men's teams' successes, means fans demand trophies and expect to see ambition.

That is no different to other big clubs, such as Liverpool, West Ham or Tottenham, who all have women's teams that have been competing at a lower level.

Spurs did not gain promotion to the WSL until 2019 and have been flirting with lower and mid-table spots until more recently under Ho.

West Ham remain the only WSL team not to have played at their men's stadium and have consistently been criticised for not investing in the transfer window.

Former West Ham head coach Rehanne Skinner had to make structural changes and ex vice-chair Karren Brady was not seen at WSL games and they frequently lost key players.

Liverpool, in particular, have faced huge scrutiny over the treatment of their women's team - who were back-to-back WSL title winners in 2013 and 2014 but were relegated in 2020.

They also faced scathing criticism about their pitch conditions in 2019.

In 2021, former Liverpool players Kirsty Linnett and Becky Jane took to social media to claim contracts they were offered were retracted by the club.

Even Chelsea, who won six successive WSL titles, were criticised for capping the number of spectators they allowed into Stamford Bridge for Women's Champions League games in order to reduce costs of running the stadium on matchdays.

Their manager Sonia Bompastor called for better recruitment and more squad depth last season.

In summary, Manchester United have faced significant scrutiny, but they are one of many WSL clubs whose decisions and progress have been closely examined.

title: Meet Liverpool's rising star who can only play friendlies
description: The emergence of teenage defender Ifeanyi Ndukwe has been one of the main storylines of Liverpool's pre-season - but why can the 18-year-old only play friendly matches?
fullText:
Liverpool's first pre-season under new boss Andoni Iraola has not been without its challenges - but one reason for optimism is the emergence of 18-year-old defender Ifeanyi Ndukwe.

The Reds have won two and lost two of their four friendlies so far - beating Sunderland and Wrexham, but throwing away two-goal leads in defeats by Leeds and Monaco.

Iraola's side are short of numbers in central defence, so Austrian teenager Ndukwe has been handed more minutes than even he might have expected.

Joe Gomez picked up an injury in Liverpool's first pre-season game, while £60m signing Jeremy Jacquet has been absent with a niggling knee issue and Giovanni Leoni is recovering from a serious knee injury - and Ndukwe has grasped his chance to impress.

With two lots of 90 minutes and an 80-minute display already under his belt, Ndukwe was handed a start alongside captain Virgil van Dijk against Monaco at Anfield on Sunday.

And it didn't take long for the imposing 6ft 6in (1.98m) youngster to draw gasps from the crowd after a neat backheel to wrong-foot Monaco's Mika Biereth, before winning important defensive duels.

After the departure of France international Ibrahima Konate, it remains unclear who will partner Van Dijk in Liverpool's opening Premier League game against Newcastle.

Post-Brexit rules mean he is not allowed to play for Liverpool in a competitive game in 2026 because he didn't reach the points target required to qualify for a UK work permit - meaning he can only play in friendly matches.

Since Brexit, and with the UK no longer part of the European Union, clubs now have to navigate a more complex work permit system to ensure players - especially those who are yet to establish themselves at the top level - are able to move to England.

Austria youth international Ndukwe doesn't currently have enough points to obtain a Governing Body Endorsement (GBE) to obtain a work visa.

There is another route into the squad, through taking up an Elite Significant Contribution (ESC) slot, which is awarded to foreign players who do not qualify for the standard GBE.

Premier League and Championship clubs have up to four ESC places available, based on the percentage of minutes clubs gave to their England Qualified Players (EQP) in the previous campaign.

But clubs are not entitled to all four spots automatically.

The magic number is 35% of minutes, which means clubs can use four ESC players. Dropping below that begins to reduce the number of ESC slots available.

Liverpool's percentage last season means they only get one ESC place, which has already been taken by Senegalese 18-year-old Mor Talla Ndiaye.

Last season, Freddie Woodman, Gomez, Rhys Williams, Curtis Jones, Trey Nyoni and Rio Ngumoha were the only English players in Liverpool's squad, playing a collective 83 times in the Premier League.

This comes after Liverpool lost the likes of Trent Alexander-Arnold, Jarell Quansah, Tyler Morton and loaned out Harvey Elliott.

Developed in the Austria Vienna academy before establishing himself in the club's reserve side, Ndukwe was included in the senior squad on several occasions - making one appearance.

An impressive Under-17 World Cup with Austria in November last year led Liverpool to add the talented youngster to their ranks.

The Reds agreed a deal in principle in January, but the £2.6m transfer became official this summer, once Ndukwe turned 18.

After excelling in pre-season and leaving fans desperate to see more of the teenager, Ndukwe will still be able to play against Como in Liverpool's final friendly on 16 August.

Van Dijk labelled Ndukwe a "big talent" after playing alongside him in the first half against Monaco.

"Obviously, I saw the games in pre-season in America," Van Dijk added.

"Big talent, big guy and he wants to learn. I had a brief conversation with him, especially in the last couple of days. For him, it is just progressing. I know he has to go on loan I think so let's see where he ends up.

"The matter of fact is that he has to go on loan and wherever he goes, he needs to learn, get better and be ready when he comes back to hopefully stay there."

A decision on Ndukwe's next steps is expected within the next fortnight.

Talking in July, Ndukwe's agent Georg Lederer told Sky Sports Austria: "A loan club will now be found where Ifeanyi can gain playing experience at a very high level.

"Despite this change, we see the situation as a great opportunity for Ifeanyi. Several top international clubs have already expressed concrete interest."

Lederer told BBC Sport on Monday that that they are still in the process of deciding where Ndukwe goes in Europe.

Ndukwe must accumulate 15 points across a number of categories while out on loan to qualify automatically for a visa.

Simply put, the better the league Ndukwe plays in, the more points towards a work permit he will earn.

It is understood that, with the right move, the necessary points tally could be achieved by January.

This means Ndukwe could potentially still feature for Liverpool this season, after the turn of the year if he was recalled, but that is a potential drawback for clubs interested in a loan.

title: Trump says it would be 'terrible mistake' to remove Infantino
description: US President Donald Trump says it would be a "terrible mistake" if under-pressure Fifa president Gianni Infantino was ousted.
fullText:
US President Donald Trump says it would be a "terrible mistake" if under-pressure Fifa president Gianni Infantino was ousted from his position.

Trump's backing followed Uefa, Concacaf and the Asian Football Confederation (AFC) issuing an open letter accusing Infantino of breaking trust "through deception" with his aborted Fifa Forward Enterprise (FFE) proposal.

FFE would have meant a new company being created to manage commercial and ticketing rights of all Fifa competitions, including World Cups, with 21% sold off to a private investment company.

Trump's comments mark the first time he has come out in defence of Infantino since the FFE plans came to light on 28 July.

"Fifa would be making a terrible mistake if, for any reason, they even considered replacing president Gianni Infantino," Trump wrote on social media.

"He is fantastic, having just presided over the most successful World Cup, by four times, ever presented. If he is gone, it will never be as successful or profitable again."

The 2026 World Cup was co-hosted by the US, Canada and Mexico this summer, with Spain crowned champions after beating Argentina in the final.

When addressing the FFE proposals for the first time on 31 July, Trump said he had not spoken to Infantino about the plans.

Thrive Eternal was expected to lead the proposed investor group for FFE.

Thrive is an American venture capital firm founded by Joshua Kushner - the brother of Trump's son-in-law Jared.

Infantino has a close relationship with Trump and awarded him the inaugural Fifa Peace Prize in December 2025.

The map showing world's division over Infantino

Infantino broke trust 'through deception' - confederation presidents

Fifa scraps controversial World Cup investment plan

European football's governing body Uefa has threatened a boycott of all Fifa competitions, as well as saying it could take legal action over the failed FFE plans.

The letter issued by Uefa, Concacaf and the AFC - the three confederations representing Europe, North America, Central America and the Caribbean, and Asia - came after Fifa said there was a "concerted and ongoing effort" to "undermine" world football's governing body and Infantino.

BBC Sport understands that there have been preliminary discussions between the three confederations over breakaway competitions, should Infantino remain in his position. However, substantive talks are yet to begin, according to others.

"When trust is broken through deception, when an individual places himself above the collective that entrusted him with authority, that duty has been abandoned," the letter from Uefa, Concacaf and the AFC read.

While the statement did not name Infantino, sources have told BBC Sport that it should be seen as an opportunity for him to resign and leave his position with dignity.

The timing of Trump's first comments on this saga is intriguing.

Could it be because on Monday, the United States Soccer Federation made clear its opposition to Infantino, calling for "meaningful change"?

Or is it a sign of the jeopardy that Infantino could now be in after Uefa, Concacaf and the AFC's joint letter?

Trump is known as someone who does not like to back a loser, so why did this support not come sooner, when Infantino's position was less vulnerable? Has Infantino urged him to step in?

Trump's claim that the World Cup will be less successful if Infantino is ousted will be contested by those who believe that the tournament has become too commercialised and expensive for fans under his leadership.

And the focus on profit is interesting given this crisis was sparked by a plan to raise even more money, on top of the record revenue that Fifa already enjoys.

It should not come as a surprise perhaps, given the close relationship between the two men, and the fact that the investment group behind the FFE plan is run by the brother of Trump's son-in-law.

While Trump's support will no doubt be privately welcomed by Infantino, it is unclear how helpful it will actually prove when it comes to shoring up support within the game. And Infantino may have hoped this backing had come sooner.

title: How £30m Charles became Northern Ireland's most expensive footballer
description: After he became Northern Ireland's most expensive player, BBC Sport NI looks at the rise of Shea Charles, from Manchester City's academy to Fulham's £30m man.
fullText:
"Shea has been so, so impressive during my time working with him. I have never seen anyone better on the ball than this kid."

It was in 2021 that the Northern Ireland youth coach Gerard Lyttle said he had never seen a youngster as comfortable on the ball as Shea Charles.

Back then, the teenager was still playing at centre-back and had yet to make a senior appearance for club or country, but he was standing out to his coaches.

Five years later, midfielder Charles has become the most expensive Northern Ireland player in history after he completed a £30m transfer from Southampton to Premier League side Fulham.

From coming through at Manchester City, to becoming one of Michael O'Neill's most important players on the international scene, the 22-year-old has taken the long way round to a top-flight return.

From when he joined Manchester City's academy as a seven-year-old, Charles' potential was clear and he quickly progressed through the ranks.

His breakout year came in the 2021-22 season, when he helped City win the Premier League 2 title as an 18-year-old playing alongside the likes of Cole Palmer, Morgan Rogers and Nico O'Reilly.

He was handed a first Northern Ireland call-up for June's Nations League window in 2022, and he made his international debut as a late substitute against Greece before he had even made a senior appearance at club level.

It was somewhat unexpected given his lack of experience, but it showcased the belief that then manager Ian Baraclough showed in Charles.

"I hope I can just push on from here and get more caps. It was a great feeling to make my debut," Charles said at the time.

"I didn't expect to be playing in this game, but I will take every chance as it comes."

Charles has certainly done that, establishing himself as a key player for Michael O'Neill, who returned as manager later in 2022 to replace Baraclough.

In fact, Charles has only missed three matches since then. One was for a suspension following a red card against Slovenia, while his absence with a hamstring injury was notable in the closing World Cup qualifiers with Slovakia and Luxembourg in November last year.

For Lyttle, having worked with Charles at age-group level with Northern Ireland, there was never any doubting his potential.

"Honestly, he is so calm, I actually haven't seen him get out of second gear yet and that is no joke - there is even 

"He plays with such a calmness, sees a pass, breaks lines, is technically very good, can hit long and short and can compete physically. He is just a proper ball-playing centre-back and a real good kid as well.

"As he goes up the levels he needs to keep progressing, but from what I've seen of young Shea he definitely has all the attributes."

It helped that Charles was learning from some of the best in the world. At Manchester City he had been training with the likes of Rodri and Fernandinho and was finally handed a Premier League chance in May 2023, by which stage he had six international caps under his belt.

Pep Guardiola's side had already wrapped up the Premier League title, and Charles made his City debut as a second-half substitute against Brentford on the final day of the season.

"When we train with the first team the standard is so high and we are always learning, every day," Charles said in 2022.

"With the likes of Rodri and Fernandinho, it is tough but enjoyable."

While learning from the best players in the world was beneficial, it did not offer a natural path of progression to the first team at Etihad Stadium.

So, a month after making his City debut, Charles signed a four-year contract with Southampton and subsequently made 32 appearances as Saints won promotion back to the Premier League.

Instead of contributing in his club's top-flight return, his development continued with a loan spell at Sheffield Wednesday, where he became a fan favourite and drew links to Arsenal.

"He's a young, high-potential player – the pity is that he is not our player," said Wednesday's manager at the time, Danny Rohl, about his loan star during his early days at Hillsborough.

Midway through his season with the Owls, Charles was handed the Northern Ireland armband by O'Neill just 10 days after his 21st birthday, the youngest player to captain the country since Terry Neill in 1963.

"Shea has got the attributes to play at the highest level of the game, and the temperament to do so, and that is what you look for as a captain," O'Neill said at the time.

"Whether he has the armband or not, he is going to be a leader on the pitch."

With Southampton back in the Championship after their relegation, Charles returned to St Mary's last season.

He contributed some big moments and chipped in with his biggest return in front of goal with six strikes in the campaign.

Moments such as his winner against eventual Premier League champions Arsenal in the FA Cup quarter-finals, or a goal against Liverpool at Anfield in the EFL Cup, will live long in the memory on the south coast.

He also netted in the Championship play-off semi-final win over Middlesbrough with a goal that would have taken the Saints to Wembley, only for the club to be denied at shot at the top flight after the Spygate drama.

While Southampton missed out on the Premier League, O'Neill was adamant that Charles has what it takes to play in the top flight. It was a matter of when, not if.

"Shea can play in the Premier League, there's no doubt about that," said Charles' international boss before June's friendlies with Guinea and France.

It was in the France game that Charles showed he belonged among the elite players, not looking out of place against a side who went on to be World Cup semi-finalists.

It was the same against Italy in March's World Cup play-off, where he was arguably the best player on the pitch against Sandro Tonali and Nicolo Barella despite the 2-0 defeat which ended NI's dreams of reaching the finals.

"I back myself against anyone," was the player's own assessment after that game.

Charles was strongly linked with a move to Leeds United, but instead Fulham will be his destination as he looks to take the next step in his career under former Real Madrid and Liverpool defender Alvaro Arbeloa, now head coach of the London side.

With 35 international caps under his belt and a host of clutch moments to his name at the age of 22, Charles could be one of the surprises of the season as he aims to have a breakout Premier League campaign at Craven Cottage.

title: Digging
description: Abdulkareem...
fullText:
Books & the Arts

 August 11, 2026

Digging

 Abdulkareem Abdulkareem 

—40,000 child miners work in southern
Democratic Republic of the Congo

We juggled boastfulness with our phones
in our hands. K said he used one before I ever knew
what it was called. Then I sliced his insolence
with a photograph of a nine-year old me
holding his point-the-light-to-the-soup phone.
I was ignorant of the genesis of phones,
how the light it opened in my face came to be—
the sweats across the neck of little boys like myself.
F said Africans are ignorant in noisemaking for our wound—
to dissect the world with a shrill.
To pull every eye into the body of our drowning.
This time, it’s not cotton picking, but metal digging,
willing & unwilling. Ripping the canopies of schooling
off the backs of little children with a sack of cobalt.
I posted a change for Congo on my Instagram
& bought a new phone a year later.
Two years later, on YouTube, I watched the cobalt hands
of kids unearth the terrain the way it reiterates
the history of rubber & mutilated hands.
In Katanga, Arthur said he digs the world to live in the world—
to battle a shovel like his parents.
Richard carries a bag big as his body—
filled with red sand. Dorsan mourns his mother
with forgetfulness, a misery so big you forget your grief.
To subsist is to be capable of mourning.
what is that bright thing up there?
He asks of the light in the bulb.
Monica sits, the four-year old child
picking stones instead of brick toys.
Natalie says, my finger hurts.
Mukumba carries a lump on his neck,
as if the woes of his country like piles
unfolded inside it. I call mama on the phone,
asks how my sister, who is 3000 km away
from Katanga, fares in school—she’s doing well,
she says. I exhume my Instagram with a new protest post.
I keep watching. The world keeps watching.
Little children with faces as if the offspring of dust.

title: Forest sign Sporting's Ivory Coast defender Diomande
description: Nottingham Forest sign Ivory Coast defender Ousmane Diomande from Portuguese club Sporting for a reported £34m.
fullText:
Nottingham Forest have signed Ivory Coast defender Ousmane Diomande from Portuguese club Sporting in a deal worth a reported £34m., external

The 22-year-old has signed a four-year contract with Forest, who have an option for a further year.

"I am very happy to be here. It is a historic club, and it motivates me to join such a club," said Diomande

"I believe we can achieve very good things this season and I am looking forward to meeting the players and head coach. I will give my best."

New Forest manager Oliver Glasner favours a 3-5-2 formation and Diomande is likely to play alongside Nikola Milenkovic and Murillo in a back three.

He has 15 caps for Ivory Coast and was part of his country's squad at the 2026 World Cup, making one appearance in a group-stage win against Curacao.

Diomande started his career at Olympic Sport Abobo in his homeland and was at Danish club FC Midtjylland before joining Sporting in January 2023.

The central defender made 132 first-team appearances for the Lisbon club and helped Sporting win consecutive Portuguese league titles in 2023-24 and 2024-25.

He was part of the side that reached the Champions League quarter-finals last season before being edged out by Arsenal.

Glasner, who took over as Forest manager earlier this summer, is a long-time admirer of Diomande and tried to sign him when he was in charge at Crystal Palace.

"He has fantastic experience for a defender of his age," said Forest's chief football officer George Syrianos.

"Playing a crucial role in title-winning teams and going into the latter stages of the Champions League puts him in a great position to integrate well at Forest.

"Ousmane is a powerful, commanding defender, and arrives with a winning mentality."

Diomande's arrival follows the signing of Austria midfielder Xaver Schlager on a free transfer in July.

title: 'I won Commonwealth bronze - then went back to work at McDonald's'
description: Summer Shaw wins Scotland's first judo medal at the 2026 Commonwealth Games and a week later is working at McDonald's.
fullText:
"Someone said to me: 'It's crazy that you can win a Commonwealth medal and then come back to work.'"

So 22-year-old Summer Shaw decided to make a TikTok video, external about her swift change of scenery while on a work break at a McDonald's restaurant.

The five-second clip that Shaw posted "for funsies" went viral, and has been watched over one million times. Then came the comments...

"People were asking: 'How is this possible?'

"They were like: 'This shouldn't be allowed.'"

Shaw won Scotland's first judo medal at the recent Commonwealth Games in Glasgow, a bronze in the 48kg event.

"It's so cool when it's something you've dreamed of doing since you were eight years old - and suddenly you're there," Shaw told BBC Sport.

"To get there was crazy, and to come away with a medal was even better."

Shaw won that medal on the last Friday of the Games. The next week, she was back at the family home in Surrey - and back to work.

"I picked up that part-time job [at McDonald's] when I was studying for my A-levels," said Shaw, who qualifies to represent Scotland through her father's side of the family.

She has recently been based largely in Birmingham while studying for a biology degree. That means she has been close to the British Judo Olympic and Paralympic National Training Centre in Walsall.

"They've been really flexible with me, letting me work when I can. They've been really good with me," she said.

"It's mostly seasonal because my job's back at home, but when I am back it is like two, three shifts a week.

"It's hard to find jobs like it though that are flexible with your hours. I've heard from other people in their part-time jobs saying their boss won't give them the weekend off."

Shaw is a world-class competitor in a sport where the rewards may not make her wealthy.

"Obviously there's football, Formula One… but I can't think of many more sports where it is a case of 'you've hit the top level and now you're financially settled'," she said.

Shaw is given what is called an 'Athlete Performance Award' (APA), a financial grant from UK Sport and the National Lottery that contributes towards her living and training costs.

There are different grades of support, external that athletes receive, depending on their results and prospect of medal-winning performances.

Shaw told BBC Sport that it was "very common" for athletes in sports like judo to have another source of income.

"The money I get [APA] covers my living expenses, which is a blessing and not to be taken for granted," she said.

"But, for example, the next competition I've paid for myself because it wasn't funded by British Judo.

"Going to Peru [for the Grand Prix] has cost me quite a bit of money and then I'm not really getting that back from anywhere else.

"I'm also a normal person! Like, I want to save for a house."

Athletes can also earn money through sponsorships, something Shaw says would be a "game-changer" for an athlete at the present stage of her career.

"It just means you can take every single opportunity… put it towards competitions that I don't get funded."

Shaw also decided to set up a GoFundMe page at the start of the year, which she sees as a way of helping to fund her dream of going to the 2028 Los Angeles Olympics.

Scroll through the TikTok comments on her video about returning to work, and you get a taste of the public reaction: "This is crazy", "insane to me".

Another comment reads simply: "Superman also had a side hustle."

Which begs the question… would Shaw continue with this work if she did have a sponsor?

"I've met so many of my close friends there, and my boyfriend! So I owe a lot of good things in my life to that McDonald's," she said.

"But obviously it means I could be more selective, rather than thinking 'I really should work because I've got a competition coming up and I don't want it to take a hit to my bank account'."

title: The map showing world's division over Infantino
description: BBC Sport uses visuals to explore the support and opposition to Gianni Infantino's leadership of Fifa from its members.
fullText:
As recently as mid-July, Gianni Infantino was considered a shoo-in to be re-elected as Fifa president next March.

All but a handful of Fifa's 210 members had endorsed his bid for a fourth term in charge of world football, and he faced no meaningful challenge from any quarter.

But that picture looks very different now, after two weeks of relentless fallout to his now-abandoned plan to sell off stakes in the World Cup and other competitions to private investors.

The world is far from united over whether Infantino should stay or go.

To illustrate that division, BBC Sport has mapped the apparent view of all 210 member associations who are able to vote (Nepal, Fifa's 211th member, is currently suspended and has no voting rights).

In some cases, countries have publicly stated their overt support or opposition regarding Infantino.

Others have directly told BBC Sport where they stand when asked to do so, while some are assumed positions based on statements made by the continental confederation the country sits within.

Trump says it would be 'terrible mistake' to remove Infantino

Whereas once Infantino looked set to saunter to a fourth term unopposed, he now might need to have enough numbers on his side to stay in post.

If a unity candidate is found to oppose him, then the election would become a direct battle.

Fifa election votes between two candidates require a simple majority - each candidate would require a total of 106 votes to win.

If there are three or more candidates, a first-round win requires two thirds of the vote. If there is no winner, there is a second round where a simple majority is needed.

Europe has 55 votes, Africa 54, Asia 46, North America 35, Oceania 11 and South America 10.

But while the current tally looks like 73 in support of Infantino, 124 in opposition to him and 13 undecided, that picture is fluid and is likely to change in the months ahead.

Several European countries, including England and Wales, have formally withdrawn letters of support for Infantino that they had sent for next year's election.

On Monday, the backlash against Infantino intensified when European governing body Uefa, North America's Concacaf and the Asian Football Confederation (AFC) signed a joint letter accusing him and Fifa of breaking their trust "through deception".

It is a significant coalition, and those regional governing bodies represent 136 associations between them.

But there are already dissenting members within the confederations, like Bhutan, the Philippines, and the UAE within Asia, who have all backed Infantino.

Indeed, Asia is considered a potential swing region for Infantino's future, with many associations not yet making their position known.

Mexico has broken ranks within Concacaf by coming out in support of Infantino, too. The USA and Canada have stated support for Concacaf's latest statement, but have not outright declared their opposition to Infantino's rule.

And the Oceania Football Confederation (OFC) has made no public comment since the whole saga began - nor have any of its members. OFC told BBC Sport they will release a statement following a meeting on Thursday.

Infantino still has staunch allies too, particularly within Africa (Caf) and South America (Conmebol), who have benefited from unprecedented investment since he took over a decade ago.

That investment could help him gain critical votes from nations within AFC, Concacaf and OFC - who are lower down the football food chain and have benefited significantly from the Fifa Forward programme, which has made billions of dollars available for investment.

And Saudi Arabia - which has yet to take a public position but was awarded hosting rights for the 2034 World Cup on Infantino's watch - will have its own football leadership elections in August. The results could dictate the kingdom's position, and influence the view of others in the region.

It cannot be guaranteed that every nation will toe the line of their confederation.

Infantino has shown no desire to step down, but there is a chance that his time in charge could be over by the autumn.

That could come to pass if Fifa Council members try to force his resignation at an emergency meeting.

Such a meeting can be called, and must take place within a fortnight, if 19 of the 37 members call for it.

The council is made up of nine members from Uefa, seven from AFC, six from Caf, five from Concacaf, five from Conmebol, and three from Oceania. Also on the panel are Infantino himself and Fifa secretary general Mattias Grafstrom.

Given its makeup, then, this approach is probably unlikely.

Which leaves the possibility of a candidate standing against Infantino next March. Nobody has put their name forward yet, but if the leaders of Uefa, Concacaf, and AFC are serious about toppling Infantino, uniting behind a single candidate is likely their best option.

The deadline for a candidate to announce their intention to stand is November.

Historically, other confederations have been angered by European dominance of football, its competitions and its wealth.

That is perhaps why Concacaf president Victor Montagliani has been consistently mooted as the most likely challenger to Infantino in recent weeks.

The map of votes could change significantly based on who stands.

If AFC president Sheikh Salman were to step forward, for example, there is a chance that could sway some of the associations in Asia that are currently supportive of Infantino towards him.

For now, the global picture remains unclear because of emerging splits within confederations, the potential for key players to declare one way or another in the coming months and the hitherto lack of a clear candidate to challenge Infantino.

What is clear is that Infantino is no longer coasting towards a fourth term, if he clings on that long.

title: One Woman’s Message From the Hell of ICE Detention
description: Maryam...
fullText:
My husband, son, and I have been locked up for months—despite being permanent residents with no criminal record. It is an unendurable, unending nightmare.

My name is Maryam Tahmasebi, and I am a professor of psychology and statistics at Los Angeles Pierce College—or, I was, until April 9, when my life, and my family’s lives, changed forever.

On that day, I was teaching a class when my son texted me, saying that my husband hadn’t picked him up from school and wasn’t answering his phone, which is very unlike him. I picked my son up from school, came frantically back home, and called the police, thinking that something horrible must have happened to him. Even so, it never occurred to me that he could have been detained by ICE. We are legal permanent residents with valid green cards. My husband, Eissa Hashemi, is also a professor, and has dedicated his life to mentoring PhD students in the Business Psychology department of The Chicago School. We have both mentored many PhD candidates, among whom are veterans who have served this country for decades. We don’t have any criminal record—not even a traffic ticket. I believed in the “rule of law,” and trusted that if there was anything wrong with our immigration status, the government would notify us through legal channels.

I was beyond shocked to realize that an online smear campaign without any merit or legal standing had convinced the US government to try to revoke our green cards overnight without due process or even telling us. The government had decided to punish my husband for being the son of a woman who was a translator for the Iranian hostage takers in 1979, before Eissa was even born.

I came here because I wanted to build a life for myself and my family that was defined by my own actions, not anyone else’s. But now our lives are being upended for something someone else did nearly 50 years ago.

Imagine that you are an independent woman wading through the waters of sexism and patriarchy every day, and then you are told that not only do your own ideas and academic achievements not matter, but you are somehow now responsible for decisions you never made, and for things that happened before you were ever born. That you don’t have an identity of your own, and that your existence can be negated based on relations. This is bloodline punishment. I was hoping that the United States of America, the country that I loved, would be different.

Eventually, my husband’s phone location showed he was at an ICE center in downtown LA. I talked to him there for a minute. He said he had been told that, while he was under arrest, our son and I were safe. That turned out to have been a lie. The next day, when I took my son to school, my car was surrounded by DHS cars, and my son and I were detained. I had to watch my son, who is in high school and has been a legal resident of California for 12 years, be handcuffed. We were shipped to Texas overnight from Los Angeles in horrible conditions that I won’t elaborate on in this letter. We have remained in Texas ever since.

My son and I have spent over 120 days in the Dilley Immigration Processing Center, away from my husband, who was taken to the South Texas Detention Center in Pearsall, Texas. There, he faces even more horrible conditions, and he faces them alone. When I requested that my husband be reunited with us in Dilley, a so-called “family detention center” (the very existence of such a term is deeply troubling), I was told that in our specific case, family separation is the policy and the rule.

I have struggled to understand how this can happen to people who have never broken the law, in a system I believed to be based on the rule of law.

We have been put through hell for the past four months, and our physical and mental health have deteriorated in ways that might not be reversible for years. We are only allowed to speak with my husband for 10 minutes every two weeks, under supervision. My son, who only speaks English and has been in California’s school system since pre-K, is struggling to understand why the only country he considers home is treating him this way.

What has happened to us was designed specifically to break our body and spirit. I am a mother, not a martyr, so I would always choose my son’s health and well-being over any dreams or aspirations I have. But even when we decided to make the difficult decision to asked to be allowed to voluntarily leave the United States—the place we consider our country and our home—the government not only opposed it but suggested that it would appeal any judicial decisions that grant us departure.

In other words, they want to continue our indefinite detention without any end in sight. But for what purpose? I have been asking myself that question over and over. I can’t think of any reason why we are being put through this punitive ordeal. We don’t have money or power to help us, shield us, or buy us favor. We are two working-class educators who had been living a working-class life in a rented apartment, and had never imagined anything like this happening to us.

This is why we need your help. We are in tremendous pain and have been trapped in an unendurable, unending nightmare. I want my son to have a normal life, not spend his days in this awful detention center in Dilley. No child deserves this. No human deserves this. We are asking anyone with a conscience to help us end this nightmare. There are more things I want to say, but this is the shackled version of what I feel safe saying right now. I will end on this: If this could happen to us, a law-abiding family of two professors and a young boy, it can happen to anyone.

title: UFC President Dana White Open to Creating Women’s BMF Title
description: UFC president Dana White said that he is open to creating a women’s BMF title for some of MMA’s best women’s fighters to compete for.The UFC has a men’s BMF title, which is currently possessed by lightweight star Charles Oliveira, but there is no women’s BMF title.However, that could potentially change, as White said for […] The post UFC President Dana White Open to Creating Women’s BMF Title appeared first on HEAVY.
fullText:
UFC president Dana White said that he is open to creating a women's BMF title for some of MMA's best women's fighters to compete for.

The UFC has a men's BMF title, which is currently possessed by lightweight star Charles Oliveira, but there is no women's BMF title.

However, that could potentially change, as White said for the first time that he's open to doing it.

Speaking to media in Las Vegas during a tour of the newly revamped Meta Apex, White said that he is open to the possibility of a women's BMF title when asked by a media member if he would consider making it.

"Yeah, anything's possible. Anything's possible," White said. "Why not?"

While White did say that he was open to a women's BMF title, he denied that the UFC would be opening any more women's weight classes anytime soon.

The UFC currently has women's strawweight (115 lbs), women's flyweight (125 lbs), and women's bantamweight (135 lbs) divisions. They previously hosted a women's featherweight (145 lbs) division, but closed it down a few years ago.

There has been some talk about a women's atomweight (105 lbs) division, giving some of the smaller women's MMA fighters a chance to fight in the UFC, but White said he has no interest in that right now.

"It screws up the other two divisions," White said. "If there was a need for it and we felt that it would work, then we would have done it already."

The BMF title was first created in November 2019, when Jorge Masvidal defeated Diaz via TKO to capture the inaugural title at UFC 244.

It would be four years before the BMF title was put on the line again, this time in July 2023, when Justin Gaethje knocked out Dustin Poirier to win the belt at UFC 291.

Gaethje then defended the belt at UFC 300 against Max Holloway, but was brutally knocked out with one second left in the fifth round as Holloway won it.

Holloway then defended it against Dustin Poirier at UFC 318 before losing it to Oliveira at UFC 326.
