title: Opinion: How the pursuit of Said El Mala could alter Borussia Dortmund's future
description: Amid an ongoing transfer saga to sign one of the Bundesliga's hottest prospects in Said El Mala, Borussia Dortmund find themselves between a rock and a hard place. Having failed with two previous bids...
fullText:
Amid an ongoing transfer saga to sign one of the Bundesliga's hottest prospects in Said El Mala, Borussia Dortmund find themselves between a rock and a hard place. Having failed with two previous bids for the 19-year-old, BVB must carefully curate the perfect third approach to get their man.

On Friday, 7 August, an offer of €45million including bonuses was submitted and quickly rejected by 1.FC Köln. With Dortmund in uncharted waters and the Cathedral City club holding out for a fee in excess of €50million, what are the implications for BVB if they fail to sign El Mala – or is it a blessing in disguise?

When Dortmund escaped the jaws of bankruptcy in 2005, a switch flicked in terms of transfer dealings. Signing superstars was no longer an option. Instead, sifting the market for young, high-potential and affordable talents became the norm. That model has largely continued to the present day.

As per Forbes' list of most valuable clubs, BVB clocks in at a cool 13th-place, priced at near $2.2billion (€1.9bn). Still, the Westphalian's record signing remains just €35million for Ousmane Dembélé in 2016 – averaging €65m less than the record spends set by teams ranked around them in 10th- to 15th-place.

Of course, this is the nature of a majority fan-owned Bundesliga club striving to compete on the global stage. There is no external investment or financial takeover. But with the transfer market inflating on a yearly basis, it begs the question of whether Dortmund need to set a new threshold to maintain their status?

Camouflage, a poker face, VPNs — Dortmund have often disguised themselves as a club with limited financial resources. They've done a good job of it too, uncovering some stars for meagre amounts in the last 20 years. However, keeping their fees below €35million is not so feasible in today's skyrocketing market.

Having pushed the boat out to €45million with El Mala (for now), some future deals may follow a similar path. Sides willing to sell their latest prodigy to the Rhurpott giants now know they can pay top dollar. Dortmund finds itself at a crossroads whereby signing El Mala could mean paying more for stars in years to come.

This isn't to say every arrival will suddenly exceed the half-century mark going forward. Take, for example, Daniel Svensson who joined for €6.5m as recently as May 2025 and is a vital cog in Niko Kovac's side. Still, adaptation must come from Ole Book & Co. to know when exactly to splash out on the perfect addition.

Transversely, going big and bringing the Köln sensation to the Westfalenstadion could bookmark a new signal of intent from BVB. For years, onlookers and even some fans have beaten the drum that Dortmund lacks ambition. Perhaps El Mala's potential arrival may help the club turn that corner.

This isn't to say that the 19-year-old will drag them to a first Meisterschale in 14 years, but rather set the tone for future campaigns. Hans Joachim Watzke often outlined the financial disparity between BVB and the superclubs. Maybe that self-fulfilling prophecy of settling for second place can be gradually banished.

Naturally, reckless spending is to be avoided at all costs, but perhaps an occasionally hefty plunge into the club's coffers could build some psychological confidence. Furthermore, securing El Mala would also lay down a marker to others interested in poaching Dortmund's targets down the line.

The on-field aspect is arguably even more important than the external side effects of securing or losing El Mala this summer. Despite finishing as runners-up last season, Niko Kovac's side encountered glaring difficulties in attack, often bailed out by defensive solidity and a stroke of fortune.

Dortmund, employing a transitional system under Kovac, were crying out for a player with the technical nous and dynamic ability of El Mala. Averaging one of the league's best rates for successful dribbles and touches in the opponents box per match, the 19-year-old could revolutionize BVB's attack.

El Mala is no slouch against the ball either. As is a prerequisite for any player in Kovac's system, diligence in defence is paramount. In this department, El Mala boasts an 85% duel success rate from last season. He also produces around 2 defensive contributions and 3 ball recoveries per game.

title: It would be a mistake: Trump warns FIFA over Infantino exit

fullText:
Donald Trump is making headlines in international football once again. The U.S. leader has posted a strong message on Truth Social to defend FIFA president Gianni Infantino amid rumors about his possible replacement at the head of the organization.

Thank you for your attention to this matter. President DJT", the message reads.

The former U.S. president praised the official's leadership, saying he has just overseen the most successful and profitable World Cup in history. According to his words, the financial figures achieved are four times higher than those of previous editions.

The American politician's message ends with a blunt warning to the leadership of world football. He maintains that, without Infantino in the position, FIFA will never again generate the same level of revenue or maintain the same degree of international impact.

This statement adds maximum pressure to the debate over the leadership of global football. The political figure's message reopens the institutional debate ahead of the governing body's upcoming Assemblies.

title: Skubal makes Dodger Stadium debut as Dodgers rally past Royals
description: LOS ANGELES — There are nights when a baseball team wins because everything clicks.
fullText:
LOS ANGELES — There are nights when a baseball team wins because everything clicks. Monday night at Dodger Stadium was not one of those nights.

The Dodgers beat the Royals, 6-5, in a game that asked them to withstand an uneven home debut from Tarik Skubal, a blown lead in the seventh and more late-inning tension than anyone wearing Dodger blue probably wanted.

And yet, when it was over, the Dodgers had exactly what they needed.

At 71-48, the Dodgers opened this seven-game homestand by doing something that has become increasingly important as the season moves toward its most consequential stretch: they found a way to win a game that didn't always look like it belonged to them.

"There's going to be no panic out of this clubhouse," Freddie Freeman said afterward.

That may have been the most important takeaway from the night.

Because there was plenty to panic about. Skubal's first start at Dodger Stadium was a grind from the beginning. The reigning ace didn't have his best command, his pitch count climbed early and, for only the fourth time in 18 starts this season, he failed to make it through the sixth inning.

He lasted five innings, allowing four hits and three earned runs while walking two and hitting another batter. He struck out six, throwing 95 pitches, 66 for strikes.

The most damaging pitch came with two strikes.

Skubal left an 0-2 slider over the plate, and Royals' Jac Caglianone didn't miss it.

The result was a two-run homer and a 3-0 Kansas City lead.

For all the anticipation surrounding Skubal's arrival in Los Angeles, this wasn't the kind of debut anyone would have scripted.

But perhaps the most encouraging part of his night was that he never let the outing unravel.

"I thought I competed well and gave our team a chance to win," Skubal said. "Our offense picked me up big time, defense picked me up big time, and the bullpen was outstanding tonight. All in all, a good team win, especially when I don't feel like I performed up to my standard."

Skubal has now made two starts as a Dodger, totaling 11 innings with 12 strikeouts. He has allowed five earned runs.

Neither start has been dominant.

And Skubal's introduction to Los Angeles has been about more than his numbers anyway.

He continues to rave about the organization and the clubhouse, saying he felt the support almost immediately after joining the team in Chicago. On Monday, he got his first real taste of the environment at Dodger Stadium.

"It felt like there were 40- 50 thousand fans 40 minutes before the game in their seats," Skubal said. "Is it Monday?"

The offense eventually showed up for him, too.

Down 3-0, the Dodgers began chipping away in the third inning.

Hunter Feduccia doubled to start the inning. Shohei Ohtani followed with an RBI double, and Freddie Freeman brought Ohtani home with another double to cut the deficit to one.

Then, in the sixth, the Dodgers finally delivered the kind of blow that changes a game.

Kyle Tucker walked to load the bases, bringing Max Muncy to the plate on his bobblehead night. Muncy made the moment count.

His bases-clearing hit, officially recorded as a double, put the Dodgers ahead 5-3.

Max clears the bases on his bobblehead night! pic.twitter.com/TvD1DXeKqc

For a moment, it looked as though the Dodgers had taken control. Then came the seventh. After Skubal and Alex Vesia exited with the Dodgers holding that two-run advantage, Jack Dreyer couldn't protect it.

The lead lasted three batters. Royals No. 9 hitter Kyle Isbel launched a two-run homer, tying the game at five.

Another Dodgers lead had disappeared.

But unlike some recent games, the Dodgers didn't let the frustration linger. They answered immediately. Ohtani singled. Then he stole second, his first stolen base in almost three months and only his seventh of the season.

And Freeman, who had already collected two hits, came through again.

His RBI single to right brought Ohtani home.

6-5 Dodgers. It would be the last run either team scored.

Freeman finished 3-for-4 with two RBIs, providing the kind of veteran presence the Dodgers have relied on so often during seasons when the margin for error gets smaller.

"It was nice," Freeman said. "50 thousand-plus on a Monday night, it felt like the fans were trying to will us to win tonight."

Because the ninth inning belonged to Edwin Díaz.

And for once, there was no drama.

Díaz needed only a 1-2-3 ninth inning to lock down the victory. He finished the job emphatically, pumping his fist as the Dodgers celebrated a win that had been anything but straightforward.

Dave Roberts saw something he wanted to see.

"I saw that urgency tonight, which we got to build on from here on out," Roberts said.

That urgency may ultimately matter more than Monday's victory. The Dodgers didn't dominate.

Skubal didn't have his best stuff. Dreyer surrendered the lead. The bullpen had to navigate some uncomfortable moments. The offense went quiet for stretches before coming alive late.

But the Dodgers scored four runs over their final three innings at the plate. They responded every time Kansas City put pressure on them. And when the game reached its final three outs, Díaz made sure there was no second comeback.

Baseball seasons are long enough that wins rarely come exactly how a team wants them to. The good teams learn to take them anyway. The Dodgers did that Monday.

It wasn't pretty. It didn't need to be.

At 71-48, with seven games at home and a long stretch of baseball still ahead, the Dodgers can build on a night like this.

As Freeman said, there will be no panic. Just another win to add to the pile.

title: Barcelona target Julian Alvarez loses patience and warns Atletico Madrid he will force the issue
description: According to Mundo Deportivo, Julian Alvarez has reached the end of his patience.The Argentine striker was left deeply frustrated after being unable to speak with Diego Simeone on Monday to ask the At...
fullText:
According to Mundo Deportivo, Julian Alvarez has reached the end of his patience.

The Argentine striker was left deeply frustrated after being unable to speak with Diego Simeone on Monday to ask the Atletico Madrid coach to help facilitate his departure, as he looks to join Barcelona.

Alvarez had expected to meet with Simeone, but the Atletico coach had left for Ibiza for two days. Miguel Angel Gil Marin, the club's CEO and another key figure in any potential transfer, was also away and unavailable.

The situation pushed Alvarez over the edge. According to the report, the striker told people around him at the training ground that they should no longer count on him and that he was prepared to take a firm stance to force the situation.

Alvarez is particularly unhappy with Simeone because he believes the coach should have been willing to confront the situation and speak with him directly.

Deeply annoyed. (Photo by Shaun Botterill/Getty Images)

The striker had made it known that he planned to meet with Simeone in an attempt to find a solution. He was therefore surprised to discover that the coach had travelled to Ibiza despite knowing that the Argentine was returning and wanted to talk.

The striker is also frustrated with Gil Marin, who could play an important role in resolving his situation but was likewise unavailable.

Alvarez had hoped to handle the matter through dialogue rather than confrontation. Instead, he feels that opportunity has been taken away from him.

The result was a dramatic escalation. Those around Alvarez at the training ground heard a clear message from the forward: "Don't count on me."

He also made it clear that he intends to stand his ground rather than simply accept the club's position.

Ready to stand firm. (Photo by Florencia Tan Jun/Getty Images)

The expectation is that Alvarez will put that stance into practice next Wednesday, when Simeone is scheduled to return to oversee Atlético's training session.

At that point, the Argentine believes the coach will have no reason to avoid the conversation.

Alvarez maintains that he has had a promise from Atletico since February that the club would allow him to leave this summer. That belief has become central to his current position.

With his patience now exhausted, the Argentine is prepared to push much harder for a move, with Barcelona remaining his preferred destination.

What began as an attempt to resolve the situation privately through conversations with Simeone and Gil Marin has now become a much more serious confrontation between Alvarez and Atletico.

And next Wednesday could be the moment when the standoff truly begins.

title: New York Knicks reporter expects Karl-Anthony Towns to sign $45 million contract extension
description: Despite not getting the $272 million supermax contract extension from the New York Knicks, Karl-Anthony Towns is likely to stay with the team. Towns was instrumental in helping the Knicks win their first NBA championship in 53 years, playing elite defense against Victor Wembanyama throughout the NBA Finals.
fullText:
Despite not getting the $272 million supermax contract extension from the New York Knicks, Karl-Anthony Towns is likely to stay with the team.

Towns was instrumental in helping the Knicks win their first NBA championship in 53 years, playing elite defense against Victor Wembanyama throughout the NBA Finals.

And even though the Knicks aren't going to sign him to a lucrative long-term extension, the former All-Star is still expected to stay in New York on a more team-friendly contract.

New York Knicks beat reporter Ian Begley spoke about the future of Karl-Anthony Towns, who is unlikely to get the $272 million contract extension from the Knicks.

He noted that Towns and the Knicks have reason to extend their partnership, with KAT likely getting a $45 million per year contract offer.

"If I had to take a guess, the two sides will reach an agreement. Towns clearly loves New York. Maybe he can make more money with another team next summer (Towns has a $57 million salary this season and his contract has a $61 million player option for 2027-28).

"But why would he leave? He won a timeless championship with his hometown team. Unless the Knicks make an insultingly low offer to Towns, I think they get something done here.

"If I'm using the recent Rudy Gobert extension as a baseline, I could see an extension for Towns starting around $45 million."

Begley added that Towns could make more money as a free agent, but with the current financial restraints placed on teams due to the NBA salary cap rules, staying with the Knicks on a team-friendly deal is a far safer option for him.

"By signing this kind of deal, Towns would obviously lose the opportunity to make more money as a 2027 free agent.

"Given all of the factors at play (the state of NBA economics, teams' approach to the second apron, the Knicks' title), there are reasons for Towns to play it safe and sign an extension.

"Towns leaving New York also would hurt the Knicks. If Towns and the team can't agree on a deal, New York would have to make a significant pivot to find another front-line center. So from the outside looking in, it seems like it makes sense for both sides to figure out a deal."

It's hard to see the Knicks letting Karl-Anthony Towns walk in free agency. Despite all the criticism they received for trading for Towns in 2024, he has rewarded their investment with a championship win.

On top of that, he has become a much better defender than he was earlier in his career, thus providing the Knicks with an elite two-way big who can stretch the floor, an archetype incredibly rare in the modern NBA.

The Knicks know that they can't keep their championship core together for much longer, but they should maximise their time together for as long as possible.

title: Donald Trump says ousting Gianni Infantino from Fifa presidency would be ‘terrible mistake’
description: The US president said world football’s governing body would ‘never be as successful or profitable again’ if Infantino leaves
fullText:
US president Donald Trump has warned Fifa would be making a "terrible mistake" if they get rid of Gianni Infantino as the head of world football's governing body.

Infantino has come under pressure following his doomed plan to sell off stakes in the men's World Cup to private investors.

But in a post on his Truth Social social media site early on Tuesday, Trump said removing the Fifa president would be a costly move.

The US president wrote: "Fifa would be making a terrible mistake if, for any reason, they even considered replacing President Gianni Infantino.

"He is fantastic, having just presided over the most successful World Cup, by four times, ever presented.

"If he is gone, it will never be as successful or profitable again!"

Trump was at the centre of another Infantino scandal in the summer after calling the Fifa president to request a "review" of USA striker Folarin Balogun's red card, which was subsequently "suspended", allowing him to play in their round of 16 tie with Belgium.

Uefa and two other confederations have held initial talks about organising competitions themselves amid the backlash against the embattled Infantino.

Europe's governing body, the Asian Football Confederation (AFC) and Concacaf, which ​oversees football in the ‌Caribbean, North and Central America, have accused Infantino of "deception" and while it is understood they want to give him the chance to resign and leave his position with dignity without seeking re-election in March next year, they want to insulate themselves from the unfolding crisis.

Uefa has previously threatened a boycott of Fifa competitions, which was reiterated even after Infantino's climbdown in an effort to oust him from power.

Infantino apologised for his proposal to create Fifa Forward Enterprise (FFE), a company to run the commercial and operational aspects of Fifa's tournaments, with an idea to sell off around 20 per cent to private investors.

But an open letter signed by the heads of Uefa, AFC and Concacaf has urged Fifa to hold an independent review into Infantino's scheme, while not naming the Swiss directly.

"Leadership in football is not a possession," the letter said. "It is not about holding – or demanding – power to be held. It is a duty of service to the football family that entrusts it.

"When trust is broken through deception, when an individual places himself above the collective that entrusted him with authority, that duty has been abandoned."

It comes after member associations began to officially withdraw their endorsement for Infantino's re-election in 2027, with England and Wales among that contingent.

title: 5 takeaways from Commanders' first unofficial depth chart
description: The Commanders released their first unofficial depth chart of 2026. Here are five thoughts on that depth chart.
fullText:
The preseason is here. Last week, we had the annual Pro Football Hall of Fame game, where the Carolina Panthers defeated the Arizona Cardinals. Now, it's time for the rest of the NFL to take the field for the first time after a long offseason. For the Washington Commanders, that means on Friday, when they host the Miami Dolphins in the preseason opener.

In the NFL, anytime there is a game, there is a depth chart. During the regular season, depth charts aren't a big deal. But for preseason Week 1, they are a big deal — to some. Washington head coach Dan Quinn said what most NFL teams feel about depth charts on Monday.

"I would say the unofficial depth chart is like as valuable as preseason rankings," Quinn said.

He's right, but the first depth chart is still interesting. And here are the five most interesting things we learned from the Commanders' first unofficial depth chart of 2026.

Someone brought up McCaffrey being WR3 to Quinn, which prompted the above quote. However, Quinn did elaborate on McCaffrey.

"What I can comment on is the intentional work by Luke in a number of areas," Quinn said. "He really kinda came on as a knack as a kick returner last year. So that kinda speaks to his competitive nature. He's improved releases off the line of scrimmage throughout techniques. And so, just seeing him with more time on task and like year three at the position, it's easy to see his ascension going up."

Is McCaffrey WR3? It's hard to know. McCaffrey had a good second week of training camp. He's also playing with more chippiness, which comes with confidence. Remember, he had only played wide receiver for two years before entering the 2024 NFL Draft. McCaffrey's biggest competition for the No. 3 spot is Treylon Burks and rookie Antonio Williams.

When the Commanders drafted Athan Kaliakmanis in the 2026 NFL Draft, many believed that would eventually end Hartman's time with the Commanders. Not so fast. Hartman and Kaliakmanis have each had some solid moments in training camp. For the most part, Kaliakmanis hasn't done enough to overtake Hartman. But he is a draft pick. The preseason will determine who the third quarterback is. It's quite possible that the Commanders keep only two quarterbacks on the 53-man roster, and slip one or two to the practice squad. We'd say Hartman and Kaliakmanis are running neck and neck for now.

This is where you can understand Quinn's point. This is not personal against Julian Good-Jones, but he's played two whole NFL snaps in his career. There is no way that Washington is strongly considering him as the starter this season, in such an important year for quarterback Jayden Daniels. That's not to say Good-Jones isn't going to be the primary backup, as he very well could be. But if healthy, Allegretti is the unquestioned starter. While the Commanders would prefer to see him return and get more time in with Daniels and his linemates, these snaps are a good thing for Good-Jones and rookie Matt Gulbin.

This is real. For now, Reaves and Quan Martin are listed as the co-No. 1 at free safety. Reaves has enjoyed a phenomenal offseason and training camp. Reaves just continues to prove to be a great story. He went from not making the initial 53-man roster in multiple seasons to being a core special-teamer to now becoming a potential starting safety. So, when you see Reaves atop the depth chart at safety, that is 100% real. Reaves has started games at safety before due to injuries. Now, he's on pace to begin the year as Washington's starting safety alongside Nick Cross.

If you were worried about how Frankie Luvu would adjust to this defense, you can put your worries aside. From all indications, Luvu is having an excellent season. He's on pace to wear the green dot this season, while rookie Sonny Styles and free-agent addition Leo Chenal share the other spot. This is more an indictment on Luvu than it is on Styles or Chenal. That's a good thing for Washington. Having Luvu return to the player he was two years ago could go a long way for the Commanders. Regardless, all three will play a lot of snaps this season.

title: The Hoddle of Coffee: Tottenham Hotspur News and Links for Tuesday, August 11
description: Oh Carlitos, where art thou? Men’s tennis is in the dog days of summer, and it’s missing its two biggest stars. Carlos Alcaraz and Jannik Sinner have both pulled out of the Canadian and Cincinnati opens – the two biggest lead-up tournaments to the US Open. For Sinner, the World No. 1 hasn’t played a […]
fullText:
Men's tennis is in the dog days of summer, and it's missing its two biggest stars.

Carlos Alcaraz and Jannik Sinner have both pulled out of the Canadian and Cincinnati opens – the two biggest lead-up tournaments to the US Open.

For Sinner, the World No. 1 hasn't played a tournament since lifting the trophy at Wimbledon on July 12. It's been an even longer wait for Carlos Alcaraz. The Spaniard and Australian Open champion has been sidelined with a wrist injury since April, missing both the French Open and Wimbledon.

We've seen plenty of tournaments to feature Sinner without Alcaraz. It isn't the same. The cool, mechanic Sinner is not compelling to watch without his freewheeling rival who prefers to hit the flair shot rather than the highest percentage possible (oftentimes to the crowd's delight). The tennis world needs its sun and moon.

Now, the two biggest men's stars on the planet are injured when the tennis calendar is supposed to be reaching its crescendo.

Instead, the men's tour is left with a wide-open field and substandard competition. The final eight of the Canadian Open consist of only one player inside the top eight: Ben Shelton. Alex Zverev lost in the early stages.

There has been some discourse about the length of these tournaments. Both Canada and Cincinnati are two-week events – which is quite a long time for a non-major (if you aren't Indian Wells or Miami). And to hold them in the tail end of the season is especially difficult. Novak Djokovic is also skipping them.

It makes for few compelling matches. Perhaps the only one that was interesting was Shelton taking on Brazilian upstard Joao Fonseca in the fourth round.

Otherwise, we're watching the meteoric rise of Rafael Jodar. The 19-year-old player from Madrid is in his first year as a pro, and he's making serious waves. He's already breached top 15 and through to the quarterfinals in Canada.

In a world where we're craving someone to challenge Sinner and Alcaraz, Jodar could be the guy. I've previously written it could be Fonseca too. It's still early days. The only thing that's for sure is we can't make any definitive statements until Sinner and Alcaraz return to the court.

title: La Liga defender back on Barcelona’s radar following Ronald Araujo exit
description: FC Barcelona are once again being linked with Natan, the 25-year-old centre-back currently at Real Betis.Indeed, according to TNT Sports Brasil (h/t Mundo Deportivo), the Catalan giants are considerin...
fullText:
FC Barcelona are once again being linked with Natan, the 25-year-old centre-back currently at Real Betis.

Indeed, according to TNT Sports Brasil (h/t Mundo Deportivo), the Catalan giants are considering the Brazilian as a possible replacement for Ronald Araujo, who has officially joined Liverpool on loan.

As per the report, Natan's name had already been discussed internally at Barcelona, but the situation has now evolved.

According to the information, the Blaugrana have opened talks with Real Betis over the possibility of negotiating a permanent transfer for the former Flamengo defender.

Barcelona like Natan. (Photo by Fran Santiago/Getty Images)

Natan had previously been offered to Barcelona by his agent, Andre Cury, following his strong performances in La Liga.

His profile is particularly interesting because he is a left-footed centre-back, a characteristic that the La Liga champions value when assessing options for the heart of the defence.

He also brings European experience and could provide Hansi Flick with another reliable option as the coach prepares his squad for the new season.

The departure of Araujo has created an opening in Barcelona's defensive planning.

As things stand, Pau Cubarsi and Gerard Martin appear to be the first-choice centre-backs for the Barça manager.

Will Barça make a move for the Real Betis man? (Photo by Fran Santiago/Getty Images)

Eric Garcia and Andreas Christensen are options to provide cover, while young prospect Alvaro Cortes could also gain prominence within the first team setup.

The club must now decide how much responsibility it wants to place on its younger defenders, such as Cubarsi and Cortes, while ensuring there is enough depth to cope with a long season.

That has brought Natan back into the conversation.

For now, however, Barcelona have other priorities ahead of strengthening the defence. The Catalans remain focused on finding a new No. 9, such as Julian Alvarez, and completing the signing of Manchester City and Spain superstar Rodri to reinforce the midfield.

Natan is therefore a name to watch rather than an imminent signing, but Araujo's departure has undoubtedly made the Real Betis defender a more relevant option for the La Liga champions than he was before.

title: Aryna Sabalenka’s ‘Tough Spot’ Involving Elena Rybakina Draws Steve Johnson’s Verdict After Toronto Exit
description: Aryna Sabalenka has not made the best start to her North American hardcourt swing, crashing out of the Canadian Open in the fourth round. Former American player Steve Johnson has shared his insight into what could be affecting the world No.
fullText:
Aryna Sabalenka has not made the best start to her North American hardcourt swing, crashing out of the Canadian Open in the fourth round. Former American player Steve Johnson has shared his insight into what could be affecting the world No. 1's performance on the court.

Following her fourth-round exit at Wimbledon, Sabalenka enjoyed a brief break before arriving at the WTA 1000 event in Toronto. She looked refreshed and in good touch as she kicked off her campaign by defeating Moyuka Uchijima and Zhang Shuai in straight sets.

However, Ekaterina Alexandrova presented a far tougher challenge in their fourth-round encounter. Although Sabalenka fought back strongly after losing the first set and even saved two match points in the decider, Alexandrova eventually claimed a 7-6 (3), 4-6, 6-4 victory.

Speaking on the "Nothing Major" podcast, Steve Johnson highlighted the world No. 1's impressive 24-1 winning record on hard courts in the first half of the 2026 season. He suggested that Sabalenka was expected to maintain that same level of dominance on the surface after relatively underwhelming results on clay and grass.

"Sabalanka, after Wimbledon, she was like, 'I'm going away from tennis.' She wants to go on vacation, get drunk, and kind of reset. And that was important for her because she was 24-1 on hard courts this year leading up to this, from obviously start of the year through Miami, she won the Sunshine double, final in Australia, won Brisbane," Johnson said.

"So, she has been absolutely dominant on the hardcourts and you felt like she was going to get back to that, but she played pretty good in her first match and then, you know, she ends up losing to Ekaterina Alexandrova in a tough three setter," he added.

However, Johnson feels that Sabalenka is in a "tough spot" as she attempts to rediscover her best level while dealing with the threat of Elena Rybakina, who is closing in on the world No. 1 ranking.

"I thought she did a good job battling back, but it just feels like she's anxious out there, right? She wants to win. She wants to get back to where she was. And that's a tough spot to be in because I feel like for Sabalenka, with how much kind of personality and fun she can have on the court, when she's having fun, I feel like she plays better," he said.

Rybakina, who is through to the quarterfinals in Toronto, would pull to within just four points of Sabalenka's top spot (8,670 to 8,666) if she clinches the Canadian Open title.

"And it just feels like right now she's gripping the racket a little tight. She could lose her No. 1 spot in the world coming up if Rybakina has a good week here in Montreal and in Cincinnati," Johnson added.

MORE: Aryna Sabalenka Defends Her Bold US Open Outfit Amid Criticism – 'You Cannot Impress Everyone'

Aryna Sabalenka will hope to deliver a stronger campaign at the Cincinnati Open, with her title defense at the US Open around the corner. The WTA 1000 event is set to begin on August 13.

title: ‘Angel Reese Hate Has To End,’ ‘Caitlin Clark Is Still Better’ — Dream Star’s Historic Performance vs. Tempo Divides WNBA World
description: Angel Reese’s latest performance added another milestone to what has already been a record-setting season for the Atlanta Dream star. The All-Star forward helped Atlanta secure a 107-95 win over the Toronto Tempo on Monday, finishing with 20 points and 14 rebounds.
fullText:
Angel Reese's latest performance added another milestone to what has already been a record-setting season for the Atlanta Dream star.

The All-Star forward helped Atlanta secure a 107-95 win over the Toronto Tempo on Monday, finishing with 20 points and 14 rebounds. The performance gave Reese a franchise-record 22 double-doubles this season, while her 71 career double-doubles moved her to No. 15 on the WNBA's all-time list, according to Real App, causing a buzz on social media.

Double-doubles have been one of Reese's biggest statistical trademarks since entering the WNBA. During her rookie campaign with the Chicago Sky in 2024, she recorded 26, a tally second only to Alyssa Thomas' 28 the previous season.

Reese now has a chance to move past Thomas. With 12 games remaining, the Dream star could add several more double-doubles before the end of the regular season and potentially climb even higher on the league's all-time leaderboard.

Her latest milestone, however, produced sharply varying reactions across the WNBA community on X.

"The Angel Reese hate really has to end. She's not just a good player. She's not just a great player. Angel Reese is Top 10 in the world. She deserves respect," ESPN's Sam Block wrote.

Block added, "This is what an elite hooper looks like."

"And Caitlin Clark is still better than her lol," an X user reacted.

"Setting franchise records she's goated fr," a Reese supporter gushed.

"They're two losses away from last year's record. She doesn't move the needle for any franchise," another X user commented.

"Angel Reese this season: 15.8 PPG (career-high), 11.9 RPG (leads WNBA), 2.3 STL + BLK. Deserves more DPOY love," Polymarket Hoops posted.

The pace of Reese's double-doubles is also staggering, drawing attention beyond the immediate franchise record. DraftKings provided additional historical context by comparing her production with the league's all-time leader.

"Tina Charles: 201 double-doubles in 473 career games. Angel Reese: 71 in just 95 games. At her current pace, Reese would have 354 double-doubles by career game 473. That's 153 MORE than the WNBA record."

The performance also marked a significant response from Reese after a difficult outing against the Washington Mystics on Friday. She scored 7 points on just 1-for-12 shooting in Atlanta's 79-74 loss.

Against Toronto, Reese returned to the statistical form that has defined much of her season.

SEE ALSO: 'It Was Funny for 4 or 5 Hours' — Right-Wing Pundit Slams Royce White for Taking Performative WNBA-Transgender Stunt 'Too Far'

The numbers continue to put Reese among the WNBA's all-time most productive rebounders and double-double threats, while the reactions surrounding her performances show how closely her success continues to be measured alongside Clark.

With 12 games still on Atlanta's schedule, Reese has more opportunities to add to the franchise record and push up her career totals.

title: One Day Cup positives for Glamorgan despite results
description: Glamorgan's One Day Cup coach David Harrison highlights the positives in developing young players despite winning only two from eight.
fullText:
Glamorgan coach David Harrison says individual players will benefit from their One Day Cup campaign despite winning only two of eight matches and finishing second from bottom in their group.

The club fielded four teenagers, including 17-year-olds Tom Edwards and Harry Wallace, and 19-year-olds Jack Hope-Bell and Romano Franco.

Three others aged 22 or under were among the 16 players used in the tournament.

"There have been so many positives in these past eight games even though we haven't got the wins we would have liked, there's so many things we've done really well," Harrison told BBC Sport Wales.

"For players getting exposure at first-team level at such a young age, like I did, like [director of cricket] Mark Wallace did, it'll accelerate their development."

Glamorgan snatch last-ball win against Worcestershire

Middlesex through as One-Day Cup nears tense finale

Hope-Bell, Edwards and Wallace made first team debuts, as did batter Callum Nicholls, 22, and Australian paceman Connor O'Riordan, whose bid to develop in Wales after missing out in New South Wales echoes the example of county stalwart Timm van der Gugten.

Wicket-keeper Alex Horton, 22, was the top run scorer.

Nicholls and Hope-Bell played major roles in the dramatic closing win over Worcestershire, with Pontarddulais product Edwards marking his potential by taking three wickets after being thrust into the squad because of injuries.

"Of the younger lads, Jack Hope-Bell has been impressive throughout the tournament and showed again [against Worcestershire] he's got a future here," said Harrison.

"Callum Nicholls has had a couple of scores and to get 70 in a chase was really good. There's a lot of experience for some of the younger players and it's shown we've got a bright future ahead."

Glamorgan are far from unique in blooding youngsters in the One Day Cup while some of their star names are away at the Hundred franchise tournament, but the perennial ambition to have a Welsh core to the team looks closer to fulfilment than has been the case since the noughties.

As well as those used, 18-year-old seam bowler Tom Norton - a breakout star of recent Championship games - missed the competition because of a back problem which will probably keep him out for the season, while batter Jacob Blades recently played for England under-19s at the age of 17.

"You've always got to plan for the future and this competition gave us that opportunity to develop a few of our players, playing against Ben Stokes for Durham is a great experience when they've watched him on TV playing for England."

Captain Andy Gorvin, the oldest player at 29 for several matches, was compared to a school-teacher in charge of the youngsters by one opposition commentator.

"My family did tell me about that! I try to help in whatever way I can and when it doesn't go right, it's how to keep the guys going," said Gorvin.

"The most important thing about sport is having the resilience to come back the next day. They've always tried to improve, it's a three-week block with eight games so you improve on the job and I've tried to guide as well as I can, and I've got to improve as well."

Glamorgan's coaching team, with Richard Dawson returning to head the operation after being linked with the England job, will have their work cut out to put together a seam bowling attack for the closing block of six Championship matches.

In addition to Norton's absence, Ned Leonard misses them all through injury, Jamie McIlroy is also currently out of action, and there is no announcement yet on an overseas bowler to replace Ryan Hadley - with Australians having domestic duties.

"I've had a couple of weeks off and I feel very fresh for me in August, but we're going to have to be knowing what we've got coming up," said opening bowler Timm van der Gugten, who was rested for the away games.

"Hopefully we can have a big push."

Glamorgan are in an unlikely fourth position in their first year back in the top flight for two decades, and could effectively ensure their status with good results against the bottom two, later in August.

"We're in a good position in Division One, there are a couple of really important games at the start at Leicester and against Hampshire, everyone's really looking forward to that," enthused Harrison, who reverts to an assistant's role.

"We've done the basics really well, and if we do the same stuff in the last six that we've done in the first eight, we'll give ourselves a good chance."

Glamorgan's season resumes in the four-day game away to Leicestershire on Thursday, 20 August.

title: Judge sides with Trump administration in Minnesota lawsuit over trans students
description: Minnesota District Chief Judge Eric Tostrud dismissed all but one of the state’s claims.
fullText:
A federal judge on Monday largely dismissed a Minnesota lawsuit that sought to challenge the Trump administration's interpretation of Title IX, the federal law that bars sex-based discrimination.

Minnesota is the only state challenging President Donald Trump's executive orders issued during his first year declaring there are only two sexes — male and female — and restricting transgender athletes from competing in women's sports.

The Trump administration has taken action to force school districts to end their trans-inclusive policies, including threatening to pull their federal education funding. Minnesota sued to stop the administration from pulling funds from schools in the state.

Minnesota District Chief Judge Eric Tostrud said in his ruling the state's case is ripe, meaning the legal issue is clear and ready for a court to make a decision on. But the state's argument failed in proving the administration violated the Administrative Procedure Act, which sets standards for how the federal government issues regulations, and the 10th Amendment, which reserves powers for the states.

The judge focused on the fact that there has not been a final action made by the administration on this issue and said its findings that the Minnesota education agency's trans-inclusive policies violate federal law and subsequent letters to the state do not count.

"Minnesota will not face legal consequences unless and until a hearing is held in which the relevant agency finds that Minnesota is not in compliance with Title IX, or a court finds, in a civil enforcement action, that Minnesota is not in compliance with Title IX," Tostrud wrote. "Neither event has occurred here. The Findings themselves impose no legal injury on Minnesota."

Additionally, Tostrud pointed to the Supreme Court's ruling this June to uphold state bans on trans athletes to support his argument.

He said that while the high court did not decide whether states and schools may allow trans athletes to compete in women's sports, "the Supreme Court's determination that 'sex' in Title IX refers to biological sex provides at least some support for the Defendant's interpretation of the statute."

The state had argued that the changes violate a Minnesota law that forbids discrimination based on gender identity. A separate state law also requires Minnesota schools to adopt and implement "a written policy to prevent and prohibit student bullying" based on "gender identity and expression."

While the case was tossed, another is still ongoing. The Trump administration is urging the Minnesota District Court to rule that the state's education department and the Minnesota State High School League violated Title IX because they allow transgender girls to play on sports teams and use locker rooms that align with their gender identity. The lawsuit stemmed from investigations from the Education Department and Health and Human Services Department.

Tostrud said the administration's arguments that Minnesota's case was not ripe were unconvincing largely because the Trump administration has also sued the Minnesota Department of Education and the state's high school sports authority over their transgender athlete policies.

"By filing that case, the United States affirmatively invoked the court's jurisdiction seeking resolution of essentially the same issues at the core of this case," Tostrud wrote. "It is difficult to understand how that case might be ripe, but this one is not."

Tostrud also agreed with Minnesota's spending clause argument that the executive orders, findings and letters impose conditions that are "unclear, are unrelated to Title IX's purpose, 'will induce recipients to violate the constitutional rights of students by discriminating against transgender individuals,' and are unlawfully coercive."

It was the main claim that was not dismissed by the judge since the state could lose roughly $2.9 billion in federal funding.

"It may be that Title IX does in fact prohibit transgender women and girls from participating on sports teams designated for women and girls or from using restrooms or locker rooms consistent with their gender identity," he wrote. "But that does not mean Minnesota had sufficiently clear notice that Title IX contained that prohibition when it decided to accept federal funding."

Minnesota Attorney General Keith Ellison said in a statement he was "pleased that a major constitutional claim against President Trump will move forward and I look forward to proving in court that the President violated the Constitution."

The Education Department did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

title: Former Air Force Secretary says he'll sue Trump administration to restore his security clearance
description: Former Air Force Secretary Frank Kendall on Monday said he'll sue to force the Trump administration to restore his security clearance, which it revoked Friday after claiming he had disclosed sensitive...
fullText:
Former Air Force Secretary Frank Kendall on Monday said he'll sue to force the Trump administration to restore his security clearance, which it revoked Friday after claiming he had disclosed sensitive information about the Qatari-gifted jet now serving as Air Force One.

Kendall, a West Point graduate who served as President Joe Biden's head of the Air Force, said on CNN Monday that he'll sue the administration, noting it has a history of retaliating against critics by stripping their clearances. "As my mother taught me years ago, you stand up to bullies," said Kendall, who has denied disclosing classified information.

Mark Zaid, a prominent national security attorney who sued the administration after his own clearance was revoked by the Trump administration, confirmed in a post on X that Kendall had hired him. "More to come,"" Zaid wrote.

Zaid specializes in helping a variety of military and civilian clients maintain security clearances in the face of investigations.

Last year he became a target of the Trump administration's efforts to strip security clearances from people they perceived to be enemies when he was named among 14 other people in an executive order signed by Trump. In a March 2025 executive order, Trump named former President Joe Biden and members of his family, Biden-era Deputy Attorney General Lisa Monaco, and New York state Attorney General Letitia James as being unsuitable to retain their clearances because it was "no longer in the national interest."

In August 2025, Trump revoked the security clearances of 37 more current and former national security officials, some of whom worked on matters that have long infuriated Trump, like the intelligence community assessment that Russia interfered in the 2016 presidential election on his behalf.

Trump has tried to squelch reports of problems with the jet that Qatar gifted him last year, which he intends to use as Air Force One for the remainder of his term. His Justice Department last month subpoenaed New York Times reporters who wrote about security concerns with the jet, which lacks the advanced anti-missile technology of its predecessor. After being criticized by a federal judge for sloppy legal work, the government grudgingly withdrew the subpoenas.

title: Jackie's care team shares 'difficult' update on beloved bald eagle
description: Jackie, the bald eagle followed by thousands online, remains critically ill and "currently unstable," according to the raptor center treating her.
fullText:
Jackie, the beloved bald eagle in Southern California, is "currently unstable" and remains "critically ill," the raptor center treating her said on Sunday, Aug. 9.

The Ojai Raptor Center said in a Facebook post that Jackie's packed cell volume fell below 6% on Aug. 8 but rose to 9% on Aug. 9. "The past 24 hours have been incredibly difficult," the center said, adding that her condition remains "extremely serious."

Jackie's health crisis, which first emerged after she was rescued following an "altercation" with two subadult eagles on July 17, has drawn concern from millions of fans. Extensive testing has ruled out several possible causes, including lead poisoning, cancer and metal objects such as fishing hooks.

The center has described the case as "complex."

"Her care and condition are being closely evaluated by a collaborative team that includes nine veterinarians, together with representatives from the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and the California Department of Fish and Wildlife," the center said.

An Aug. 7 post from the raptor center said that tests "provided important new information" but did not elaborate on what the bird's care team discovered.

The beloved bald eagle is known for appearing on Big Bear Valley's Big Bear Eagle Nest Cam, managed by Friends of Big Bear Valley (FOBBV). FOBBV shared the Aug. 9 health update on its Facebook page, writing, "Please allow others to take in this information and comment what they are feeling without judgement. Please be kind to each other in these emotional times."

Lookin' for love? Who is Jolene, the bald eagle in Jackie's territory

Jackie was rescued following the altercation from near Dana Point Park, where she was "found grounded and unable to fly."

"Initial bloodwork" had indicated the eagle "is experiencing severe anemia and inflammation affecting the kidneys," the center said on July 21. Vets had begun "supportive treatment based on the information available," with guidance from wildlife professionals globally.

Jackie received a "life-saving" blood transfusion from another eagle on July 20 and underwent oxygen therapy as part of her treatment. She also received treatment for rodenticide toxicity, which occurs when humans or non-target animals ingest rat or mouse poisons, though caregivers do not believe that is the primary cause of her illness.

The eagle has been at the raptor center for roughly three weeks. During that time, the center has faced harassment and warned against AI-driven misinformation about Jackie.

FOBBV said Jackie's ill health marks a "season of uncertainty" for the beloved eagle family.

"This season certainly has had its ups and downs, sad times and good times," FOBBV said Aug. 5.

Jackie's partner, Shadow, meanwhile, is on "his summer vacation," FOBBV said. "He has been and will likely continue to be seen on camera occasionally."

Millions of fans are worried about the power couple's fate after a new young female, believed to have attacked Jackie before her hospitalization, was seen perched with Shadow. Many on social media have nicknamed the new eagle "Jolene" after the Dolly Parton song.

But experts believe Shadow isn't likely to be ready to move on from his life with Jackie. The pair have been together for nearly a decade and have shared eight eaglets.

Contributing: Michelle Del Rey, Anthony Thompson, Amanda Lee Myers, and Julia Gomez, USA TODAY

This article originally appeared on USA TODAY: Jackie's care team shares 'difficult' update on beloved bald eagle

title: No evidence of data breach after Chinese-made component found in Navy drones, MoD says
description: The Royal Navy's new sea drones were found to include a Chinese-made component which sent communication to a Chinese IP address.
fullText:
The Ministry of Defence (MoD) said there is no evidence to suggest a systems or data breach after the Royal Navy's new sea drones were found to include a Chinese-made component.

During what the MoD called a "routine cyber vulnerability assessment" of the drones, the cameras were found to have sent a squark – also known as a heartbeat communication – to a Chinese IP address.

A squark can signal when the system is switched on, is functioning properly, but it can also carry location information.

"A thorough investigation found no evidence of MoD data or systems being accessed, compromised or transmitted externally," an MoD spokesperson said.

"Our assurance and testing processes are designed to identify and address potential vulnerabilities early, and we continue to undertake routine security activity across our systems and equipment," the MoD added.

This is embarrassing for the MoD which, like most Nato countries, has banned Chinese components from military equipment - not least over fears of spying.

The K3 Scout sea drones can remotely carry out surveillance, and according to their supplier, "support a wide range of mission profiles including maritime awareness, force protection, logistics and precision strike".

The supplier of the Royal Navy's 20 new K3 sea drones, Kraken, said it was given assurances about security. But a third party supplier of the drone camera still had Chinese-made components.

Kraken has said it is confident no sensitive information has been shared.

The story was first reported by The Telegraph.

The security lapse has been addressed, but it is a reminder of the heavy dominance on Chinese supply chains.

Even the defence sector – which has taken measures to prevent espionage – still struggles to source materials, and technologies that are China free, or as cheap.

title: Iran installs new war chiefs as Tehran signals ‘prolonged confrontation,’ expert warns
description: Iranian Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei named six military commanders as an expert says Tehran is preparing for prolonged confrontation, not settlement.
fullText:
Iranian Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei formally appointed six senior military commanders Monday, cementing a wartime reshuffle as Tehran rebuilds a command structure impacted by months of U.S. and Israeli strikes.

The appointments, announced by Khamenei's office and promoted on social media, fill posts across Iran's armed forces, the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) and the Basij paramilitary force, with a counterterrorism expert warning the timing and language of the decrees signal Tehran is preparing for "prolonged confrontation" and not a settlement with Washington.

"Strategically, the announcements made were issued in English, on X, while Iranian and Omani negotiators finalize the coordinates of a proposed shipping route through Hormuz, which is deliberate sequencing," Dr. Omar Mohammed, director of the Antisemitism Research Initiative at George Washington University's Program on Extremism, told Fox News Digital.

"Tehran is establishing its command structure as a fact on the ground before it signs anything."

Trump Says Iran Will Pay — What It Takes To End The War Remains Unclear

Mohammed also pointed to language in the appointment announcements blaming the deaths of predecessors on what Iran called the "Zionist-American enemy."

"That phrase, in formal state documents, codifies the United States as a co-belligerent," Mohammed said.

Khamenei appointed Ali Abdollahi as chief of staff of the armed forces and Kioumars Heydari as his deputy. He also formally named Ahmad Vahidi commander-in-chief of the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps, promoting him to the rank of major general.

Mostafa Izadi was named deputy IRGC commander, Ali Azmaei as commander of the IRGC Navy and Hossein Taeb as commander of the Basij.

Mohammed said Vahidi was also instructed to maintain readiness for "powerful offensive operations against the enemy," by the Supreme Leader, while Abdollahi was tasked with completing the integration of the General Staff into the Khatam al-Anbiya wartime joint command.

"States exiting a conflict dismantle their wartime command arrangements, but Iran is now institutionalizing its own," Mohammed said. "The decrees here describe a leadership planning for a prolonged confrontation, not a settlement."

Several of the newly appointed commanders have previously faced U.S. or European sanctions or allegations tied to terrorism and violent crackdowns.

Vahidi is the subject of an Interpol Red Notice requested by Argentina over his alleged involvement in the 1994 bombing of the AMIA Jewish community center in Buenos Aires, which killed 85 people.

Taeb, a former chief of the IRGC Intelligence Organization and former Basij commander, is on the U.S. Treasury Department's sanctions list.

The United States first designated him in 2010 over serious human rights abuses following Iran's disputed 2009 presidential election.

Heydari was also sanctioned by the United States in 2022 after the Treasury Department said he had publicly acknowledged his forces' involvement in the violent response to Iran's November 2019 protests, in which hundreds of protesters were killed.

The European Union has also sanctioned him.

Iran's Unseen Supreme Leader Becomes Weapon In Escalating Power Struggle, Experts Say

The reshuffle comes as Iran continues rebuilding its political and military leadership after a series of U.S. and Israeli strikes killed senior figures across the regime.

Ayatollah Ali Khamenei, who had served as supreme leader since 1989, was killed in a Feb. 28 strike at the start of the war. Mojtaba Khamenei, was selected as Iran's new supreme leader in March.

Ali Larijani, then secretary of Iran's Supreme National Security Council and a major figure in the country's security and foreign policy establishment, and Gholamreza Soleimani, commander of the Basij, were killed in strikes on March 17.

The latest appointments come amid continuing questions about Mojtaba Khamenei's health and public absence.

President Masoud Pezeshkian claimed Monday that he had held a nearly seven-hour meeting with Khamenei, only the second meeting the president has publicly disclosed since the new supreme leader took office, Iran International reported.

Khamenei has not appeared publicly since being selected in March and is believed to have been wounded in the Feb. 28 strike that killed his father.

Pezeshkian said the two discussed economic conditions, sanctions and other domestic challenges and that Khamenei emphasized the need for "unity and cohesion."

The military rebuild, however, has not extended fully into Iran's sensitive intelligence apparatus, according to Mohammed.

"The IRGC Intelligence Organization and its counterintelligence arm have no announced chiefs, and Iran has no permanent defense or intelligence ministers," the expert said.

"The appointments require assigning responsibility for the counterintelligence failures that enabled the February decapitation.

"Whoever wins that argument — the supreme leader's circle or the Guard's institutional leadership — is the actor actually in control."

Original article

title: Trump pivots back to sanctions for Iran as other strategies to end his war fizzle
description: President Donald Trump likes to say that he started his war with Iran after 50 years of economic pressure had failed to stop its nuclear weapons ambitions — but he’s now betting that another financial...
fullText:
WASHINGTON (AP) — President Donald Trump likes to say that he started his war with Iran after 50 years of economic pressure had failed to stop its nuclear weapons ambitions — but he's now betting that another financial squeeze can bring an end to that war.

The Trump administration is hoping that months of bombing have pushed Iran's economy to a breaking point that will force its leadership to cave to demands to end its nuclear program and fully reopen the Strait of Hormuz to oil and natural gas tankers.

The president on Monday said that since Iran is seeking compensation as part of any peace talks, he now intends to demand the same for the U.S. side. It's part of a larger pivot this weekend by Trump to argue that Iran is now on the cusp of financially collapsing, even though it has already endured decades of financial sanctions, which are often a longer-term strategy rather than an immediate tool of warfare that can halt a conflict.

The shift comes as U.S. stockpiles of key weapons have dwindled and as stop-start talks seem again to have stalled. But Trump insists the pressure can lead to a breakthrough.

"Yeah, they can make trouble, but they're broke," Trump told reporters. "They have no money. You know, Iran is broke, totally broke. And, they're not paying their soldiers. They have inflation of 300%."

Inflation is running high in Iran, although Trump's estimates were higher than what administration officials have been citing to reporters. But the prospect of a longer war also carries inflation risks for other nations, including the U.S. — where the war and higher gasoline prices are unpopular.

Crude oil prices climbed on Monday as investors interpreted Trump's comments as a sign that fewer ships would be traversing the Strait of Hormuz, continuing to limit global supplies of gasoline, jet fuel, natural gas and other forms of energy. The Iran war largely closed the waterway involved in shipping roughly 20% of global oil supplies before the conflict — and attempts to reopen the strait have been short-lived as it has become a source of leverage for the Iranians in negotiations.

Iran does not appear to be publicly intimidated by the prospect of more financial sanctions.

"Whenever Washington proves itself incapable of pursuing diplomacy, it retreats into sanctions; and whenever those sanctions fail to produce results, it simply increases the dose," said Esmaeil Baqaei, spokesman for Iran's Foreign Ministry, on social media. "The real risk is that American politicians, clinging to this bad habit, will instead strangle their own remaining chances of a less humiliating exit from a crisis of their own making."

The president didn't say what additional financial pressure would be applied, but the administration has since April 16 been engaged in what it calls " Operation Economic Fury " against Iran. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent called this component the "financial equivalent" of a bombing campaign as the countries that buy oil from Iran or bank with it could be sanctioned.

But one problem with this pivot is that the sanctions are unable to bite as quickly as the impact of the largely shuttered strait, said Richard Nephew, a senior research scholar at Columbia University who helped direct Iran sanctions strategy in the Obama administration.

Nephew stressed that the value of sanctions as a tool is limited because Trump has not articulated clear strategic goals for the war, at times stressing that it can't have a nuclear weapon, then emphasizing the strait and then talking about ballistic missiles. Instead, Trump has engaged in a massive series of aerial assaults and a level of destruction that has not produced the quick end that he initially promised.

"Economic pressure is a possible element in his strategy, but he's yet to explain the purpose," Nephew said. "Trump has systematically weakened his own hand through his inadequate use of force, inarticulate elucidation of an objective, and vacillation on negotiations."

Still, the sanctions and the ongoing U.S. naval blockade of Iranian ports give the U.S. economic and financial leverage, said Juan Zarate, a deputy national security adviser in the George W. Bush administration. Zarate said the U.S. sanctions threatening third-party countries doing business with Iran also have an impact. But these things take time, he noted.

"The ultimate question will be how far the United States is willing to go to constrict Iran's oil trade and threaten third countries with severe sanctions -- and whether it has the patience to test whether the economic pain will change the regime's behavior," Zarate said.

Trump's latest pivot to economic issues with Iran is something of a flip-flop. Trump has long derided past presidents who used sanctions to limit Iran's economic ability to pay for its military and nuclear development. In a speech last week in Las Vegas, he defended the bombing, missiles and drone attacks that began on Feb. 28 by indicating that the sanctions from previous administrations that date back to November 1979 had failed to succeed.

"It's been 47 years, but really, it's been 50 years because they've been saying 47 for three years, it's been 50 years," Trump said. "And no other president has done what you should have done a long time ago, because Iran cannot have a nuclear weapon, can't have it."

The Iranian economy has suffered gravely because of the war, with the International Monetary Fund estimating the overall economy shrinks by 5.4% and the Iranian government recently reporting an annual inflation rate of 88.6%. The U.S. Treasury Department said average loadings of Iranian oil have decreased from 1.8 million barrels per day before the war to less than 500,000 barrels per day over the past month.

The U.S. economy — the world's largest — has continued to grow, but inflation is elevated and borrowing costs have risen in ways that have hurt Trump's popularity and led to disapproval of the Iran war.

A senior U.S. official, insisting on anonymity to discuss strategy, said the U.S. military has set back Iran's ability to produce, sell and ship oil and other energy resources. The administration sees the naval blockade of the strait and sanctions as effective and views Trump as having additional options that can be cranked harder in the weeks and months ahead.

Trump is essentially arguing that U.S. voters are better able to tolerate any economic inconveniences than Iranians, who have been in a state of economic hardship for years.

"It's not just what the military can do — we've got the most powerful economy in the world as well," Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth said Monday in a joint appearance with Bessent. "And when you've got a motivated treasury secretary who can pull a lot of levers because he knows how to do it, you can put a lot of pressure on adversaries."

AP White House reporter Aamer Madhani contributed to this report.

title: RFK Jr. is targeting a decades-old loophole allowing chemicals in food supply
description: Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. on Monday unveiled a plan aimed at tightening a decades-old loophole that has allowed food companies to put certain chemicals in their products without first not...
fullText:
Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. on Monday unveiled a plan aimed at tightening a decades-old loophole that has allowed food companies to put certain chemicals in their products without first notifying the nation's food regulators, according to federal health officials.

The practice known as "generally recognized as safe" (GRAS) allows companies to self-certify the safety of certain food chemicals or substances. The Trump administration's new proposed rule would require food companies to notify the Food and Drug Administration when they make such determinations and include the basis for those conclusions.

"Shifting to a mandatory notification system closes a decades-old information gap," Kyle Diamantas, the acting FDA commissioner, told reporters Monday. He said the plan "improves transparency" while "respecting the limitations of our authority," adding that officials would work with Congress to further address the loophole.

Companies have not been mandated to tell the FDA when they include some chemicals or substances in their products for uses viewed generally as safe, though they can opt to do so. That means there are probably hundreds of such ingredients added to the food supply without strict government oversight. Chemicals that have been generally considered safe include those acting as preservatives in some breakfast cereals, emulsifiers in certain ice creams and salad dressings, and select low calorie sweeteners that are found in sugar-free desserts and candies. They can often be found in ultra-processed foods that make up more than half of Americans' diets and which studies have increasingly linked to health problems.

Overhauling the loophole has been part of Kennedy's food agenda as the nation's top health official as well as a priority for the Make America Healthy Again (MAHA) movement he champions.

Some food safety and nutrition experts said they welcomed the proposal, referring to it as a long-overdue change. Others said they feared the FDA does not have the resources to review the submissions from companies, potentially leading to substances continuing to flood the market without regulators having time to adequately review them.

Melanie Benesh, vice president for government affairs for the advocacy nonprofit Environmental Working Group, called the move the "first step toward meaningful reform."

"True GRAS reform requires more than mandatory notification," she said in a statement. "It must also include strong, science-based safety standards and thorough, independent FDA review before chemicals are allowed in our food. And it must address the thousands of substances already on the market that have not been meaningfully reviewed in decades."

In one of Kennedy's first food-related moves as secretary, he declared an intent for the FDA to "explore potential rulemaking" to tighten the GRAS loophole.

Since 1958, the FDA has been charged with evaluating the safety of new food additives. However, exceptions were made for substances generally deemed safe, such as vinegar, flour and standard spices.

While the specific rules have changed over time, companies are allowed to make their own determinations on whether certain substances are considered safe, which food safety advocates say has been expanded to a variety of ingredients over time, without informing the FDA. That has become the primary way the majority of substances are entering the nation's food supply, Diamantas said.

"Industry hijacked the loophole and drove a convoy of chemical trucks through it straight into the American food supply," Kennedy said at a Monday news conference.

There have been instances when additives included in food through the GRAS loophole had later raised safety concerns, such as tara flour used in a leek-and-lentil crumble that was associated with at least 130 people being sent to the hospital and sickening hundreds of others.

The FDA will review what each company submits within 45 days to ensure all that the relevant information is included. Within 180 days, the agency will review the submission more substantively, Diamantas said.

Under the proposal, companies won't be prohibited from adding the substances to their food while that process is ongoing, and there is no requirement that the FDA must formally approve or review the chemical, which Diamantas suggested would have required an act of Congress. Kennedy called on Congress to give the FDA more resources "to keep pace with the changing food supply."

For substances already in the food supply, the FDA is aiming to create a process for companies to submit information about how the chemical is used in food.

Some in the food industry prefer changes to be done through Congress, rather than through regulation. One person involved in the food industry, who spoke on the condition of anonymity to be candid, said the industry has been concerned that it would take time for the FDA to comb through companies' information on potential new substances, adding they believe changes should be done through legislation and come with more funding for the agency.

Americans for Ingredient Transparency, a coalition launched last year backed by the food industry and other lobbying groups, said in a statement that Congress should establish "a transparent, nationally uniform framework for food ingredient oversight."

David Kessler, a former FDA commissioner under both Republican and Democratic presidents, petitioned the FDA last year to revoke the GRAS status of some commonly used ingredients in ultra-processed foods.

Of the announcement Monday, Kessler said that "the proposed GRAS actions do not tackle the root causes of chronic disease in this country."

The White House's budget office finished reviewing the GRAS proposed regulation on July 31, an indication that a rule would be released for public comment soon. On CNN earlier this month, Kennedy said the proposal would come out "within probably a month," saying it had undergone an "extensive interagency process."

Federal officials have also been crafting a definition of "ultra-processed" foods, and as of last week, the White House budget office received for review a white paper on a proposed definition.

This comes as Kennedy, the founder of a prominent anti-vaccine group, has for months been publicly leaning into his work on food and nutrition ahead of the midterm elections and downplaying the push to overhaul vaccine policy. GOP pollsters have referred to vaccine skepticism as politically risky. However, White House officials are working to draft an executive order focused on the childhood vaccine schedule and autism amid President Donald Trump's push.

The MAHA movement was formed after an unlikely political alliance between Kennedy and Trump during the 2024 campaign. It has various factions that defy traditional partisan lines, such as those pushing for changes to the food supply, tighter regulations over pesticides and eliminating vaccine mandates.

title: Mamdani clashes with Democratic Socialists' push to abolish police and prisons
description: New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani defended police, prisons and jails on air, distancing his administration from the DSA's abolition platform.
fullText:
New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani defended police, prisons and jails during a Friday appearance on "The Clay Cane Show," putting distance between his administration and the Democratic Socialists of America (DSA) platform as political streamer Steven Bonnell, known online as "Destiny," told Fox News Digital that Mamdani would likely govern moderately while helping more radical candidates gain power.

Bonnell said Mamdani's control of a prominent and politically secure office could allow him to build support for other socialist lawmakers without implementing the DSA's most radical proposals himself.

"I think that Mamdani holds a very powerful, very safe office where he can be entrenched for a long time in order to 'hold the door open' for other, (arguably) more radical lawmakers in the future," he said.

Harris Reaches Out To Socialist Mayor Mamdani In Latest Sign She's Shoring Up Support For Possible 2028 Bid

Mamdani addressed his differences with the DSA after host Clay Cane noted that the organization's platform calls for abolishing institutions including prisons, the Senate and the presidency.

"I would say, especially when it comes to public safety, I've been very clear that we have our police force, we have prisons, we have jails [and] the purpose of these is also to ensure that we are delivering safety and justice hand in hand. And what that means is that New Yorkers need not choose between the two," Mamdani said.

He also credited the NYPD with driving down violent crime while emphasizing that public safety should not come at the expense of justice.

"I am proud of our police department for their work in delivering the lowest levels of murders and shootings and even the number of shooting victims in recorded history over seven months over this year," Mamdani said.

Mamdani Walks Back Plan To Increase Nypd Headcount Following Dsa Pressure

The NYPD reported 381 shooting incidents, 462 shooting victims and 149 murders during the first seven months of 2026, the lowest record totals for that period. Major crime declined 6.6% compared with the same period in 2025.

The position contrasted with the DSA's official platform, which describes defunding law enforcement and weakening police unions as steps toward eliminating police and prisons.

DSA co-chair Megan Romer defended the organization's approach to police and prisons during an interview with New Yorker editor David Remnick Monday on "The New Yorker Radio Hour." Romer rejected eliminating law enforcement, while defining defunding as redirecting department money into social programs.

"I am not in favor of getting rid of police entirely tomorrow," Romer said. "I think it means taking funding back and moving it elsewhere, right?"

"It's not communities with cops on every corner. It's communities that have good schools, good jobs, good park systems, good recreation for their teenagers, things like that," she added.

Dsa Co-chair Pushes Back On Soviet Union Comparisons, Wants Prisons To Be 'Less Necessary'

Bonnell predicted to Fox News Digital that the demands of running the nation's largest city would keep Mamdani from applying the DSA's policies, even as the mayor used his popularity to promote other socialists.

"As someone who has to actually govern, though, I don't see him applying any of the more radical DSA positions," he said. "Rather, he'll govern moderately, remain decently popular, market well, then use that position and popularity to promote others."

Republican New York City Councilwoman Vickie Paladino's office told Fox News Digital that Mamdani's remarks were intended to obscure an agenda that remained central to the DSA.

"Mamdani is politically savvy and understands that DSA messaging on police and prison abolition has been embarrassing and deeply problematic for Democrat candidates heading into the midterms," Paladino said. "As the top DSA figure in the country, he's trying to deploy some smokescreen on behalf of the party, nothing more."

"Make no mistake, abolishing police and prisons is now a baseline policy position for the DSA, regardless of what Mamdani is saying at the moment," she added.

Despite distancing his administration from that platform, Mamdani praised NYC-DSA during the interview for helping elect minority candidates.

"And I think to me, one thing I've appreciated about New York City DSA is that it has been one of the engines behind the creation of a new generation of Black and Brown leadership, the likes [of which] we haven't seen in quite some time," he said.

Fox News Digital reached out to Mamdani's office, the national DSA and NYC-DSA for comment on whether the mayor's position conflicts with the organization's platform, but did not immediately receive a response.
