Instead, something incredible happened. The majority of the committee members slowly began to convince themselves that Charlotte was the right choice. She had extensive work experience, had a history of teaching interdisciplinary courses, and had developed DEI programs at her current institution. This was all true. But it also did not change the fundamental fact that Charlotte was a remarkably low-wattage academic. The fact that we would entertain giving her a job seemed mostly due to her pigmentation and her enthusiasm for DEI bureaucracy.

The committee’s letter to the dean, who had final say over the decision, summarized the rationale for hiring Charlotte. It was a marvel of sugarcoating, describing her research as “primarily observational and centered on the distribution of species in different kinds of environments.” (In other words, she walked around and counted animals.) It confessed that “we were uncertain whether her research program would develop into something that used some of the most modern tools.” (Which is to say, we weren’t sure if she was capable of abandoning her 1970s methodologies and joining 21st-century science.) And it noted that we were not confident she had the “ability to help our students develop skills that would be most helpful for going into the increasingly digital and computational workplace.” (She might not be able to help our students develop the kinds of proficiencies that would make them employable.) Still, we made the case for giving Charlotte a tenure-track job at one of the most selective liberal-arts colleges in the country.

Thankfully, the dean saved us from ourselves. Although he was a primary cheerleader for DEI on campus—and although he was afflicted with a degree of racial neurosis that would have made Rachel Dolezal blush—the dean was also a biologist, and he must have known that Charlotte had no business at Bates. He voiced “significant concerns” about her research quality, questioned whether she could meet tenure standards, and said he was “very concerned” by the idea that we would knowingly hire someone who lacked the ability to prepare our students for this millennium’s job market.

In the end, Charlotte did not get the offer. But the entire episode left me distressed by what it seemed to suggest about the way many of my colleagues at Bates viewed scholars of color.

Did they really believe, however deeply in the recesses of their subconscious, that the only way to get “marginalized” faculty on campus was to lower academic standards to the subbasement? The idea made me irate, not only because it was racist, but because, selfishly, it made me look bad. Maybe I was not an academic rock star, but I thought I was doing quite respectably at Bates; by any reasonable metric, I was meeting, even exceeding, the college’s expectations for tenure-track faculty. I was placing articles in well-respected journals. An editor at one of the top university presses was interested in my book project. I’d received glowing internal reviews from members of my tenure committee.

I had spent my entire adult life at college, in grad school, and now working as a professor, and I had never before been self-conscious about being a beneficiary of affirmative action. I had always assumed that if I simply worked harder than the people around me—if I read more, went to more conferences, published more and in better venues—then nobody would question whether I deserved to be there. My experience on that search committee, though, disabused me of the notion that any of this mattered at Bates. The school’s culture encouraged us to see professors of color as vehicles for achieving the college’s diversity goals. The inescapable conclusion I arrived at was that I had been hired to be visibly Black first and a scholar second, if at all.

Even more upsetting, my experience on that committee changed how I viewed other newly hired minorities on campus. I sometimes found myself reflexively wondering whether Bates’s professors of color were up to the job, or whether they were underqualified fodder for the school’s social-engineering regime. I could not unlearn what I had discovered: that more than a few people at this elite little college seemed happy not just to move the goalposts for people like me, but to take them down entirely.

The dean, of course, happened to be familiar with Charlotte’s research areas. But if she had been a sociologist or a historian, would he have deferred to the expertise of the faculty on the committee? How many other Charlottes had already been hired at Bates? And how common was this kind of thing at other colleges around the country? It seemed highly unlikely that I had landed at the only school in America so hell-bent on getting minorities through the door that it would make a mockery of academic standards if need be.

I never stopped believing in affirmative action in principle, but I slowly stopped believing in it in practice. I’d understood the spirit of affirmative action to be about recognizing that people from historically underrepresented groups often face additional barriers, about affirming that talented minorities who may be less connected and superficially less refined can nonetheless rise to the occasion if given the opportunity. It seemed to me that the Bates administration’s push to diversify at all costs had led some of my colleagues on the faculty to internalize the opposite idea: that it is not especially important to find minority candidates who are capable of being held to traditional academic norms. Justice and anti-racism required a two-tiered system, a sort of woke Jim Crow, in which radically separate standards were applied to white and nonwhite candidates. In short, I came to see Bates College, self-styled beacon of progress, as an institution that was deeply, incorrigibly racist.

One of my friends, a Black software engineer, has a theory about navigating the 2020s job market as an African American. He jokes (but it is not really a joke) that there are “replaceable negroes” and “irreplaceable negroes.” The goal, he says, is to become an irreplaceable negro: someone who is unfireable because they are too good at their job, because they work for a company that doesn’t have a lot of Black people and can’t afford to lose any, or, ideally, both.

I was angry about the culture at Bates. I was sick of being treated like a racial prop rather than a professor, which included being continually recruited to do Minority Work I found silly or degrading. In addition to serving on the MLK committee, which I did for several years, I had been asked to be on multiple committees related to the college’s metastasizing diversity bureaucracy—work it seemed that my white faculty friends were rarely asked to do.

But more than this tokenizing, it was the disconnect between the college’s progressive patter and its labor practices that was pushing me toward a breaking point. Environmental studies had lost several non-tenure-track faculty members since I’d arrived, each a fantastic professor. Watching this happen as the administration continued to spend most of its time bleating about social justice left me considerably less patient when college leadership made its next cartoonishly progressive move.

Bates’s Academic Affairs Council was a small but powerful committee composed of the dean and four senior faculty members drawn from the humanities, social sciences, sciences, and interdisciplinary studies. In December 2022, the council circulated draft legislation for a version of the proposal that the Curricular Working Group had suggested back in 2021: the Race, Power, Privilege, and Colonialism requirement, or RPPC, as it came to be known. If the proposal passed a faculty vote, every major would be required to offer at least one course related to “race, power, privilege, colonialism, and their consequences.” Students would be required to take two such courses, one of these in their major. That the council was composed of five white people, with nary a professor of color among its ranks, added a degree of bleak hilarity to the whole affair.

I found it less funny, though, that the council was determined to have its way seemingly regardless of broader faculty sentiment, which early polling had shown was thoroughly skeptical of such a plan. At a March 2023 faculty meeting, the RPPC requirement was put up for debate and comment. I commented.

Standing at the mic in a cramped auditorium, I laid out my case against the requirement: It was a clear violation of academic freedom. The burden for teaching these new courses would probably default to minority faculty members, who would be further pigeonholed into race work that they may not want to do. And asking professors in the sciences to teach courses on race and colonialism would likely be a disaster. Most Bates science faculty lacked any expertise in these areas, nor did they have much experience discussing fraught social issues in the classroom. I argued that pushing them to act as bigotry experts not only was of dubious educational value, but would likely do more harm than good, especially to students of color who would be subject to their fumbling attempts at teaching racially sensitive topics.

I leaned on this last point especially hard. If my time at Bates had taught me anything, it was that the most reliable way to get progressive white academics to do what you wanted was to translate your concerns into the therapeutic language of racial harm. As if on cue, a professor on the council whom I will call Sandra hastened to assure me that she took potential trauma to minority students very seriously. She insisted that there would be ways to ensure that classroom dynamics did not become unpleasant for them; the key, she explained, would be to foster a “culture of repair.”

When I said that I had no idea what a culture of repair meant (really, I just wanted to see her try to substantiate her hollow jabber), Sandra gave a helpful example of what “repair” might look like in action. She suggested that perhaps there could be a system in which students of color could call out “oops” or “ouch” if somebody accidentally said something racist—as though these were not young adults with basic human dignity paying minor fortunes to be taught by ostensible subject-matter experts, but toddlers learning not to bite their friends when someone grabbed their toy truck. It took every last ounce of my already threadbare professionalism not to lean into the mic and say “Oops.”

I had long privately believed that the specter of student demand was being used as justification to pass legislation that only senior administrators and a few tenured radicals were excited to see put in place. A strange email I received a few days before the March 2023 faculty meeting appeared to confirm this. In it, a member of the student government not so subtly nudged me to support the requirement. When I wrote back explaining the various reasons I did not, she confessed that she and her peers had been asked by the council to encourage (read: guilt-trip) their professors to endorse it. I was disturbed that students were apparently being recruited for an influence campaign. The student told me, too, that she and her peers had been “blindsided” by the proposed requirement, but had been presented with an almost uniformly favorable faculty view of it.

I also got an email, after the meeting, from “oops, ouch” Sandra, who seemed quite anxious that a young Black professor with leftist politics objected to the committee’s vision. During our exchange, she noted that my views on academic freedom were also found among “faculty with libertarian leanings”—as though the mere fact that my opinion was shared by professors who were not liberal progressives was proof that the opinion was illegitimate. She added, “I do have some suspicion about white people using arguments like this to avoid addressing systemic racisms.” To me, it seemed obvious what she meant: Did I, a Black man, really want to be on the same side as people who didn’t want to Do the Work?

I told her that I saw Bates’s new scheme as simply the liberal mirror image of what was already happening in places like Florida, where the state government was policing curricula to advance a racist, homophobic agenda. “I’m not willing to support violating intellectual freedom in higher education just because it happens to be my team that’s doing it,” I wrote.

Sandra seemed stuck: Some minority professors supported the requirement, while others, like me, did not. In my observation, woke white academics—who are largely acculturated to defer to the “lived experience” of their Black and brown students and colleagues—had next to no ability to make decisions when confronted with minorities who disagreed with one another. Encountering “marginalized” people with opposing views tended to create a kind of cognitive paralysis in some of my white co-workers, and I noticed that, in such cases, they usually followed the recommendation of the most recent minority they’d spoken with about the issue. With my friends, I jokingly called this the “last Black person I talked to” problem.

But this problem was also an opportunity: If you could manage to be the last minority voice that a white professor or administrator heard before they made an important decision, they’d often just do what you told them to. With Sandra, apparently, it worked. My rebuttals to the RPPC started to land, and she asked if I could support a version of the proposal that would still force students to take two courses on racism without requiring every major on campus to furnish these courses.

I told her that I could. Although I still privately disliked what seemed to me a naked politicalization of our curriculum, my core objections had always centered on the faculty’s academic freedom, and the absurdity of making chemists teach courses on white supremacy. If the requirement could be fulfilled with classes that were already being taught, or voluntarily added, that compromise seemed worth making, especially if it meant that students would be less likely to be subjected to “Mathematics for Social Justice” slop. Sandra said she would suggest this modification at the next Academic Affairs Council meeting. Less than two weeks later, a new version of the legislation was distributed, now with the major requirement removed. The vote to pass or kill the legislation would take place at the April faculty meeting.

I thought, briefly, that my side had won. Yet a week later, a counterproposal came across the transom, this one buoyed by a small but vocal corner of the faculty that was especially militant about social justice. It restored the original demand that every major create required courses on racism.

I later learned that professors in the Africana program, one of the centers of performative radicalism at Bates, stood outside the meeting distributing flyers that announced they would effectively hold the curriculum captive if they didn’t get their way. They informed the rest of the faculty that they would not allow their classes to count for the requirement if the less aggressive version of the legislation passed. This would have made any implementation logistically challenging, leaving students to fight over spots in a smaller number of courses that could fulfill their obligations. In what seemed to be an even more cynical manipulation, a number of students—many of them minorities—were brought to the meeting by a white faculty member, apparently as visual aids; they audibly cheered for the counterproposal.

Perhaps some professors were uncomfortable striking down an anti-racism requirement in front of the students, or maybe they recognized that Africana’s threat had put everyone in a difficult spot. It’s possible, I suppose, that the light of truth and progress had simply warmed their frigid hearts. Whatever the reason, Bates’s faculty relented: The vote was 73 percent in favor of a measure that only a small minority had originally supported.

The vote and all that preceded it finally pushed me to speak up in a forum that was more public than a faculty meeting. It didn’t help my less-than-rosy outlook that, just a couple of weeks before the April faculty meeting, the union effort had officially failed. That June, I published an op-ed in The Boston Globe titled “I Am the Wrong Kind of Black Professor.”

Voicing the frustrations that I had long kept mostly private was cathartic. I was also about to begin a yearlong break from Bates, a combined research sabbatical and parental leave. I convinced myself that I could stick it out when I got back. I still adored my students, and loved sharing books and films I cared about with them. And even if my views frequently differed from those of my colleagues in environmental studies, they were kind and open-minded people.

The year that I was away, I tried to find humor, sometimes dark, in the glimpses of Bates madness that blipped on my radar: an email sent to the entire faculty to complain that a campus “Scholar Tea” event was appropriating “Black Queer Southern traditions.” A Martin Luther King Jr. Day meeting I attended where a white social scientist argued that putting a silhouette of a farmer on a poster was problematic—that year’s MLK theme was “Food Justice”—because farmers “default to whiteness” and “tractors reflect whiteness.” The Center for Inclusive Teaching and Learning hosting a “DeStress Fest” for faculty featuring a “Lunch & Play” (Play-Doh, LEGO, “other fun ‘toys’ ”), arts and crafts, and “a soft bunny in the next room to pet.” It was incredible to learn that I worked at an adult day care.

But nothing seemed as humorous after I came back to campus.

My leave had started just a few months after OpenAI’s breakthrough model of ChatGPT was released, leaving dazed professors and administrators flailing in their response to a technology that seemed poised to make the college essay obsolete. I assumed that by the time I came back in the fall of 2024, Bates would have a strategy for dealing with this existential threat to American higher education.

Yet upon my return, I found that, even as Bates faculty panicked about AI-enabled cheating, many of my colleagues seemed to have little collective will to do anything about it. Nor did the administration seem especially concerned that our students now had at their disposal a tool that could do their reading, writing, and thinking for them. I was distressed to find that safeguarding the basic tenets of liberal arts, or providing students with an experience that might still be recognizable as an education, seemed to be a low priority at Bates.

A search committee I joined that fall compounded my disillusionment. By this point, I had mostly lost the capacity to be scandalized by the administration’s questionable DEI policies, or by those policies’ deep tension with the college’s labor conditions. During this search, however, that tension became impossible to ignore. One of the many “diverse” candidates in our search pool was a non-tenure-track professor—I’ll call her Mia—who had been teaching at Bates for multiple semesters. Her research was exciting, her courses were compelling, and she was a hardworking and thoughtful colleague.

Further, it is routine for colleges to give tenure-track jobs to non-tenure-track faculty members: These “internal candidates” have the advantage of being a known quantity, and departments are often eager to do right by a co-worker who has been stuck in career limbo. The path to becoming a tenure-track professor can be grueling—the system asks people to spend the prime of their life moving from low-paying job to low-paying job, from one state to another to another, all in the hopes of one day getting a permanent position. Because many universities cap the number of courses that adjuncts can teach (to avoid having to comply with federal health-care mandates), many of them have to teach half a dozen or more per semester spread across different local colleges—a practice known as “freeway flying”—to cobble together a living. One in four non-tenure-track college educators relies on public assistance. One in three earns less than $25,000 a year.

Mia’s position at Bates was about to expire, and so I assumed that we would take the rare opportunity to hire her onto the tenure track. Once again, I watched a committee talk itself out of an obvious choice.

On a cold morning a few days into 2025, the group arrived at its final decision: We would not be hiring Mia, a result that made it likely that this would be her last semester at Bates, and perhaps her last semester as an academic. If Mia had been a mediocre teacher or scholar, that would be one thing. But the committee agreed that she was absolutely qualified. There just happened to be another “diverse” candidate who was judged to be a marginally better fit, and who did more to expand our curricular offerings. I had watched the college chew up and spit out enough non-tenure-track professors that Mia’s fate shouldn’t have come as a surprise, but it did.

I saw clearly now what should have been obvious all along. Bates was not a good place to work, nor a moral one. And the problem went beyond a single college: Bates was a node in a higher-education system that offered teenagers an uncertain future in exchange for often unpayable debt, and that asked scholars—enticed by the tweedy dream of a kind of faculty life that has long since been clubbed to death—to keep waiting for the real job that would surely come after the temporary job, and the next temporary job, and the next.

I had been spared all that. And I was on the cusp of getting the very thing I had wanted since I was a 21-year-old English major in my modernism professor’s wood-lined office, declaring that I would like to do her job one day. My senior colleagues in environmental studies talked about my tenure as if it were a foregone conclusion and openly discussed how I was next in line for program chair. The same January morning we decided not to hire Mia, Bates’s president announced that I was one of four professors—and the only non-tenured faculty member—whom my colleagues had voted onto the powerful Strategic Planning Steering Committee, a body composed of the president himself, various vice presidents, and a member of the board of trustees. I was on the inside track of an inside track, but it felt hollow.

Sitting in that last search-committee meeting, deliberating the fate of a person who, like me, had spent years chasing after a career that felt more like a calling, I was unexpectedly gripped by a granite certainty. I did not want to keep doing this. My academic Stockholm syndrome—You do not leave the tenure track—subsided in a rush. Five years after my adviser had likened me to the last dinosaur, I decided to walk my academic career into a tar pit rather than wait for the asteroid. I sat in my car after the deliberation about Mia ended and sent an email to a confidant explaining that I intended to leave Bates.

The story of elite higher education’s hiring and labor practices and the story of its decades-long creep toward progressive extremism are not separate or even contradictory. They are the same story. In 1969, a survey of 60,000 professors found that 27 percent identified as moderate, 28 percent as conservative, and 46 percent as liberal or left. Now, at some of this country’s top universities, only single-digit percentages of faculty identify as conservative. A 2025 survey of Harvard faculty placed that number at 9 percent.

How this happened is no mystery: The very system that was designed to protect the faculty’s right to free thought collapsed. By 1980, as many as two-thirds of American college professors were tenured. Today, only about a quarter are. We went from a world where most faculty members could say what they think without fear of being fired to one where most people teaching college courses have to worry that their contract won’t be renewed if they cause intellectual offense. It is not surprising that a professoriat disproportionately composed of contract workers would also be one that could be pressured into groupthink.

In a consultant-led meeting I attended near the end of my time at the college, one month into Donald Trump’s second term, the small group of professors and senior administrators present was asked to share what it saw as Bates’s greatest strengths and weaknesses. One of my colleagues said that the college’s greatest strength was its commitment to DEI. Another said that the college’s greatest weakness was that it could be even more committed to DEI. Someone lamented that our ties to the Wabanaki Nations could have been stronger.

As snow turned into slush, I walked by a flyer pasted to a campus building announcing the college’s annual sex week. The technicolor poster proclaimed that Bates would be hosting a game of “dildo ring toss” and would provide “exploration tables” replete with sex toys. Once, I might have seen in that poster a symptom of everything wrong with the college—money wasted on weird bullshit, organized by bureaucrats whose jobs nobody could explain. Now I found it all oddly refreshing. What was Bates if not a place devoted to risk-free ideological masturbation? For a week, at least, we could be honest about it.

Months later, I joined The Atlantic as a full-time staff writer. I was busy enjoying my first fall free from academia when I heard the news: At the November faculty meeting, Bates professors would vote on whether to suspend the Race, Power, Privilege, and Colonialism requirement, which was set to begin in 2026. Cooler minds at the college had evidently judged that, given the political climate, now was not exactly the best time for mandatory courses on the physics of white supremacy or the chemistry of colonialism; such a nakedly politicized curriculum, in fact, could make Bates a target of the current administration. The new legislation proposed that implementation of the requirement be paused until 2029—not coincidentally, after the next presidential election.

I thought I’d feel vindicated. I had argued all along that the RPPC was pointless, unworkable, mad. Now it was dead. Yet, unexpectedly, I was disappointed. Here was one last sign that it had all meant nothing. I recalled the dean’s faint embarrassment, years earlier, when I’d said that I was proud to join a school with an abolitionist past. Although the dead cannot speak, I must assume that embarrassment runs both ways.

Bates was founded in 1855 on the principle that a man is a man wherever he is found and whatever color his skin. In the decade that followed, the college furnished from its ranks 173 students willing to spill their blood for the cause of the Union and human liberation. One of these abolitionist-educated men was Holman S. Melcher, who left Bates to join the 20th Maine Regiment. A year later, at Gettysburg, he helped lead the bayonet charge down the hill at Little Round Top and into the maw of an advancing Confederate force.

Now this same college could not find the spine required to simply stand by a curricular change that its faculty and administrators had breathlessly, earnestly, performatively insisted was an imperative because it was nothing less than a matter of justice.

This article appears in the September 2026 print edition with the headline “Confessions of a Token Black Professor.”

title: Harry Potter fans force diverting UK-Ireland power link to avoid Dobby's grave
description: Potter fans complained after a project manager suggested cables would go under the grave in a BBC interview.
fullText:
Harry Potter fans succeeded in diverting a multimillion-pound power link between the UK and Ireland after they complained it would disturb a "memorial" to Dobby the House Elf.

The £430m Greenlink interconnector links the National Grid to Ireland via 125-mile cable between County Wexford and Freshwater West, a beach in Pembrokeshire where the death of fictional character Dobby was filmed in the Potter films.

Project manager Simon Ludlam told the Energy Revolution podcast the cable was originally "going to go straight through" the tribute, before fans left his firm "hundreds of calls".

"Actually we went quite close to some real Bronze Age remains, but we avoided Dobby's grave," he said.

Ludlam, founder of Etchea Energy, said a BBC News interview about the project had turned into a public relations nightmare after fans got wind of what was to happen.

He told the podcast that during the filmed interview he had pointed out where the cable would go underground, saying: "We did the shot, we finished I went back to London, and they then aired it a couple of weeks later.

"And we got hundreds of calls, I mean hundreds of calls."

A colleague told him the nature of the calls, and that "apparently, we're going to go straight through Dobby's grave".

"I said, 'Dobby, who's Dobby? I don't know Dobby?'

"I said, 'he's a fictitious character in a fictitious book, the whole thing is fictitious, what are you talking about?'

"[The colleague] said 'no it's very, very serious'."

Ludlam discussed with planners "exactly how to reroute the cable so we wouldn't go anywhere close to Dobby's grave".

He added: "A lot of people were very happy about that, and the project is now going [ahead] and Dobby's happy."

The Bronze Age remains the cable went close to were mentioned in Pembrokeshire council planning documents about the power link.

It said archaeological trenches dug near the route of the underground cable "contained the rim of an inverted pottery vessel whose fabric suggests a Bronze Age collared urn circa 1700-1500BC, typically associated with human burial".

The cable diversion is not the first time Dobby's grave has been saved.

In 2022 the National Trust agreed it could remain in place following a consultation, but urged visitors not to leave souvenirs.

Fans were asked not to leave socks on the mock grave, made of pebbles with messages written on them, because the beach was environmentally sensitive.

title: Road deaths in the US have fallen more slowly than in other rich countries
description: Most high-income countries have reduced road deaths substantially over the past decades. But the United States has made much less progress than other rich countries, and has even gone backward since the mid-2010s.
fullText:
Many cities across East Asia and Latin America have grown quickly over the last few decades. Since 1950, São Paulo’s population has grown sixfold. Shanghai’s nearly tenfold.

This rapid growth is now ending. São Paulo is near its population peak, and Shanghai is projected to peak around 2050.

The fastest-growing megacities are now emerging elsewhere. In the chart, you can see various examples: Karachi in South Asia, and Dar es Salaam, Addis Ababa, and Luanda in Africa.

Luanda, the capital of Angola, is an interesting case. It gets much less attention than well-established megacities, but as the chart shows, it's on track to overtake São Paulo in about 20 years and Shanghai in about 60.

In this dataset from the European Commission's Joint Research Centre, only 24 of today’s 100 largest cities are projected to still be growing by 2100; of those, 12 are in Africa, and 5 are in South Asia.

Of course, these rely on projections — often many decades ahead — and those come with a lot of uncertainty. Nonetheless, they provide a useful perspective on what the future of cities across the world might look like.

title: Using AI while exercising your critical thinking
description: It doesn't matter how capable a lab claims a latest model is, every single AI model suffers from the same problems of regularly jumping to conclusions, forgetting instructions, and hallucating information.
fullText:
The industry has been using the term AI Psychosis to describe a person who “blindly” believes everything that AI says, leading to scenarios where, if the person fails to realize the AI may be mistaken about a particular subject, they may develop strong beliefs in concepts that were based on either false assumptions or outright made-up information on behalf of the AI.

In software engineering, one common example that the industry has been observing is when someone opens a pull request with a very long AI-generated description of a problem and a very confident description of why the proposal in the PR is the correct solution for it, but one deep look is all it takes to realize that nothing in that description actually makes sense. The PR doesn’t really solve anything, at best it’s just moving the problem elsewhere. Every claim made by the description turns out to be false, making it just a big word salad that looks convincing at a glance but is complete nonsense when you take the time to analyze it.

This is a very real problem. But I think “psychosis” is a really bad way to describe it. Psychosis is a medical condition, and there’s nothing medical about this. It’s simply the consequence of trying to use AI without first understanding what AI “is” and how the tech that powers it works.

I personally think the term cognitive surrender (or the recently coined more casual equivalent meat proxy) is a much better way to describe it because it perfectly captures the problem: it’s not that people are getting “crazy”, but rather that they are failing to apply critical thinking to the AI’s responses, often simply due to a lack of understanding that the AI can (and will, constantly) make mistakes.

I’ve written posts in the past about how there’s no right or wrong in software engineering, but I think this topic is a valid exception as I cannot think of a single reason why acting as a “meat proxy” for the AI could be a good idea. If a person simply proxies what the AI says, are they really bringing any value to the table? Anyone can prompt AI nowadays, so there is no value in simply relaying its responses. If someone just bounces whatever the AI tells them, it would be easier for someone interacting with said person to just prompt the AI directly and skip the person entirely, wouldn’t it?

This means that what has value in this new way of working and sets you apart from other engineers is your ability to apply critical thinking to what comes out of the AI. It’s then critical that when you work AI, you need to be aware of the technology’s shortcomings and have strategies to manage each of them.

Given this context, here are my personal guidelines and advice on how to avoid this problem and use AI without losing grasp of your critical thinking skills:

It doesn't matter how capable a lab claims a latest model is, every single AI model suffers from the same problems of regularly jumping to conclusions, forgetting instructions, and hallucinating information. Newer models will not solve this, this is a flaw of LLMs as a technology and will continue to exist for as long as the underlying tech itself doesn't change. Any time you see a lab claim that they solved any of these problems is pure marketing. Remember when OpenAI said that GPT-2 was too dangerous to be released? The same model turned out to barely stay in line for more than a prompt!

This means that for complex prompts where you expect the AI to do a lot of research, you should always watch the AI as it does its thing and make it sure it's going the right way. If it starts to make weird assumptions, you should interrupt it and guide it back the right way. I find that letting the AI work on its own with zero oversight can work well for simple requests, but in my experience this rarely works for complex pieces of work. No matter how many details you provide it's pretty much guaranteed that it will make wrong assumptions at some point and start building the wrong thing.

If you want to develop a deeper understanding of why LLMs suffer from these problems, I find that there's nothing better than building one yourself. Andrej Karpathy (arguably the number 1 expert on the topic in the world) has several educational videos and tutorials on how LLMs work and how to build them, and they are all incredibly well written and easy to follow.

You should also have a habit of challenging and double-checking everything the AI produces. I originally did this by asking things such as "how do you know this?" or "give me proof", but nowadays I'm using a stop hook to do that automatically every time the AI claims to have found something. This nudges the AI to not jump to conclusions and actually perform research and provide proof. Note that using a system prompt will not work because one of the issues we're fighting here is that the AI tends to sometimes ignore instructions, so system prompts alone are not reliable in this case.

When the AI provides proof for a claim, endure the urge to blindly believe it. If it's a link for example, actually open the link and confirm that the information is there (and that it's not also AI-generated). This is because there will be many cases where the "proof" is also something the AI completely made up. This challenging process thus goes on until the proof is indisputable.

This issue is something that I do think newer models will improve, but I think it will always be good to do regardless to prevent you from losing your coding knowledge.

If you followed the previous two guidelines, you will end up with code that works. However, that doesn't mean the code is structured the best way it could. At least with today's models, the result will probably be massively overcomplicated, full of duplication, zero separation of concerns, wrong handling of edge cases, basically all the mistakes you'd do as a beginner.

I then think it's a good idea to go over the generated code for two reasons: 1) to make sure the code is structured correctly and handles the neccesary edge cases, and 2) to make sure you actually understand what has changed in the code. This second reason is particularly important because many have been feeling that they are losing their programming skills as a result of their AI usage, so I think that even though newer models might eliminate the code quality problem, going over the code may always be useful at least to prevent you from losing your skills and knowledge and retain your understanding of how the code works.

title: US court rules Meta, other tech companies must face thousands of lawsuits over social media addiction
description: A U.S. appeals court on Monday allowed thousands of lawsuits to move forward against Meta Platforms, Alphabet's Google, ByteDance's TikTok, and other social
fullText:
Aug 10 (Reuters) - A U.S. appeals court on Monday allowed thousands of lawsuits to move forward against Meta Platforms, Alphabet's Google, ByteDance's TikTok, and other social media companies over claims they designed their products to be addictive to ‌young users.

The San Francisco-based 9th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals rejected the companies' bid to reverse a lower court's ruling forcing them ‌to face more than 3,000 lawsuits over the claims filed in federal court, concluding that the appeal came too early in the litigation.

The defendants, which also include Snap Inc's Snapchat, ​had argued that Section 230 of the Communications Decency Act of 1996 -- which generally shields online companies from claims over content posted by their users - also bars lawsuits claiming they failed to warn the public about the addictive nature of their platforms.

Most appeals come after a case has concluded with a ruling or a verdict. Meta had argued that Section 230 provided it broad immunity and that it should be able to appeal the lower court's decision immediately. But ‌the 9th Circuit said Section 230 provides a ⁠defense to liability, not immunity from lawsuits, so the appeal was premature.

The court also denied Meta's bid to postpone a trial beginning Wednesday in a lawsuit brought by 29 state attorneys general alleging that the company illegally collected and ⁠used children's data, designed their social media platforms to keep young users hooked, and misled consumers about their safety. The company had argued that the trial couldn't go forward while the appeal had been outstanding.

A representative for Meta and a spokesperson for the lead attorneys in the appeal did not immediately respond to requests for ​comment.

Filed by states, municipalities, school districts and individuals, the lawsuits allege that social ​media companies intentionally addicted young users, contributing to surging depression, ‌anxiety and body-image issues and a broader mental health crisis among American youth in recent years.

Parents, school districts, states and other plaintiffs had argued that the trial court's ruling was not final and therefore could not be appealed. But they also objected to the companies' arguments about Section 230, saying it does not cover claims related to how they operate and design their products.

The cases, which have been centralized before U.S. District Judge Yvonne Gonzalez Rogers in Oakland, California, seek damages, penalties and restitution from the companies. The companies appealed Rogers' orders in 2023 and 2024 that largely allowed the ‌litigation to move forward.

The companies are facing hundreds of additional lawsuits over similar claims ​in state court, with approximately 3,300 of them in a consolidated proceeding in California ​state court.

In the first lawsuit to go to trial in the ​California litigation, and a closely watched test of how juries might respond to similar claims, a Los Angeles jury in ‌March found Meta and Google negligent for designing social media ​platforms that harm young people. The ​jury awarded $6 million to a now‑20‑year‑old woman who says she became addicted to Instagram and YouTube as a child.

And, Meta lost both phases of a landmark lawsuit brought by New Mexico in state court. A jury in March ordered it to pay $375 million after finding ​it had misled consumers about the safety of its ‌platforms. On Thursday, a judge found Meta had created a public nuisance and ordered it to pay an additional $567 million and ​implement youth-safety measures.

Both Meta and Google, which have denied the claims in those cases, said they would appeal.

title: Mark Zuckerberg says the future will have an ‘abundance of jobs’—and predicts a wave of new careers like world builders and personal biologists
description: Despite predictions of a job apocalypse, Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg sees a future of economic and financial prosperity.
fullText:
The rise of superintelligence—technology capable of surpassing human cognitive abilities—has fueled fears ranging from an elimination of human labor to more dystopian, Terminator-like visions of what happens when technology goes rogue. But now, Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg is pushing back against the predictions of a job apocalypse once made by his fellow tech CEOs, including Anthropic's Dario Amodei and OpenAI's Sam Altman.

"I do not understand why anyone who believes that AI will eliminate most jobs and much of humanity's relevance would rush to build that future," Zuckerberg wrote in an essay posted to Meta's website Monday.

"The notion that AI is so dangerous that the only safe path is an extreme concentration of power seems inherently problematic. Historically, hoping that an absolute power will benevolently provide for humanity if sufficiently enlightened has not led to safe or positive outcomes."

Zuckerberg, who is the world's sixth-richest person with a net worth of $211 billion, sees AI as a catalyst for an "abundance of jobs in the future," arguing that people will continue to invent new products and services—and the jobs needed to bring them to life.

He pointed to the fact that a generation ago, commonplace jobs like app developers, social media creators, electric vehicle technicians, and data center operators barely existed.

And moving forward, the 42-year-old expects a new set of careers to come into being, such as one-person-studio designers creating physical products, world builders devising virtual experiences, and personal biologists formulating individualized treatments.

Despite Zuckerberg's largely optimistic tone, he acknowledged that the transition could still come with growing pains. If automation outpaces workers' ability to develop new skills, job displacement could create a "difficult period" for society.

That disruption could be particularly painful without greater investment in training workers in career paths less vulnerable to automation, such as in the skilled trades.

"Unlike the concern about knowledge work displacement, there is a shortage of skilled tradespeople like carpenters, electricians, and construction workers to support the demand for infrastructure buildout," he said.

Earlier this year, Meta committed $115 million into building out America's Workforce Academy—a training program designed to prepare workers for data center technician roles. The five-week program provides training at no cost, and graduates are guaranteed a job at one of Meta's data center sites.

title: You Can (Maybe) Run Meta's Latest AI Model Locally on Your Computer
description: Muse Glimmer is designed to run locally—if your hardware can keep up.
fullText:
On Monday, Meta announced its latest AI model: Muse Glimmer. The company isn't necessarily advertising this model as its biggest and best, however. While Meta has plenty to say about Muse Glimmer's performance potential, there are two key selling points for the model in the company's eyes: The fact that it's open-weight, and that it's designed to run locally on "consumer" Macs and PCs—though perhaps not on your computer.

According ot Meta, Muse Glimmer is a 30-billion-parameter AI model optimized for "always-on local agent workflows." What that means is Glimmer is designed to run autonomously directly on your machine, rather than outsourcing that processing to the cloud. Local AI is much more secure than cloud-based, as your data stays within your system. When you tap into cloud servers, you're at the mercy of whichever company owns that network, potentially putting your data in jeopardy.

While there are many use cases for a model like Muse Glimmer, Meta is emphasizing its use for agentic AI. AI agents can perform tasks on your behalf and are growing in popularity, as users and developers can ask their agents to do any number of functions. Running agents locally is also quite popular, as evidenced by OpenClaw's infamous year, but the most demanding models also require powerful hardware. If you're working with a laptop, you might not have the energy necessary to run AI agents.

That's part of Meta's pitch here. The company says Muse Glimmer was trained to balance performance with limited hardware. Meta says it puts Muse Glimmer through three sets of training to achieve this: a "Pre-Training," which trained Muse Glimmer on Muse Spark's outputs; "Mid-Training," which trained the model on more "agent-heavy" data; and "Post-Training," which fine-tuned the model across a number of parameters. Meta says Muse Glimmer can handle end-to-end agentic task completion, multi-step reasoning, recovery when a tool call fails, and multi-model input and reasoning, among other functions. It is also trained on data from over 100 languages. The company says the model performs "strongly for its size class" against many standard LLM benchmarks.

While Muse Glimmer isn't as demanding as other models, it likely won't run well on the average laptop. Meta says that a 30-billion parameter model would typically require more than 55GB of memory, but through "quantization techniques," Muse Glimmer can use less than 20GB. When you take its "working memory" into consideration, Muse Glimmer will likely use 24GB or 32GB of memory. If you have a "Pro" MacBook or PC, that might suit you well. But if you're like me, your laptop has 16GB or less of RAM—not quite what Muse Glimmer requires. Still, it's a step forward for local AI use. (For reference, Meta says it tested Muse Glimmer on MacBook M4 Max, M5 Max, and with an RTX-5090 GPU.)

Meta says Muse Glimmer is "open," which means Meta released the model's training weights. As such, not only can anyone use the model, but they can tune it as well. If you have specific needs for your AI model, you can tinker with Muse Glimmer to better serve your usage.

There are a lot of AI models on the market these days, but Meta only has direct comparisons with two other models: Google's Gemma4-31b and Alibaba's Qwen3.6-27B. According to Meta's benchmarks, Muse Glimmer beats both models in the following 12 tests: MCP Atlas, DeepSearch QA, 𝜏³-banking, WildClawBench, GAIA2, SWE-Bench Pro, Sci Code, Charxiv Reasoning, IFBench, AIME 2026, AA-LCR, and Beam 128K. Gemma4-31b still has the crown in four of the benchmarks, while Qwen3.6-27B leads in eight.

Meta didn't provide similar comparisons with models from industry leaders, like OpenAI, DeepSeek, Z.ai, or Moonshot AI. However, Artificial Analysis has a ranking of all open-weight models on the market. As of this article, Muse Glimmer (high) is actually in 18th place. Moonshot AI's Kimi K3 (max) is in the lead, with Z.ai's GLM-5.2 (max) in second, DeepSeek's V4 Flash (max) in third, and Kimi K3 in (low) in fourth. For reference, Gemma4-31b is in 32nd, while Qwen3.6-27B is actually in 17th. There are many variables here, but this leaderboard gives us a quick glance at how Meta's latest model ranks amongst the competition.

You can try Muse Glimmer right now by downloading the weights from Hugging Face. Meta says the model will be available in the coming days from apps like Ollama, LM Studio, and Unsloth.

title: Harris becomes accidental SAVE Act ‘saleswoman’ as Trump attack spectacularly backfires
description: Kamala Harris posted a video criticizing the SAVE Act's voter ID requirements, but conservatives say she inadvertently made the case for the bill.
fullText:
Conservatives piled on former Vice President Kamala Harris after she warned Americans would have to "prove who you are" under the SAVE America Act, arguing her criticism inadvertently turned into a sales pitch for the Republican-backed bill.

"Incredible SAVE America Act saleswoman," wrote conservative commentator Eric Daughetry on X.

Harris posted a video on her X account Friday discussing midterm elections while highlighting the SAVE Act, including lamenting to voters that "you're going to have to have proof of who you are."

She added the bill will require "a passport, which a lot of Americans don't have, or a birth certificate. Same point, obstacles to make it difficult for you to register to vote."

Schumer Said 'Democrats Support Voter Id' — Then Every Senate Democrat Voted Against Gop Bill

Trump has made passage of the SAVE Act a top priority for his administration, pushing the stalled election legislation through a series of pressure tactics, including tying it to defense spending and threatening housing legislation.

The clip went viral among conservatives, with Trump even pinning the video to the top of his profile on Truth Social.

"The Jim Crow comparisons are tired. The poll tax is gone. Jim Crow is gone. Proving you're an American citizen before voting in an American election is not oppression. It's common sense," said Texas Rep. Wesley Hunt in response.

Watch: Elissa Slotkin Says Save America Act Would Make It 'Hard For Any Democrat' To Win An Election

"This is CRAZY- imagine a world where you have to prove who you are," said former White House press secretary Sean Spicer.

"She needs to hang it up," wrote Oversight Project vice president of litigation Jeff Clark.

"Kamala Harris complains that if the SAVE America Act passes, people will have to prove who they are in order to register to vote," wrote conservative commentator Benny Johnson.

"Wonder why Kamala Harris thinks this is a bad thing," posted Elon Musk's political action committee America.

"Kamala Harris on the SAVE Act: it would require Americans to 'prove who you are' to vote. Trump reposted her clip himself," said Fox News anchor Sean Hannity.

Republican Says Trump's Top Election Priority 'Dead' In Senate As Gop Fractures Ahead Of Midterms

Trump has warned about the need for voter ID laws for years, including from the 2016 campaign trail.

With Congress out of session and the midterms approaching, Trump is continuing to push lawmakers to prioritize passage of the SAVE Act, keeping pressure on Republicans to act when they return to Washington.

Democratic lawmakers have argued the SAVE Act would create unnecessary barriers for eligible voters, most notably potentially disenfranchising them.

Fourteen states and Washington, D.C., do not require most voters to present identification when voting in person.

title: Trump wins permission to file amended complaint in $10B defamation lawsuit against BBC
description: President Donald Trump won permission to amend his $10 billion defamation lawsuit against the BBC over its edited "Panorama" documentary about Jan. 6.
fullText:
President Donald Trump notched a legal victory on Monday when a district judge granted his Leave to File First Amended Complaint in Trump v. British Broadcasting Corporation (BBC), allowing the president's legal team to amend his complaint against the global broadcaster.

Trump filed a lawsuit against the BBC in December in a personal capacity for both defamation and for a violation of Florida's Deceptive and Unfair Trade Practices Act for $5 billion apiece, seeking $10 billion total. Trump was seeking permission to modify his original lawsuit, but the BBC insisted he missed the deadline and was playing tactical legal games to avoid financial disclosures.

United States District Judge Roy K. Altman sided with Trump, granting him permission to file an amended complaint and wiping out the BBC's previous motion to dismiss as "moot."

Judge Limits Bbc From Relitigating Jan 6 In Trump Lawsuit Over Misleading Documentary Edit

"Today's strong and thoughtful ruling is a major win for President Trump's powerhouse lawsuit against the formerly respected and now disgraced BBC, which defamed President Trump by intentionally, maliciously and deceptively doctoring his speech in a brazen attempt to interfere in the 2024 Presidential Election. President Trump is holding the leftist BBC, along with all of its comrades in the mainstream media, accountable for their peddling of Fake News through deception and maliciously defamatory conduct," a spokesman for Trump's legal team told Fox News Digital.

The BBC did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

The BBC has faced scrutiny over the 2024 "Panorama" documentary about Trump's speech on Jan. 6, as the documentary — titled "Trump: A Second Chance?" — stitched together remarks Trump made nearly an hour apart during his address that made it appear as if he had told his supporters to "fight like hell" at the Capitol, shortly before the riot there that day.

The issue surrounding the documentary's editing integrity comes after a report from The Telegraph revealed excerpts from a whistleblower dossier compiled by Michael Prescott, a communications advisor hired by the BBC to review its editorial standards.

Trump, Bbc Agree On Mediator For $10 Billion Lawsuit Over Jan 6 Documentary Editing Controversy

The whistleblower alleged the network's documentary spliced two separate comments made by Trump nearly an hour apart on the day of the Capitol riot, which erroneously implied that the president was calling for violence from his supporters.

"We're going to walk down to the Capitol. And I'll be there with you. And we fight — we fight like hell," the documentary showed Trump saying, without noting that the statement had been edited.

In reality, Trump said, "We're going to walk down to the Capitol. And we're going to cheer on our brave senators and congressmen and women, and we're probably not going to be cheering so much for some of them, because you'll never take back our country with weakness. You have to show strength, and you have to be strong."

Legal Analyst Predicts Trump Could Win 'Considerable' Damages From Bbc Documentary Lawsuit

Trump called on his supporters 54 minutes later to "fight like hell" for election integrity. The controversy ultimately led to the resignations of BBC CEO Deborah Turness and Director-General Tim Davie last year.

Trump must file the new version of the complaint by Monday. He is expected to focus on personal reputational harm and is still seeking $10 billion in damages. The BBC will have the opportunity to file a new motion to dismiss targeting the revised allegations.

Fox News Digital's David Rutz contributed to this report.

title: Captain charged after boat capsizes near Statue of Liberty, killing mother and infant daughter
description: A woman and her baby died after a boat carrying 14 people capsized near the Statue of Liberty on Saturday night, authorities said — triggering a multiagency search for the victims in the busy waters o...
fullText:
A woman and her baby died after a boat carrying 14 people capsized near the Statue of Liberty on Saturday night, authorities said — triggering a multiagency search for the victims in the busy waters of New York Harbor.

The captain of the boat, Manuel Hernandez, 46, of Manhattan, was arrested early Sunday and charged with 13 counts of reckless endangerment, the New York Police Department said.

The US Coast Guard is investigating what caused the boat to capsize and whether the vessel was operating illegally as an uncredentialed charter, the agency said. The investigation is being conducted with the Coast Guard Investigative Service and the NYPD.

An illegal charter is a passenger-for-hire operation that lacks required Coast Guard credentials, safety equipment and a certificate of inspection, according to the Coast Guard.

"We are committed to holding illegal operators accountable to (the) highest extent of the law to ensure the safety of everyone on our waterways," said Capt. Doreen McCarthy, the Coast Guard's Sector New York commander.

It's not clear what type of boat the passengers were on, but a law enforcement source briefed on the investigation told CNN investigators believe the boat was likely over capacity.

Twelve of the 14 people on the boat had been pulled from the water before police arrived, the NYPD said. Eleven of them were saved by the captain and crew of the first boat to arrive on scene, a hot tub boat – a small vessel outfitted with two full-size hot tubs that takes passengers on tours around New York Harbor, according to Adam Schwartz, the owner of the tour company, Sea the City.

After authorities arrived, search-and-rescue teams located Sara Sanchez, 27, and her 5-month-old daughter, Antonella Garcia, both of Queens, in the water, police said. Both were taken to NYU Langone Hospital-Brooklyn in critical condition, where they were later pronounced dead, police said. The baby's father was also on the boat and is among the survivors, a law enforcement official briefed on the investigation told CNN Sunday.

The remaining survivors are in stable condition, the US Coast Guard said.

Police said they received a 911 call at about 10:25 p.m. Saturday reporting an overturned vessel near Liberty Island, home to the Statue of Liberty. The boat was in the Hudson River near Buoy 32, between the Statue of Liberty and Bay Ridge Anchorage, police said.

The capsizing triggered a large emergency response in the dark waters near Liberty Island, located south of Manhattan, between New Jersey and Brooklyn. The response involved air and water rescue teams from three agencies – the Coast Guard, the city's fire department and the NYPD. The NYPD's Harbor Unit, SCUBA Team and Aviation Unit – all part of the department's specialized operations teams that help handle search-and-rescue missions – responded to the scene.

The area around Liberty Island is a high-traffic part of New York Harbor, used by commercial and recreational vessels. The island is one of New York's top tourist destinations, with various charter companies and boat tour operators offering trips to view the Statue of Liberty from up close.

Temperatures Saturday night were about 80 degrees Fahrenheit under clear skies, with light westerly winds of around 10 mph, according to the National Weather Service.

"I saw three helicopters, two active boats on the water, and just a lot of NYU (Langone hospital) ambulances, cops, firefighters, trucks," witness Madeleine Montero told FreedomNewsTV.

CNN affiliate WABC reported the capsized boat was a 22-foot bowrider, a common type of recreational powerboat. CNN has reached out to authorities 

In July 2022, a boat chartered by a group of family and friends capsized in the Hudson River off Midtown Manhattan, killing 7-year-old Julian Vasquez and 47-year-old Lindelia Vasquez. The boat's owner and captain later pleaded guilty to a federal charge of misconduct and neglect of a ship officer resulting in death; prosecutors said he had run paying tours without the required Coast Guard credentials.

This story has been updated with additional information.

title: FAA to pause flights at Washington airport to support Freedom 250 Grand Prix
description: The U.S. Federal Aviation Administration said on Monday it expects to temporarily pause flight operations at Washington's Reagan National Airport from 10:15 a.m.
fullText:
Aug 10 (Reuters) - The U.S. Federal Aviation Administration said on Monday ‌it expects to temporarily pause ‌flight operations at Washington's Reagan National Airport from 10:15 ​a.m. (1415 GMT) to 1:15 p.m. on August 23 to support the Freedom 250 Grand Prix IndyCar race.

The IndyCar race will roar ‌through the streets ⁠of Washington August 22 to 23 to celebrate the 250th birthday ⁠of the U.S. General admission tickets are free, though spectators can pay to be ​part of ​the "Champions Club" and ​have an "exclusive race weekend ‌experience," according to the event website. The cost is $5,000 per person for a two-day package.

The FAA has closed the airspace above Washington's Reagan National Airport a few ‌times in recent months ​for anniversary celebrations. The FAA ​closed the ​airport on July 4 to ‌accommodate Independence Day events ​in the ​nation's capital, forcing the cancellation of hundreds of flights. The airport suspended operations ​on June ‌14 for U.S. President Donald Trump's ​Army anniversary parade.

title: Rahmanullah helps Afghanistan see off improved Ireland
description: Rahmanullah Gurbaz's 71 helps Afghanistan to victory over Ireland at Stormont to take a 2-0 lead in the five-match one-day international series.
fullText:
Ireland 206 all out (46.3 overs): Carmichael 32 (52); Ghazanfar 3-29, Rashid 3-44

Afghanistan 207-7 (44.5 overs): Rahmanullah 71 (77); Hoey 4-34

Afghanistan win by three wickets

Rahmanullah Gurbaz's 71 helped Afghanistan to victory over Ireland at Stormont to take a 2-0 lead in the five-game one-day international series.

After the first match fell victim to the weather, the visitors powered to victory in the second game of the series on Friday and while Ireland produced much better this time, Afghanistan extended their ODI winning streak between the nations to eight.

Gavin Hoey took four wickets for the hosts whose tally of 206 with the bat fell one run short of Friday's total, but was not enough for Gary Wilson's side as three wickets apiece from Rashid Khan and AM Ghazanfar helped set a manageable target for Afghanistan.

The visitors won the toss and put Ireland into bat.

Once again, Rashid proved a thorn in Ireland's side with ball in hand, taking the wickets of captain Cade Carmichael, Harry Tector and Mark Adair with just 44 runs coughed up.

Ghazanfar would surpass Rashid with his three wickets coming at the cost of just 29 runs, but it was Fazalhaq Farooqi who made the first breakthrough with Andrew Balbirnie removed for just seven runs which immediately put the hosts on the back foot.

When Stirling [23] and Carmichael [32] fell to Yamin Ahmadzai and Rashid respectively, it was already looking ominous for the hosts with Ghazanfar then stepping up to take Lorcan Tucker and Curtis Campher in quick succession.

Tector and Adair were next to go thanks for Rashid, but Ireland managed to show some resistance with Ben Calitz chipping in with 20 before Gavin Hoey [36] and Jai Moondra [31] proved a fruitful partnership, finding the boundary seven times between them, but would ultimately fall before the end of the innings.

Afghanistan wasted little time in making inroads with Rahmanullah building his tally, although they would lose Ibrahim Zadran for 12 with Byron McDonagh taking the wicket.

Sediq Atal was next to go with 27 off 25, balls, while Adair struck early against visitors' captain Rahmat Shah.

While Hashmatullah Shahidi chipped in with 22 before becoming Hoey's second victim, Rahmanullah continued to lead the way for the visitors with five sixes and two fours before Hoey removed him and then Darwish for 13.

Ireland had a glimmer of hope when Adair removed Azmatullah Omarzai, but Rashid's 37 helped the visitors home before the sides meet again at Stormont on Wednesday.

title: West Ham sign winger Solomon from Tottenham
description: West Ham United sign winger Manor Solomon from Tottenham on a three-year contract.
fullText:
West Ham have completed the signing of winger Manor Solomon from Tottenham on a three-year contract.

The Championship club did not disclose the fee, but the Hammers are understood to have paid about £5m to make the Israel international their third permanent signing of the summer.

Solomon, 27, made 19 appearances for Italian side Fiorentina on loan last season.

He also spent time on loan at Leeds United and Spanish club Villarreal after joining Spurs in 2023.

"I know West Ham have a rich history both in the Premier League and in Europe," said Solomon, who will wear the number 10 shirt for the side gearing up for their first season outside the top flight since 2011-12.

West Ham comeback sees off Portsmouth in cup

London Stadium seeks concerts to cut £19m losses

"It's a club that won a European trophy just three years ago, and I think this is where the club should be, and I'm here to help the club and to be where it belongs.

"Of course, our first task is to get promoted, to go back to the Premier League."

Capped 49 times by Israel, Solomon won three titles during his time in Ukraine with Shakhtar Donetsk before a loan move to Fulham, and also helped Leeds win the Championship in 2024-25.

He follows Venezuela midfielder Keiber Lamadrid and former Netherlands defender Joel Veltman in joining the club this summer.

West Ham have sold winger Crysencio Summerville to Al-Hilal and midfielder Mateus Fernandes to Tottenham, among others, after their relegation.
